    Journey stage

    Stage

    Description.

    Get noticed at all

    • Salience, the option or detail that visually or emotionally stands out gets weighted far past its actual importance.
    • Illusory Truth Effect, hearing a claim repeated makes it feel truer, whether or not it's been verified.

    Get trusted before anyone's verified anything

    • Framing Effect, the same fact, worded two ways, changes how it feels before the facts are weighed.
    • Order Effect, and whichever fact arrives first sets the frame the rest gets read through.
    • Social Proof, seeing others already interested makes it feel safer to pay attention.
    • Social Norm, and whether that interest looks common or rare changes how much it matters.
    • Halo Effect, and one strong, visible impression gets extended, unverified, to everything else about the same source.
    1. Salience, the thing that visually or emotionally stands out gets noticed first.
    2. Illusory Truth Effect, repeated exposure makes a claim start to feel true.
    3. Framing Effect, how that claim is worded shapes the feeling before the facts are checked.
    4. Order Effect, and whichever fact arrives first sets the frame the rest gets read through.
    5. Social Proof, seeing others already interested makes it feel safer to pay attention.
    6. Social Norm, and whether that interest looks common or rare changes how much it matters.
    7. Halo Effect, and one strong impression, once formed, gets extended unverified to everything else about the same source.

    How the option set itself is built

    • Decoy Effect, a deliberately worse option makes a specific other one look better.
    • Compromise Effect, a middle option absorbs indecision, whether or not it's objectively best.
    • Similarity Effect, a near-duplicate option splits attention and share with an existing one.
    • Not Enough Choice, removing an option can make people want it more, and trust the chooser less.
    • Choice Overload, past a point, more options make choosing itself the hard part.

    How the comparison gets shaped once it's in front of them

    • Anchoring, the first number seen becomes the reference point everything after is judged against.
    • Salience, the option that visually stands out gets weighted past its actual merits.
    • Ordering Effects, the same options, in a different order, get chosen differently.
    • Order Effect, and the same information, in a different order, changes the judgement of any one option.
    • Signpost Effect, and the same fact, expressed in different terms, can wake up a value that changes which option looks right.
    • Tradeoff Transparency, showing what's being given up, not just gained, changes the decision.
    • Mental Accounting, and which mental "budget" the cost gets charged against changes how it feels.

    How people actually simplify the decision

    • Social Proof, what other people picked leaks into the decision.
    • Take-the-Best Heuristic, one good cue can out-predict weighing everything.
    • Chunking, breaking a long option set into smaller groups makes it easier to hold in mind.
    • Choice Bracketing, deciding once for a whole set produces different choices than deciding one at a time.

    How much effort stands between them and the choice

    • Good Friction, a few extra seconds, placed on purpose, can be the only thing that stops an impulsive pick from locking in.
    1. Choice Overload / Not Enough Choice, first, how many options even exist shapes everything that follows.
    2. Similarity Effect, near-duplicate options split attention.
    3. Decoy Effect, a deliberately worse option can make a specific other one look better.
    4. Compromise Effect, a middle option starts absorbing the indecision.
    5. Anchoring, whatever's compared first sets the scale for everything after.
    6. Salience, the option that visually stands out gets weighted past its actual merits.
    7. Ordering Effects, position in the list starts doing some of the choosing.
    8. Order Effect, and the order any one option's own details arrive in shapes how it's judged.
    9. Signpost Effect, and the same fact, expressed in different terms, can wake up a value that changes which option looks right.
    10. Tradeoff Transparency, what's being given up becomes visible, or stays hidden.
    11. Mental Accounting, and which mental "budget" the cost gets charged against changes how it feels.
    12. Social Proof, what other people picked leaks into the decision.
    13. Take-the-Best Heuristic, under time pressure, most people lean on one good cue instead of weighing everything.
    14. Chunking, breaking the option set into smaller groups makes the whole thing easier to hold in mind.
    15. Choice Bracketing, deciding once for a whole set, versus one at a time, changes the answer.
    16. Good Friction, and a few extra seconds, placed on purpose right here, can be the only thing that stops an impulsive pick from locking in.

    Make the price feel smaller

    • Zero Price Effect, demand jumps disproportionately the moment a price hits $0.
    • Left Digit Bias, $2.99 gets processed as "two dollars something," not $2.99.
    • Pain of Paying, the more directly you feel the act of paying, the less you enjoy what you bought.
    • Mental Accounting, and which mental "account" the spend comes out of changes how much that pain registers.
    • The Precision Effect, a precise number and a round one trigger different reactions, and not always in the direction you'd guess.
    • Translating Information, the same total cost feels smaller split into "per day" terms.

    Shape the comparison right before the decision

    • Anchoring, the first number seen sets the scale the final price gets judged against.
    • Decoy Effect, a deliberately weaker option makes the intended one look like the obvious pick.
    • Compromise Effect, a middle tier absorbs the indecision.
    • Framing Effect, how the offer is worded shifts the feeling before the number is parsed.
    • Endowment Effect, and if a trial or a cart already feels half-owned, giving it up starts to feel like a loss.
    • Loss Aversion, the general asymmetry behind that: giving something up is felt more sharply than gaining the identical thing.

    Build trust at the moment of paying

    • Price Transparency, the full, all-in price upfront changes what people choose, not just how they feel.
    • Tradeoff Transparency, whether what's given up was ever made visible.
    • Perceived Fairness, and whether a price change reads as protecting a real cost, or exploiting the moment, decides how it lands.
    • Zero Price Paradox, sometimes free converts worse than a small positive price, because it invites scrutiny.
    • Operational Transparency, visible effort behind the product adds to what it feels worth.
    • Reciprocity, and an unsolicited gift right before the ask creates a felt obligation to say yes.
    • Halo Effect, and one great channel or product can raise trust in every other channel the same brand touches, whether or not those other channels changed at all.

    Remove the need to decide at all

    • Default Effect, whatever's pre-selected gets chosen at a dramatically higher rate.
    • Smart Defaults, and timing a default against a future gain instead of a felt loss makes it work with someone's biases instead of against them.
    • Good Friction, and collapsing several small decisions into one pre-filled “yes” raises follow-through on the ones people already meant to make.

    Create urgency to act now

    • Scarcity, a countdown or a “only 2 left” label makes the decision feel time-limited, whether or not supply actually is.

    2. Decoy Effect, a deliberately weaker option makes the intended one look like the obvious pick.

    4. Framing Effect, how the offer is worded shifts the feeling before the number is parsed.
    5. Scarcity, and a countdown or an “only 2 left” label makes the decision itself feel time-limited, whether or not supply actually is.
    6. Left Digit Bias, then the sticker price itself gets read, digit by digit, from the left.

    What keeps them engaged

    • Goal Gradient Effect, effort and motivation increase the closer you get to a goal.
    • Pseudo-Set Framing, a group of steps framed as one thing to complete pulls people to finish it, even when the grouping is arbitrary.
    • Medium Maximisation, a points or stamps system can start mattering more than the reward it stands for.
    • Emergency Reserves, a pre-approved allowance for slipping up keeps a broken streak from becoming a cancelled account.
    • Smart Defaults, committing today to a future raise that hasn't arrived yet keeps a good habit escalating on its own.
    • Precommitment Devices, and setting a costly, binding deadline for yourself today makes a future lapse expensive enough to actually avoid.
    • Behavioural Labels, being called "a member," not "someone who uses this," reinforces the identity that keeps them coming back.
    • IKEA Effect, and having customised or set the thing up themselves makes it harder to walk away from.
    • Symbolic Rewards, and a purely honorific badge, worth nothing, keeps people contributing anyway.

    What the experience is remembered as

    • Peak-End Rule, the relationship gets remembered by its worst or best moment, and how it ended, not the average.
    • Operational Transparency, visible ongoing effort keeps the value feeling earned, not assumed.
    • Social Norm, seeing what similar people are still doing reinforces, or undermines, that identity.
    • Shooting the Messenger, and how badly a piece of bad news lands depends on how, not just what, it's delivered.
    • Reciprocity, and an unconditional gesture along the way builds goodwill that outlasts any one transaction.

    What makes them leave, or stay

    • Sludge, friction deliberately added to a cancellation flow turns a quiet decision to leave into a fight.
    • Default Effect, whatever's pre-selected at renewal decides more outcomes than persuasion does.
    • Price Transparency, a bill with no surprises rarely triggers a cancellation on its own.
    • Pain of Paying, but a payment that feels worse than expected chips away at renewal intent regardless.
    • Endowment Effect, and simply having owned it this long makes giving it up feel like a loss, not just a lapsed habit.
    • Ostrich Effect, while not checking usage or billing at all keeps a bad-fit subscription alive by default.

    01

    Anchoring

    Why does the first number on the page set what a fair price feels like afterward?

    Whichever figure arrives first becomes the yardstick. Later numbers get judged against it, even when that first figure was arbitrary.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA first number anchors judgment, and adjusting away from it stops too early

    The psychology. Kahneman and Tversky named this anchoring-and-adjustment. People rarely build an estimate from a blank slate. They begin at the anchor, move away from it, then stop once the adjusted figure feels plausible, often well before it is accurate.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Kahneman and Tversky named this anchoring-and-adjustment. People rarely build an estimate from a blank slate. They begin at the anchor, move away from it, then stop once the adjusted figure feels plausible, often well before it is accurate.

    Where it causes errors

    A struck-through “was” price lifts the reference, so the sale figure looks like a bargain. An aggressive opening offer rewrites what both sides treat as reasonable. Even a number everyone knows is meaningless, like a rigged wheel spin, still pulls the estimate.

    Where it can help

    A carefully set first offer puts the negotiation on ground that shapes both sides' next moves. Offering a realistic reference figure before someone decides can stop them from overshooting or undershooting for lack of any starting point.

    Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases." Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131
    The foundational paper: anchoring is one of three heuristics it identifies, alongside representativeness and availability.
    StrengthA wheel of fortune, visibly set to stop on either 10 or 65, came first. Only then did people estimate what share of UN members are African countries. Randomness was on full display, so the starting number could not count as useful information.
    WeaknessSample sizes were small and unrepresentative, in line with 1970s lab psychology. The task was also a single numeric estimate. Extending the finding to decisions such as pricing had to wait for later replications.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“the median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations were 25 and 45 for groups that received 10 and 65, respectively, as starting points. Payoffs for accuracy did not reduce the anchoring effect.”
    ParaphrasedThe paper frames anchoring as a general-purpose heuristic underlying everyday probability judgment, not a quirk specific to one task.
    See also: Behavioural Economics vs. Behavioural Science vs. Psychology vs. UX, on why this particular finding kept its original name across psychology, economics, and product design, when most don't.
    Run this one live: Live Sessions: Anchoring, the same paradigm and the same two anchors (10 and 65), run with a real room instead of a 1974 lab.
    02

    Sludge (Obstruction)

    Why does cancelling take five clicks when signing up took one?

    Friction placed in the way on purpose, against the person's interest: a cancel path that inserts a retention pitch instead of letting them leave.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe effort of a hard step is felt right now; the benefit it unlocks feels distant and abstract

    The psychology. Present bias and effort aversion do the work. The cost of fighting through the friction lands now and feels concrete. The payoff, money saved or an unwanted service ended, sits later and stays abstract. People drop the effortful path far more often than they still want the outcome.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Present bias and effort aversion do the work. The cost of fighting through the friction lands now and feels concrete. The payoff, money saved or an unwanted service ended, sits later and stays abstract. People drop the effortful path far more often than they still want the outcome.

    Where it causes errors

    Subscriptions keep getting paid after someone has already decided to leave. Leaving simply costs more perceived effort than staying. That is design friction overriding intent, not a reconsideration.

    Where it can help

    The inverse is sludge removal: strip friction from actions that help people, such as auto-enrolling employees into retirement savings or offering a one-click opt-out. The FTC's Click-to-Cancel rule is built on that inverse. Cancellation has to be no harder than sign-up.

    Mathur, A., et al. (2019). "Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites." Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
    The largest systematic study of dark patterns to date, sludge is one of several categories it documents.
    StrengthThe authors crawled 53,180 product pages on 11,286 shopping sites by machine. The taxonomy that came out of that sweep is still cited in FTC enforcement work. No hand-picked case study reaches that scale.
    WeaknessA crawler misses friction that appears only deep in a multi-step path, such as a cancellation that requires a phone call. Prevalence figures are therefore likely too low.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Analyzing ~53K product pages from ~11K shopping websites, we discover 1,818 dark pattern instances, together representing 15 types and 7 broader categories.”
    Verbatim“We identified 22 third-party entities that provide shopping websites with the ability to create and implement dark patterns on their sites.”
    Verbatim“Obstruction makes it easy for users to sign up for recurring subscriptions and memberships, but it makes it hard for them to subsequently cancel the subscriptions.”
    ParaphrasedThe paper documents this specific pattern, which it calls Hard to Cancel, on 31 of the ~11,000 shopping websites it crawled.
    Also worth citing: FTC v. Amazon (2025): $2.5B settlement over a Prime cancellation flow requiring 4 pages, 6 clicks, and 15 options.
    See also: Good Friction, the same mechanism, pointed the other way: friction added against your interest here, in your interest there. Which one you're looking at depends entirely on who it protects.
    03

    Zero Price Effect

    Why does free feel like a different universe from one cent?

    Free sits in its own decision category, not merely at the bottom of a price scale. Demand jumps out of proportion the moment the price hits $0 .

    ›
    Likely mechanismZero treated as a categorically different price, not just a low one

    The psychology. Textbook price theory treats cost as a smooth scale. A one-cent gap ought to feel similar wherever it sits. People treat free as a separate category instead. At $0 there is no downside to weigh, so the exchange registers as pure gain.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Textbook price theory treats cost as a smooth scale. A one-cent gap ought to feel similar wherever it sits. People treat free as a separate category instead. At $0 there is no downside to weigh, so the exchange registers as pure gain.

    Where it causes errors

    People take a free but weaker option over a cheap better one. They do it even when the cent gap matches a gap elsewhere that barely moves preference at all.

    Where it can help

    A genuinely useful free tier or sample lets people try real value at no risk. That only holds when the free offer is not bait for later obstruction (see Sludge) or a hollowed-out product.

    Shampanier, K., Mazar, N., & Ariely, D. (2007). "Zero as a Special Price: The True Value of Free Products." Marketing Science, 26(6), 742–757
    The paper that gives this principle its name: the ordinary vs. luxury chocolate study.
    Experiment Teardown
    398 participants
    Only the Hershey's price moved, to zero
    Cost condition
    1¢ Hershey's, 15¢ Lindt
    Picked one, or neither
    Free condition
    0¢ Hershey's, 14¢ Lindt
    Picked one, or neither
    Result Cost Free Swing
    Hershey's 14% → 42% +28
    Lindt 36% → 19% −17

    Only the zero moved. The 14¢ gap between the two chocolates was identical in both conditions, yet making the Hershey's free flipped which one people picked.

    Internal validityThe paper itself notes that conditions rotated in fixed time blocks instead of being randomised person by person. Percentages come from a live chocolate booth in MIT's student center (n=398). A second field replication at an MIT cafeteria, with different price points, used n=232.
    External validityThe goods were small, low-stakes candy. Whether the same swing size appears at higher prices has not been shown.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedChoosing between a 1¢ Hershey's Kiss and a 15¢ Lindt truffle, participants picked the Lindt over the Hershey's by more than two to one (36% vs. 14%). Dropping both prices by exactly one cent, making the Hershey's free, reversed the pattern: the now-free Hershey's was chosen more than twice as often as the Lindt (42% vs. 19%), even though the 14-cent gap between them never changed.
    Verbatim (abstract)“After documenting this basic effect, we propose and test several psychological antecedents of the effect, including social norms, mapping difficulty, and affect. Affect emerges as the most likely account for the effect.”
    Also worth citing: Pantry Story, a bakery and café at 336 Parramatta Road, replaces the usual request for a jug of water with a self-serve Purezza tap built into the counter, sparkling and still, poured free into a paper cup with no barista to ask. It's a real, uncontrolled example rather than a study, but the same zero-price pull shows up: a water station that costs nothing and requires no request gets used far more freely than the identical water would if it carried even a token price or a wait for staff.
    See also: Zero Price Paradox, free doesn't always win. When people suspect a hidden catch (shipping, data, lock-in), zero pricing can backfire instead.
    See also: Reciprocity, related but distinct: this is demand jumping at a $0 price point, regardless of who's giving it or how personal it feels; that's the felt obligation triggered specifically by an unsolicited personal gift. A free sample handed to you by name can trigger both at once.
    04

    Decoy Effect (Asymmetric Dominance)

    Why does adding a worse option make a different choice look more attractive?

    Insert a third option that is clearly dominated, and preference shifts toward the option the decoy flatters. Nothing about that preferred option itself has changed.

    ›
    Likely mechanismAn easy win against a decoy colours a harder comparison it never actually settled

    The psychology. People choose by relative comparison. Absolute merit barely enters. A decoy makes one pairing easy to call ("B beats C on everything"), and that easy win bleeds confidence into the harder A-versus-B choice the decoy never settled.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    People choose by relative comparison. Absolute merit barely enters. A decoy makes one pairing easy to call (“B beats C on everything”), and that easy win bleeds confidence into the harder A-versus-B choice the decoy never settled.

    Where it causes errors

    Someone pays for an upgrade or bundle they would have skipped on a plain two-option menu. A deliberately weak third option was added only to manufacture comparative confidence.

    Where it can help

    The useful skill is mostly defensive: spotting when a weaker third option exists only to pull people off their real preference. Tools meant to support decisions should strip decoys out rather than invent them.

    Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (1982). "Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives: Violations of Regularity and the Similarity Hypothesis." Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90–98
    The original paper, still taught as a foundational violation of rational-choice theory.
    StrengthRegularity says adding an option should never raise another option's share. These experiments put that axiom under a direct test and broke it cleanly.
    WeaknessChoices were hypothetical. Nobody spent real money. Confirming the exact size of the effect waited on later real-money replications.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)"An asymmetrically dominated alternative is dominated by one item in the set but not by another. Adding such an alternative to a choice set can increase the probability of choosing the item that dominates it."
    ParaphrasedAcross 153 students choosing among six product categories (cars, beers, restaurants, lotteries, film, and TV sets), adding the decoy raised the target's average share by 9.2 percentage points between subjects, and from 53% to 56% within the same subjects when the decoy was removed two weeks later.
    Also worth citing: Dan Ariely's Economist-subscription classroom demonstration (from Predictably Irrational, 2008) is a popular illustrative case, not a peer-reviewed study.
    05

    Operational Transparency

    Why does watching food get made make it taste better?

    Seeing the work happen raises how much people value the result. Effort that is visible feels more worth paying for.

    ›
    Likely mechanismVisible effort is read as value, and watching someone work hard invites returning the favour

    The psychology. A labour illusion shortcut equates effort with value. Watching work also cues reciprocity: when a provider visibly works hard, people feel inclined to value that effort back. The same service can feel thinner when it looks effortless.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A labour illusion shortcut equates effort with value. Watching work also cues reciprocity: when a provider visibly works hard, people feel inclined to value that effort back. The same service can feel thinner when it looks effortless.

    Where it causes errors

    Outcomes get overvalued just because effort was put on display, including staged effort such as a search slowed on purpose, whether or not that display improved anything real.

    Where it can help

    Honest transparency also fixes the reverse problem: excellent, fast work getting undervalued because the skill stayed invisible. Showing the real process, without fake theatre, restores a fair sense of what went into it.

    Buell, R. W., & Norton, M. I. (2011). "The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value." Management Science, 57(9), 1564–1579
    Harvard Business School: the paper that names this specific mechanism.
    StrengthAcross five experiments, some people watched a visible “searching” process and others got an instant answer, with the outcome held fixed. That setup pins the cause on the display of process itself.
    WeaknessThe services were simulated in lab and online settings. Higher-stakes professional work, where a fake-looking wait might backfire once spotted, was left for later research.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedGiven a straight choice between an instant result and one that took longer, participants chose the slower option 62% of the time at a 30-second wait and 63% of the time at 60 seconds when that wait visibly showed work being done, versus just 42% and 23% when the identical wait showed a plain progress bar.
    Verbatim (abstract)“When websites engage in operational transparency by signaling that they are exerting effort, people can actually prefer websites with longer waits to those that return instantaneous results.”
    Verbatim“Operational transparency is positively associated with perceptions of effort (β = 0.23; p < 0.01), which in turn is positively associated with reciprocity (β = 0.58; p < 0.01), which has a positive association with perceived value (β = 0.68; p < 0.01).”
    Also worth citing: Domino's Pizza Tracker (~26% associated sales lift), Kayak's deliberately delayed search results, TurboTax's "checking 350 deductions" messaging.
    See also: Tradeoff Transparency, this principle shows that work happened; that one shows what you gave up to get it. Related instinct, different job.
    06

    Not Enough Choice

    Why does taking an option away make people want it more?

    Cutting an option does more than shrink the menu. Desire for the eliminated choice can rise, and trust in whoever removed it can fall.

    ›
    Likely mechanismLosing an option makes people want it more, simply because it was taken away

    The psychology. Psychological reactance kicks in when a freedom people already had, including the freedom to pick an option, is threatened or removed. Motivation shifts toward restoring that freedom. Desire for the eliminated option can rise precisely because it was taken away.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Psychological reactance kicks in when a freedom people already had, including the freedom to pick an option, is threatened or removed. Motivation shifts toward restoring that freedom. Desire for the eliminated option can rise precisely because it was taken away.

    Where it causes errors

    A retailer drops a low-margin but familiar item to “simplify” the range, then faces complaints out of proportion to how often that item was actually bought. The option's presence on the shelf mattered on its own, separate from its sales.

    Where it can help

    When a restriction is genuinely necessary, explaining the reason helps. Reactance fires hardest when the cut feels arbitrary or unexplained. Saying why an option went away defuses far more anger than narrowing the set without comment.

    Naming the freedom outright works even when nothing is being restricted. In a street experiment, adding one line, “but you are free to accept or to refuse,” to an otherwise identical bus-fare request lifted compliance from about 10% to about 47.5%. Restoring the freedom a plain request seemed to threaten stopped reactance before it started, without cutting anyone's real choice.

    Hammock, T., & Brehm, J. W. (1966). "The Attractiveness of Choice Alternatives when Freedom to Choose Is Eliminated by a Social Agent." Journal of Personality, 34, 546–554
    The founding experiment behind psychological reactance theory.
    StrengthThe key contrast was a social agent taking a choice away, set against a choice that had never been on offer. Reactance tracked the act of restriction. Mere absence of an option did not produce the same response.
    WeaknessThe paradigm used children and candy bars, and it has been replicated many times. Showing that the same mechanism covers adult purchases and subscriptions still took decades of follow-on work.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedChildren rated a candy bar as more attractive after being told an adult had eliminated it as an option, compared to an equally unavailable bar that wasn't actively taken away by someone.
    ParaphrasedThe result generalised into psychological reactance theory, now used broadly to explain resistance to advice, warnings, and restricted choices well beyond the original experiment.
    Also worth citing: Guéguen, N., & Pascual, A. (2000). “Evocation of Freedom and Compliance: The ‘But You Are Free’ Technique.” Current Research in Social Psychology, 5, 264–270. A real street experiment: asking passersby for coins for a bus fare, a plain request got about 10% compliance, the identical request followed by “but you are free to accept or to refuse” got about 47.5%, naming the freedom explicitly defused the reactance a bare request would otherwise trigger. A later meta-analysis (Carpenter, 2013) found a real but smaller pooled effect across many replications than this original study.
    See also: Choice Overload, too little and too much choice can both backfire, for opposite reasons.
    07

    Choice Overload

    Why do more options sometimes mean nobody picks anything at all?

    A wider set can look generous. Past a point it stops helping. Choosing becomes the hard part, and many people walk away with nothing.

    ›
    Likely mechanismComparison cost outweighing the value of more options

    The psychology. A large set raises cognitive load and the fear of picking badly. Once the assortment passes a certain size, the mental cost of comparing outweighs the benefit of the extra options. Deferring the whole decision becomes more attractive than choosing imperfectly.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A large set raises cognitive load and the fear of picking badly. Once the assortment passes a certain size, the mental cost of comparing outweighs the benefit of the extra options. Deferring the whole decision becomes more attractive than choosing imperfectly.

    Where it causes errors

    A page with dozens of variants can convert worse than one with six, even when the wider range was meant to serve more customers. Abundance reads as effort saved for the seller, and as work dumped on the shopper.

    Where it can help

    Curating a smaller, well-chosen set, or grouping a large range into simple categories first, raises both satisfaction and completion. Fewer, better options is a real service to the decision-maker.

    Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). "When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?" Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995–1006
    The famous "jam study."
    Experiment Teardown
    502 shoppers passed the booth
    Only the number of jams on display changed
    6-jam display
    6 jams on the table
    Stopped, or walked on
    24-jam display
    24 jams on the table
    Stopped, or walked on
    Result 6 jams 24 jams Swing
    Stopped to look 40% → 60% +20
    Purchased (of stoppers) 30% → 3% −27

    More choice drew a crowd, not a sale. The 24-jam display attracted more browsers, but of everyone who stopped, ten times as many bought from the small display as the large one.

    Internal validityShoppers bought real jam in a real grocery store; the outcome was purchase, not a preference rating. Displays switched hourly across two Saturdays, and day counterbalanced which display came first.
    External validityThe setting was one product category, jam, in one upscale store. Later meta-analyses treat the effect as real, yet smaller and more dependent on context than this original study alone implies.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Nearly 30% (31) of the consumers in the limited-choice condition subsequently purchased a jar of Wilkin & Sons jam; in contrast, only 3% (4) of the consumers in the extensive-choice condition did so.”
    ParaphrasedFollow-up meta-analyses since have found the "too much choice reduces satisfaction or completion" effect is real but variable across contexts, strongest when options are hard to compare or the chooser lacks expertise.
    Also worth citing: A 2025 randomised trial of 402 primary care physicians found the opposite pattern in a different context, showing two or three appropriate treatment alternatives (instead of just one) in the electronic health record increased how often physicians chose a more personalised care plan, from 44% to 62%. A genuine boundary condition, not a contradiction: it depends on how comparable the options are and who's choosing, not a universal rule that fewer options always wins. Altinger, G., et al. (2025). "Multiple Suggested Care Alternatives and Decision-Making of Primary Care Physicians: A Randomised Clinical Trial." JAMA Network Open
    Also worth reading: The Biases Draining Your Super Could Also Fill It, on how every unintended duplicate super account multiplies the number of fund and insurance decisions a saver would need to make to actually opt out.
    08

    Zero Price Paradox

    Why would a $0 price sell worse than a 99-cent one?

    Free does not always win. An exact $0 price can convert worse than a small charge, because people start hunting for the catch instead of feeling the pull of free.

    ›
    Likely mechanismScrutiny of the “catch” overriding the zero-price emotional pull

    The psychology. A $0 tag fires two responses at once: the emotional pull of the Zero Price Effect, and closer scrutiny of whatever the catch must be. When incidental costs of free are obvious, shipping, time, data, a longer commitment, scrutiny can beat the emotional pull, and demand falls below what a small paid price would get.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A $0 tag fires two responses at once: the emotional pull of the Zero Price Effect, and closer scrutiny of whatever the catch must be. When incidental costs of free are obvious, shipping, time, data, a longer commitment, scrutiny can beat the emotional pull, and demand falls below what a small paid price would get.

    Where it causes errors

    Teams assume free always converts best, then stare at a $0 offer losing to a $1 one. Resources get poured into chasing the wrong emotional lever for the offer actually on the page.

    Where it can help

    Choose deliberately between free and a small nominal price, matched to how honest the offer is. Use free when any catch is truly invisible, as with a frictionless trial. Prefer a token price when people will reasonably suspect a catch, such as data collection or an upsell funnel.

    Fan, X., Cai, F. C., & Bodenhausen, G. V. (2022). "The Boomerang Effect of Zero Pricing: When and Why a Zero Price Is Less Effective Than a Low Price for Enhancing Consumer Demand." Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 50(3), 521–537
    Directly tests the boundary condition of the original Zero Price Effect.
    StrengthThe paper asks when Shampanier et al.'s (2007) classic zero-price effect fails. Boundary-condition work like this is scarcer than another confirmation study.
    WeaknessIn four of five studies the incidental cost is effort: a commute, a long survey, or writing a resume. Cash stakes show up only in the field data, a K-12 tutoring market with prices up to about $25 an hour. Physical risk appears in just one study, a hepatitis C vaccine offer. A pure money frame such as a shipping fee or deposit was not tested.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)"Zero pricing triggers both positive affect and cognitive scrutiny of incidental costs; when incidental costs are high, the scrutiny pathway overrides the affective pathway and decreases demand."
    ParaphrasedThe reversal specifically shows up when the "free" offer carries non-obvious costs, making this a boundary condition of the original effect, not a contradiction of it.
    See also: Zero Price Effect, the two aren't opposites. Zero pricing pulls demand up when there's no catch to suspect; it can push demand down when people sense there must be one. The paradox is knowing which situation you're in.
    What the paper actually tested: The main field study analysed 3,502 short-term K-12 tutoring classes in China, comparing online classes (low incidental cost, no commute) against offline classes (high incidental cost, a real commute). Demand for online classes rose the closer the price got to zero. Demand for offline classes followed an inverted U, peaking at a small positive price and dropping at exactly $0, the boomerang this principle is named for. A follow-up study used a hepatitis C vaccine offer to show the same reversal with a risk-based incidental cost instead of a time-based one.
    09

    Tradeoff Transparency

    Why does showing what someone would give up change what they choose?

    Put the downside next to the upside, what people give up as well as what they get, and decisions improve compared with a benefits-only pitch.

    ›
    Likely mechanismNaming the tradeoff forces a real comparison instead of a quick gut reaction

    The psychology. Most pitches default to benefits and leave costs implied. Spelling out the tradeoff, what someone gets and what they surrender, pulls in more deliberate comparison than the quick, affect-led judgment a benefits-only page invites.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Most pitches default to benefits and leave costs implied. Spelling out the tradeoff, what someone gets and what they surrender, pulls in more deliberate comparison than the quick, affect-led judgment a benefits-only page invites.

    Where it causes errors

    A plan comparison that only lists inclusions lets people commit without clocking what they traded away. The cost shows up later as a missing feature, a longer lock-in, or a charge that appears only on the first real bill.

    Where it can help

    This is the constructive end of the subject. Naming a product's real drawbacks beside its strengths is a direct path to better decisions, and more than a shield against manipulation. The study below found the business did not have to sacrifice take-up to do it.

    Buell, R. W., & Choi, M. (2025). “Improving Customer Compatibility with Tradeoff Transparency.” Management Science, 71(2), 1335–1355
    A field experiment run inside Commonwealth Bank of Australia's real credit card acquisition funnel, not a lab survey.
    Experiment Teardown
    393,036 prospective credit card customers
    Only whether drawbacks were shown as prominently as benefits differed
    Standard marketing
    Card pages led with strengths; drawbacks minimised or absent
    Tradeoff transparency
    Each card's drawbacks shown with equal billing to its strengths
    Result Hidden Shown Swing
    Monthly spend — → — +9.9%
    Cancel rate — → — −20.5%

    Naming the downsides didn't cost CBA customers. It earned better ones. Take-up was statistically unchanged, but customers who saw each card's drawbacks went on to spend more, cancel less, and make late payments less often.

    Internal validityA large randomised field experiment (n=393,036, split roughly evenly across conditions) tracked real spending, cancellation, and payment records. Satisfaction surveys were not the outcome.
    External validityThe trial sat inside one nationwide bank's credit card funnel. Other financial products and markets with different disclosure norms were outside the design.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Although we find tradeoff transparency to have an insignificant effect on acquisition rates, customers who were shown each offering's tradeoffs selected different products than those who were not.”
    ParaphrasedA supplementary analysis found early, mixed evidence that this shift moved customers toward cards suited to their financial profile: customers with fewer existing banking products became more likely to pick the lower-rate card under transparency, though not every one of these secondary patterns reached significance.
    Verbatim“Customers who were randomly-selected to experience transparency into each offering's tradeoffs, and who moved forward in opening an account, used their cards more intensively, spending 9.9% more per month, and were 10.8% less likely to make late payments on a monthly basis. Furthermore, customers who experienced transparency were 20.5% less likely to cancel their credit cards during the first nine months of their relationships.”
    Also worth citing: Buell, R. W., “Commonwealth Bank of Australia: Unbanklike Experimentation,” Harvard Business School Case 619-018, the teaching case documenting how CBA's Behavioural Economics team designed and ran this “Good and the Bad” experiment inside the bank.
    See also: Operational Transparency, related instinct, different job: that one shows work happened, this one shows what you gave up to get it.
    Tested as an experiment: Does tradeoff transparency work between products, not just within one?, taking CBA's own finding one level up, from comparing cards to comparing ways to pay.
    10

    Behavioural Labels

    Why does calling someone “a voter” make them more likely to vote?

    Name the identity behind the behaviour, “a voter” rather than “someone who votes,” and people act to stay consistent with that label.

    ›
    Likely mechanismBeing given an identity nudges people to keep acting consistently with it

    The psychology. Under self-perception theory, people partly learn their own traits by watching what they do. Once an identity is named for them, they work to keep later behaviour consistent with it. A noun such as “a voter” names a stable identity; a verb such as “voting” only describes a one-off act. Identities pull harder on what happens next.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Under self-perception theory, people partly learn their own traits by watching what they do. Once an identity is named for them, they work to keep later behaviour consistent with it. A noun such as “a voter” names a stable identity; a verb such as “voting” only describes a one-off act. Identities pull harder on what happens next.

    Where it causes errors

    The same lever runs backward. Stick someone with a negative identity (“you're lazy,” “you're bad with money”) and the label can lock in the behaviour someone hoped to change. People conform to identities imposed on them as readily as ones they chose.

    Where it can help

    A positive identity label, “you're someone who shows up,” “you're a voter,” “you're a saver,” reliably beats a plain exhortation to act. It is one of the most replicated, low-cost, and ethical levers in the field. It works by affirming an identity someone already holds or wants, without hiding anything.

    Bryan, C. J., Walton, G. M., Rogers, T., & Dweck, C. S. (2011). "Motivating Voter Turnout by Invoking the Self." PNAS, 108(31), 12653–12656
    Field experiments across two real state elections, not just survey responses.
    StrengthTurnout was checked against official state voting records across two real elections. Self-report was never the outcome measure. That design is far stronger than a typical attitude study run in a single lab session.
    WeaknessGains of 10.9 to 13.7 percentage points across the two elections sit at the extreme end of this literature. The authors themselves put them among the largest effects ever recorded on objectively measured turnout. Effects that large often shrink at population scale or in later replications, so the result warrants caution.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“[T]he personal-identity phrasing significantly increased interest in registering to vote (experiment 1) and, in two statewide elections in the United States, voter turnout as assessed by official state records (experiments 2 and 3).”
    Verbatim (abstract)“These results provide evidence that people are continually managing their self-concepts, seeking to assume or affirm valued personal identities.”
    Also worth citing: Miller, Brickman & Bolen (1975): labelling children "neat and tidy" cut littering far more effectively than repeatedly telling them to be neat and tidy, with the effect still holding two weeks later. An older, foundational demonstration of the same mechanism.
    See also: Framing Effect, easy to confuse with this one, but different: that's about how the same fact is worded ("75% lean" vs. "25% fat"); this is about naming a person's identity ("a voter").
    11

    Framing Effect

    Why does the same surgery sound safer as “90% survive” than as “10% die”?

    Identical information can land as reassuring or alarming once it is worded as a gain versus a loss.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe same fact feels different depending on whether it's framed as a gain or a loss

    The psychology. Attribute framing: stating a fact as “75% lean” produces a different immediate emotional read than stating the same fact as “25% fat.” The product is unchanged. The wording sets the first impression.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Attribute framing: stating a fact as “75% lean” produces a different immediate emotional read than stating the same fact as “25% fat.” The product is unchanged. The wording sets the first impression.

    Where it causes errors

    Someone picks a product off a positively worded label (low-fat, “90% success rate”) without registering the matching negative frame (still contains fat; still fails one in ten). The choice moved on labelling alone.

    Where it can help

    Labels that print both frames, or one shared comparable metric such as nutrition panels and energy ratings, let people reach the underlying fact. Honest labelling remains one of the cheapest, most reliable nudges available.

    Spotted in the wild

    The identical mechanism, live on a real McDonald's Australia promotion.

    McDonald's Australia's own promo page: a real, capped McGold Card prize worded as “free Macca's for life,” captured September 2026.

    The same prize's real terms, on McDonald's own McGold Card page: eight winners, a fixed weekly allowance, not the unlimited windfall “for life” suggests.

    Full decode: Why does a $2.50 fries deal come with a chance to win free food for life? This is McDonald's own marketing language, not proof the framing changed anyone's actual purchase.

    Levin, I. P., & Gaeth, G. J. (1988). "How Consumers Are Affected by the Framing of Attribute Information Before and After Consuming the Product." Journal of Consumer Research, 15(3), 374–378
    The classic "75% lean / 25% fat" framing study.
    StrengthFraming was measured before people tasted the meat and again afterward. Most framing studies stop at the pre-experience judgment. Repeating the measure after real sensory information shows whether the frame still holds once people know what the product is like.
    WeaknessOnly one product category appears, and the frame is a simple lean/fat binary. Multi-attribute nutrition panels or financial disclosures could behave differently.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“The consumers’ evaluations were more favorable toward the beef labeled ‘75% lean’ than that labeled ‘25% fat.’”
    ParaphrasedThe framing effect was strongest before consumers tasted the product and measurably weaker afterwards, direct experience partially, but not fully, corrected the labelling bias.
    See also: Behavioural Labels, related but different: this is about how the same fact is worded; that's about naming a person's identity.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: Why does Bankwest say you're “still a winner” even when you lose the draw?, where a savings account's ordinary consolation rate gets relabelled a “win.”
    Also decoded on The Science Behind: Why does a $2.50 fries deal come with a chance to win free food for life?, where a real, capped $30-a-week prize gets worded as unlimited “free food for life.”
    12

    Illusion of Explanatory Depth

    Why does someone freeze when asked to explain how a zipper works, after being sure they understood it?

    Confidence that a zipper, a bill, or a policy “makes sense” holds until someone has to walk through the mechanism step by step. Then the gaps show.

    ›
    Likely mechanismFamiliarity gets mistaken for actually understanding how something works

    The psychology. The failure sits in metacognition. People treat familiarity, having seen or used something many times, as if it were a working causal model. The model feels finished because it has only ever been skimmed, never run end to end. Generating a real explanation exposes the gap. Asking “do you understand this?” does not.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    The failure sits in metacognition. People treat familiarity, having seen or used something many times, as if it were a working causal model. The model feels finished because it has only ever been skimmed, never run end to end. Generating a real explanation exposes the gap. Asking “do you understand this?” does not.

    Where it causes errors

    Strong opinions on a tax policy, a treatment, or a technical claim often rest on a mental model never tested out loud. Confidence and real understanding stay only weakly linked until someone has to walk the mechanism. At that point confidence, and sometimes the opinion itself, softens.

    Where it can help

    The remedy sits inside the same mechanism. Ask for a step-by-step causal explanation of a claim, plan, or product before anyone commits. That contact test is one of the few debiasing moves that holds up. Distrust is optional; trying to explain is the work.

    Rozenblit, L., & Keil, F. (2002). “The Misunderstood Limits of Folk Science: An Illusion of Explanatory Depth.” Cognitive Science, 26(5), 521–562
    Twelve studies establishing the core effect across knowledge domains.
    StrengthTwelve within-subject studies asked for a self-rating of understanding, then had people attempt an explanation, then asked again. Domains spanned mechanical devices, natural phenomena, procedures, and narratives. The design captures how the rating moves after the attempt.
    WeaknessBoth ratings sit on a numeric self-report scale, a subjective score of a subjective state. Part of the drop may be people revising the answer they think the experimenter expects after being put on the spot, instead of a clean recalibration of belief.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Nearly all participants showed drops in estimates of what they knew when confronted with having to provide a real explanation, answer a diagnostic question, and compare their understanding to an expert description.”
    Verbatim“[W]e found no decrease in knowledge ratings over time with procedures or narratives, and a significantly smaller drop with facts.”
    Also worth citing: Fernbach, P. M., Rogers, T., Fox, C. R., & Sloman, S. A. (2013), “Political Extremism Is Supported by an Illusion of Understanding,” Psychological Science, 24, 939–946, found that asking people to explain a policy mechanistically moderated their stated position. Honest caveat: a 2021 preregistered replication attempt (published in Cognition) failed to closely reproduce that political-moderation extension specifically, the core illusion-of-explanatory-depth effect itself remains well-replicated, but this particular applied extension should be treated as unsettled.
    13

    Social Proof

    Why does a restaurant with a line outside feel safer to pick?

    Under uncertainty, people treat what everyone else appears to be doing as a signal of quality. Popularity itself becomes the evidence.

    ›
    Likely mechanismOther people's visible choices are read as evidence about what's actually good

    The psychology. Ambiguity pushes people to treat others' visible behaviour as information. The shortcut is often sound: if 500 people chose this, it is probably fine. It fails when the crowd's choice was shaped by something other than quality, such as which option simply got noticed first.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Ambiguity pushes people to treat others' visible behaviour as information. The shortcut is often sound: if 500 people chose this, it is probably fine. It fails when the crowd's choice was shaped by something other than quality, such as which option simply got noticed first.

    Where it causes errors

    A product, app, or song can grow more popular because it was displayed as popular early, even when a better alternative sat nearby. Visible popularity then draws still more followers, compounding regardless of the real quality gap.

    Where it can help

    Real, verified figures (checked reviews, actual completion rates) help people decide faster under genuine uncertainty. The test is whether the number is representative of real behaviour, or built to manufacture a herd.

    Spotted in the wild

    Two examples from the same real checkout flow, a domain registrar upselling an add-on, then asking for payment on the very next screen. Both lean on the identical mechanism this principle names: let a crowd's size stand in for a quality judgment the buyer hasn't made themselves.

    GoDaddy, domain checkout upsell. “CHOSEN BY OVER 225,000 CUSTOMERS EACH MONTH” sits directly under a $13.95/yr add-on marked “RECOMMENDED,” right where a buyer is deciding whether to add it. Captured 2026-08-26.

    Same checkout, order summary screen. A 4.4-star Trustpilot rating and “139,923 reviews” count appear directly above the “Complete Purchase” button, the last thing shown before payment. Captured 2026-08-26.

    Both numbers are GoDaddy's own claims, not independently verified figures, the same honesty check this site applies to every citation. Showing them here demonstrates the tactic in current, active use, not that it worked on these particular screens. The actual evidence that the mechanism is real is the cited study below.

    Salganik, M. J., Dodds, P. S., & Watts, D. J. (2006). “Experimental Study of Inequality and Unpredictability in an Artificial Cultural Market.” Science, 311(5762), 854–856
    The “MusicLab” experiment.
    StrengthIn a live field experiment, 14,341 participants downloaded real songs from previously unknown bands. One group saw no information about others' choices; another saw download counts. Visible social proof could then be separated from song quality as a cause.
    WeaknessEvery song came from an unsigned band with no prior track record. The outcome was downloads, short of payment or lasting engagement. That is a lower-stakes behaviour than many of the purchase or voting decisions this effect is later applied to.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Increasing the strength of social influence increased both inequality and unpredictability of success.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Success was also only partly determined by quality: The best songs rarely did poorly, and the worst rarely did well, but any other result was possible.”
    See also: Social Norm, related but distinct: this is about copying others' visible choices under uncertainty; that's about which specific message (what's common vs. what's approved) actually changes behaviour, and when.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers?, where a real-time feed of other people winning a promotion runs alongside a visibly draining prize pool.
    14

    Social Norm (Descriptive vs. Injunctive)

    Why can a message that “most people still do this” raise the very behaviour it meant to cut?

    Two different messages both claim to be “the norm”: what most people actually do (descriptive), and what most people approve of (injunctive). Confusing the two can push behaviour the wrong way.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA norm only changes behaviour if it's front of mind at the moment of choosing

    The psychology. Norm messaging moves behaviour only when the norm is “in focus” at the decision. Truth alone is not enough. Descriptive norms (“most people do X”) say what is typical; injunctive norms (“most people approve of X”) say what is sanctioned. Highlight the wrong type, or advertise that the unwanted act is common, and the campaign can raise the behaviour it meant to cut.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Norm messaging moves behaviour only when the norm is “in focus” at the decision. Truth alone is not enough. Descriptive norms (“most people do X”) say what is typical; injunctive norms (“most people approve of X”) say what is sanctioned. Highlight the wrong type, or advertise that the unwanted act is common, and the campaign can raise the behaviour it meant to cut.

    Where it causes errors

    A campaign that says “too many people still litter here” can be factually right and still raise littering. It broadcasts a descriptive norm (littering is common) that undercuts the injunctive message (littering is frowned on), including among people who had no plan to litter.

    Where it can help

    Stating the real descriptive norm, “most guests in this room reuse their towels,” reliably beats appeals to abstract values such as environmental protection. No deception is required. The norm has to be true.

    Cialdini, R. B., Reno, R. R., & Kallgren, C. A. (1990). “A Focus Theory of Normative Conduct: Recycling the Concept of Norms to Reduce Littering in Public Places.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 58(6), 1015–1026
    Study 1: the parking-structure littering experiment.
    Experiment Teardown
    139 drivers
    Only the visible state of the parking structure changed
    Clean environment
    No litter visible on arrival
    Found a handbill on the windshield
    Littered environment
    Litter already scattered around
    Found the same handbill
    Result Clean Littered Swing
    Littered the handbill 11% → 41% +30

    The environment did the persuading. Seeing existing litter nearly quadrupled the littering rate, same handbill, same parking structure, just a different visible norm.

    Internal validityResearchers physically altered real environments and observed actual littering without participants knowing. Surveys and self-reports were not the measure.
    External validityLittering was the sole behaviour under study, though the paper ran it in several physical settings: two hospital parking garages, a walkway, dormitory mailboxes, and a library car park. Focus theory in the paper predicts the mechanism should travel to other behaviours; that claim needed separate confirmation elsewhere.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedAcross five experiments, a relevant norm (against littering) only shaped behaviour when something in the environment made that norm psychologically salient at the moment of the decision, the same norm, unfocused, had little effect.
    ParaphrasedMaking people aware of a norm that runs counter to what's wanted (pointing out that a space is already littered) could increase the undesirable behaviour, by making the descriptive norm salient instead of the injunctive one.
    Also worth citing: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., & Griskevicius, V. (2008), “A Room with a Viewpoint: Using Social Norms to Motivate Environmental Conservation in Hotels,” Journal of Consumer Research, 35(3), 472–482, two real hotel field experiments found a sign stating the majority of guests in that specific room reuse their towels outperformed a standard environmental-appeal sign.
    See also: Social Proof, related but distinct: that's about copying others' visible choices under uncertainty; this is about which specific norm message actually changes behaviour, and when.
    15

    Compromise Effect

    Why does the middle option win so often, simply by sitting in the middle?

    Insert a middle option into a two-item lineup and people flock to it. It is often the easiest choice to justify, even when it is not the best value.

    ›
    Likely mechanismExtremeness aversion, avoiding the risk of looking wasteful or cheap

    The psychology. Extreme options carry social risk. The priciest choice can look wasteful; the cheapest can look stingy. A middle option dodges both charges at once, especially when someone expects to justify the pick to another person. The decision almost reasons itself, without weighing the real attributes.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Extreme options carry social risk. The priciest choice can look wasteful; the cheapest can look stingy. A middle option dodges both charges at once, especially when someone expects to justify the pick to another person. The decision almost reasons itself, without weighing the real attributes.

    Where it causes errors

    A three-tier price menu reliably shifts share toward the middle tier, whether or not that tier is the best value. The same product sells differently as the extreme of a two-option set than as the safe middle of three.

    Where it can help

    The useful skill is mostly defensive. Before taking “the middle one,” ask whether it would still win if it were labelled the cheapest or the dearest option in a differently bounded set. If the answer flips, the compromise slot made the call.

    Simonson, I. (1989). “Choice Based on Reasons: The Case of Attraction and Compromise Effects.” Journal of Consumer Research, 16(2), 158–174
    The paper that names and formally tests the compromise effect.
    StrengthThe design asked whether “need for justification” enlarges the compromise effect. People told they would have to explain their pick to someone else showed a larger shift toward the middle than people who were not. That pattern backs the reason-based account.
    WeaknessScenarios were hypothetical forced choices in the lab. Real money never changed hands. How large the effect is in high-stakes purchases still needed field replication.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“[T]he market shares of alternatives in the TV, apartment, calculator, mouthwash, and calculator battery categories were, on average, 17.5 percent larger when they were compromise brands than when they were not.”
    ParaphrasedThe attraction effect was measurably stronger among participants who expected to justify their decision to someone else. An earlier pilot study found the same pattern for the compromise effect, but that difference wasn't statistically significant in the main study, so the compromise result is less settled than the attraction one.
    See also: Decoy Effect and Similarity Effect, collectively known as “context effects”: how a choice set is built changes which option wins, independent of anyone's actual preferences.
    16

    Similarity Effect

    Why does a near-identical new option make the current best look weaker?

    Add a second option nearly identical to one already on the menu, and the pair splits attention and share. A more distinct rival gains relatively, even though its own quality never changed.

    ›
    Likely mechanismTwo near-identical options split the same pool of support instead of adding to it

    The psychology. People compare options partly by how easy they are to tell apart. Two near-identical options fight over the same slice of consideration, dividing their combined share rather than growing it. A more distinctive option skips that internal fight and keeps its share.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    People compare options partly by how easy they are to tell apart. Two near-identical options fight over the same slice of consideration, dividing their combined share rather than growing it. A more distinctive option skips that internal fight and keeps its share.

    Where it causes errors

    A retailer or platform that adds a near-twin of a bestseller can cannibalise that bestseller and hand a relative edge to a totally different product. The near-duplicate does not steal share evenly. It mostly takes from its closest twin.

    Where it can help

    Deliberately separating similar options, instead of letting them cluster, helps people compare on attributes that matter. It keeps choosers from stalling between two options that are hard to tell apart for reasons unrelated to quality.

    Tversky, A. (1972). “Elimination by Aspects: A Theory of Choice.” Psychological Review, 79(4), 281–299
    The foundational paper identifying similarity, attraction, and compromise as distinct context effects.
    StrengthThe paper derives the similarity effect as a falsifiable breach of “regularity” and “independence of irrelevant alternatives,” two foundational axioms of rational choice, then tests the prediction in probabilistic choice experiments rather than informal demos alone.
    WeaknessChoice sets were abstract and hypothetical, typical of choice-theory work from this period. Later applied research (Huber & Puto, 1983) took the effect into real product categories to check it outside the lab.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedThe model, and the accompanying experiments,showed that adding a close substitute for an existing option reduces that option's relative share by more than simple probability models predict, because the two similar options compete directly with each other for the same underlying preference.
    ParaphrasedThe paper formally derives and tests the similarity effect itself, using classic thought experiments (choosing between records, travel agencies, trips to Paris or Rome) to show that adding a near-duplicate option violates basic axioms of rational choice like regularity and the constant-ratio rule. It doesn't name “attraction” or “compromise” effects: those specific effects and terms came later, from Huber, Payne, and Puto (1982) and Simonson (1989), building on the elimination-by-aspects framework this paper introduces.
    See also: Decoy Effect and Compromise Effect, together, the three classic “context effects”: similarity splits share between near-twins, attraction (decoy) boosts a dominant option via a deliberately worse one, and compromise favours the safe middle. Same underlying lesson: how a menu is built shapes the outcome as much as what's actually on it.
    17

    Goal Gradient Effect

    Why does effort rise faster once a loyalty card is eight stamps in than at two?

    Effort and motivation rise as a goal draws nearer. A loyalty card that already shows two stamps filled gets used faster than a blank one, for the same reward.

    ›
    Likely mechanismFeeling closer to a finish line speeds people up, even when the real distance hasn't changed

    The psychology. First seen in animals running a maze: they speed up as the food nears. The same gradient shows up whenever people chase a goal with a visible finish line. Felt proximity to completion drives the acceleration as much as objective distance. Pre-filling a loyalty card with “free” stamps that were never earned still speeds people up, even though the real purchase count required is unchanged.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    First seen in animals running a maze: they speed up as the food nears. The same gradient shows up whenever people chase a goal with a visible finish line. Felt proximity to completion drives the acceleration as much as objective distance. Pre-filling a loyalty card with “free” stamps that were never earned still speeds people up, even though the real purchase count required is unchanged.

    Where it causes errors

    A 10-stamp loyalty card leaves the same real distance as an 8-purchase card that starts with 2 stamps already filled. The second version reliably speeds purchasing by manufacturing a felt sense of progress.

    Where it can help

    Honest progress bars use the same mechanism to help people finish things they already want to do. They show real distance left on a form, a course, or a savings goal. The progress displayed matches what has actually been done.

    Spotted in the wild

    Exactly this kind of genuine progress bar, live in Up Bank's own savings account list.

    Up Bank, Savers list. Every Saver renders its own progress bar against its real target, right in the account list, not buried a tap away.

    Full decode: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers? A $0-of-$157,100 bar describes the identical remaining task very differently to a $140,000-of-$157,100 one, the same mechanism this principle's cited study documents.

    Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., & Zheng, Y. (2006). “The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention.” Journal of Marketing Research, 43(1), 39–58
    The real coffee-card field study.
    StrengthOne strand was a café field study: real customers, a real 10-coffee loyalty card, and purchase records over time. A second online field study ran in parallel. Evidence therefore comes from two different real-world reward programmes.
    WeaknessThe main acceleration pattern is observational: customers opted into the loyalty programme on their own, so card records are not a randomised experiment. A separate 10-stamp versus 12-stamp comparison was randomly assigned, yet only among 108 customers at one café.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedCafé customers bought coffee at an increasing rate the closer they got to their free 10th coffee. In a separate randomised test, 108 customers given a 12-stamp card with 2 stamps already filled in finished their 10 required purchases in 12.7 days on average, 20% faster than the 15.6 days it took customers given a blank 10-stamp card, for the identical real distance to the reward.
    ParaphrasedAfter earning a reward, participants' effort dropped and then re-accelerated as they approached the next reward, the gradient resets and repeats with each new goal, rather than motivation simply declining over time.
    See also: Medium Maximisation, a related but different reward-programme mechanism: this one is about accelerating effort near a finish line; that one is about chasing the reward token itself past the point where it still tracks real value.
    The finish line doesn't have to be external: Law of Round Numbers is the same acceleration effect aimed at a number someone sets for themselves rather than a card a business hands them.
    Experiment built on this: Does showing progress through a home loan appointment booking increase completion?, testing the exact mechanism proposed above on a real multi-step lending form.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: Why does GoalSaver's 4.75% bonus feel like money you'd be losing, not money you haven't earned yet?, where CommBank's Goal Tracker breaks a savings target into weekly milestones using this exact acceleration effect.
    Also decoded on The Science Behind: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers?, where every Saver renders its own visible progress bar against its real target, right in the account list.
    Special report built on this: Breaking a Form Into Steps Changes How It Feels. It Doesn't Always Change How It Performs., where this exact mechanism explains the Progress Flow form pattern, and a real head-to-head test finds it can backfire on a phone.
    18

    Medium Maximisation

    Why do people chase airline miles that are worth less than the cash spent to earn them?

    Hand people a token that stands in for a reward (points, miles, stamps), and they sometimes maximise the token itself, even when that leaves them worse off in cash terms.

    ›
    Likely mechanismChasing more points crowds out what the points are actually worth

    The psychology. A medium such as points or miles is meant to stand transparently for the value it can be traded for. Once effort is tallied in the medium's own units, people can lose the thread back to cash value. They chase “more points” the way they would chase more money, even when the points-maximising option is worth less once redeemed.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A medium such as points or miles is meant to stand transparently for the value it can be traded for. Once effort is tallied in the medium's own units, people can lose the thread back to cash value. They chase “more points” the way they would chase more money, even when the points-maximising option is worth less once redeemed.

    Where it causes errors

    Someone picks the option that earns more loyalty points over one that earns fewer but is worth more once redeemed. The token becomes the goal. That is especially likely when the point-heavy option makes an otherwise weaker choice feel “certain” or advantageous.

    Where it can help

    There is no clean way to exploit this in others. The honest use is defensive: convert any points-based choice back into its cash equivalent before deciding, instead of ranking options by the point totals alone.

    Spotted in the wild

    A real McDonald's app push notification and points balance, showing the same medium doing the work Hsee's study describes.

    McDonald's Australia app, push notification. The incentive to order is stated entirely in points, doubled for the day, never in what those points are actually worth.

    McDonald's Australia app, Deals screen. A running points balance sits permanently in view; there's no equivalent running total of what those points are worth in cash.

    Real screens from a currently operating McDonald's Australia promotion, captured 2026, shown to illustrate the medium at work, not to claim the notification's odds or prize terms are accurate. Points balances and promotions change; check the app directly for what's live today.

    Hsee, C. K., Yu, F., Zhang, J., & Zhang, Y. (2003). “Medium Maximization.” Journal of Consumer Research, 30(1), 1–14
    The paper that names the effect: Study 1 is the ice cream/task experiment.
    Experiment Teardown
    96 students recruited
    Only a points system was added
    Control condition
    6m6 min→—→vanilla
    7m7 min→—→pistachio
    Chose a task
    Medium condition
    6m6 min→60 pts→vanilla
    7m7 min→100 pts→pistachio
    Chose a task
    Result Control Medium Swing
    Chose long task ~25% → ~53% +28
    Preferred pistachio ~27% → ~29% +2

    Choice moved, taste didn't. In the control condition, task choice and flavour preference tracked closely together. Add points, and choice of the long task roughly doubled, while real preference for pistachio barely shifted at all.

    Internal validityBoth conditions used the same recruitment path and the same follow-up preference question. How people were assigned to groups is not stated in the paper.
    External validityThe first study used one campus and one reward. Study 2 applied the same logic to a bank CD scenario and recovered the same pattern.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedIn Study 1, participants offered a points-based reward chose the longer, more point-heavy task at a significantly higher rate than participants offered the identical flavour tradeoff directly (χ² = 7.43, p < .01), even though a separate question showed their actual flavour preference didn't differ between the two groups.
    ParaphrasedThe effect traces to specific illusions the medium creates, for example, a medium can make an option feel more certain or more proportionally rewarding than it actually is, rather than simple confusion about how the redemption maths works.
    See also: Goal Gradient Effect, related reward-programme mechanism, different failure mode: that one is about accelerating effort as a goal nears; this one is about losing track of real value while chasing the token itself.
    See also: Symbolic Rewards, related but different: this is a token that stands in for a real reward and gets over-optimised for its own sake; that one is a token with no exchange value at all, that still motivates through recognition alone.
    19

    Noise

    Why can the same judge, same case, on different days, reach different verdicts?

    Ask the same expert to judge the same case twice on different days, and the answers often diverge. The drift usually comes from scatter in judgment itself, rather than a consistent directional bias.

    ›
    Likely mechanismUnwanted, inconsistent scatter in judgments, not a bias pointing the same way every time

    The psychology. Bias and noise fail in different ways. Bias is a consistent skew in one direction (a scale that always reads 2kg heavy). Noise is scatter: the same judge, on the same case, lands in different places depending on mood, the day, or other factors that should not matter. Scatter that points nowhere is harder to spot than a consistent skew, and can cost just as much.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Bias and noise fail in different ways. Bias is a consistent skew in one direction (a scale that always reads 2kg heavy). Noise is scatter: the same judge, on the same case, lands in different places depending on mood, the day, or other factors that should not matter. Scatter that points nowhere is harder to spot than a consistent skew, and can cost just as much.

    Where it causes errors

    Two identical insurance claims, loan applications, or court sentences can receive meaningfully different outcomes based only on who reviewed them and on which day. A single case hides that inconsistency. Show the same case to the same expert twice and it jumps out.

    Where it can help

    Structured judgment cuts noise without asking anyone to care less or know less. Break a decision into independently scored parts. Aggregate scores from several independent judges instead of relying on one. Use checklists and decision rules.

    Hodgson, R. T. (2008). “An Examination of Judge Reliability at a Major U.S. Wine Competition.” Journal of Wine Economics, 3(2), 105–113
    The wine-judges reliability study.
    StrengthAcross four years of a major live competition, expert judges unknowingly re-tasted the same wine, poured from the same bottle, several times within a single flight. That reliability check sat inside the contest itself.
    WeaknessScoring wine is a hard sensory task with high natural variance from palate fatigue and order effects. The same size of inconsistency should not be assumed for very different expert judgments, such as medical diagnosis or legal sentencing, even when the broad mechanism is shared.
