    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Between 65 and 70 judges were tested each year. About 10 percent of the judges were able to replicate their score within a single medal group.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Another 10 percent, on occasion, scored the same wine Bronze to Gold.”
    Also worth citing: Kahneman, D., Sibony, O., & Sunstein, C. R. (2021), Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (Little, Brown Spark), the book that popularised “noise” as a concept distinct from bias, and that specifically cites Hodgson's wine-judge findings as a real-world illustration. It's a trade book rather than a peer-reviewed study, so treat it as a synthesis and framework, not itself the primary evidence.
    20

    Price Transparency

    Why does burying the total inside fees change what people buy?

    An all-in price shown from the start changes what people buy, how much they buy, and how carefully they choose, relative to a low headline figure with fees added later.

    ›
    Likely mechanismLimited attention anchoring on the headline number

    The psychology. Splitting a price into a low headline figure plus later add-on fees exploits limited attention. People anchor on and remember the first, smaller number, then partially discount or forget the fees stacked afterward. Putting the full price in view from the start closes that gap, so real cost is weighed against the decision before commitment begins.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Splitting a price into a low headline figure plus later add-on fees exploits limited attention. People anchor on and remember the first, smaller number, then partially discount or forget the fees stacked afterward. Putting the full price in view from the start closes that gap, so real cost is weighed against the decision before commitment begins.

    Where it causes errors

    Drip pricing (a cheap-looking base with mandatory fees revealed at checkout) reliably raises what people pay versus the same total shown upfront. It exploits the anchoring and attention gap. That is a major reason many jurisdictions now require all-in pricing by law.

    Where it can help

    Showing the complete real price from the first screen protects buyers. The same research also found purchases shift toward products people actually value more, because decisions are made against real cost rather than a distorted one.

    Blake, T., Moshary, S., Sweeney, K., & Tadelis, S. (2021). “Price Salience and Product Choice.” Marketing Science, 40(4), 619–636
    A real field experiment on StubHub's live marketplace.
    StrengthStubHub's live marketplace hosted a large field experiment with real buyers and real money. The usual drip-priced checkout ran against an all-in, full-price-upfront version. Outcomes came from transaction and click-stream records.
    WeaknessThe setting is one marketplace, ticket resale, where the gap between sticker price and all-in cost is unusually large. Categories with proportionally smaller fees were not tested directly in this study.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Making the full purchase price salient to consumers reduces both the quality and quantity of goods purchased.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“The effect of salience on quality accounts for at least 28% of the overall revenue decline.”
    Also worth citing: Morwitz, V. G., Greenleaf, E. A., & Johnson, E. J. (1998), “Divide and Prosper: Consumers' Reactions to Partitioned Prices,” Journal of Marketing Research, 35(4), 453–463, the earlier classic study establishing the underlying mechanism: splitting a price into a base plus a separate mandatory surcharge lowers what people recall as the total cost and increases demand, compared to one combined price.
    21

    Salience

    Why does one bold number on a bill outweigh the total?

    Whatever option, number, or detail stands out visually or emotionally gets weighted far above its real importance, simply because it was the thing noticed.

    ›
    Likely mechanismWhatever visually stands out gets weighed more heavily than what actually matters more

    The psychology. Attention is scarce, and choice asks people to compare several attributes across several options at once, a task they cannot do exhaustively. Salience theory describes what fills the gap. Attributes and outcomes that stand out (extreme, unusual, or visually loud relative to the immediate set) get disproportionate weight. Equally or more important details that catch the eye less get systematically underweighted.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Attention is scarce, and choice asks people to compare several attributes across several options at once, a task they cannot do exhaustively. Salience theory describes what fills the gap. Attributes and outcomes that stand out (extreme, unusual, or visually loud relative to the immediate set) get disproportionate weight. Equally or more important details that catch the eye less get systematically underweighted.

    Where it causes errors

    A single dramatic, low-probability outcome (a jackpot, a worst-case warning, a shock discount) can dominate a decision even when it is the least likely or least relevant number in the set. It wins because it is the detail that jumps out visually or emotionally.

    Where it can help

    Making the genuinely important number the salient one uses the same mechanism to weight decisions by what matters. Lead with true total cost, or the risk that actually counts, ahead of the most visually dramatic figure.

    Bordalo, P., Gennaioli, N., & Shleifer, A. (2012). “Salience Theory of Choice Under Risk.” Quarterly Journal of Economics, 127(3), 1243–1285
    The formal, unifying theory of salience in choice.
    StrengthOne formal model produces quantitative, testable predictions for several familiar anomalies in risky choice, including the Allais paradox and specific risk-seeking patterns that had previously been treated as separate puzzles. Unification across those anomalies is the contribution.
    WeaknessThe paper is mainly theoretical. It is fitted and checked against existing risky-choice experiments rather than a new field study of its own. How well it predicts everyday consumer decisions, outside gambling-style risk tasks, depends on later applied work.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“This leads the decision maker to a context-dependent representation of lotteries in which true probabilities are replaced by decision weights distorted in favor of salient payoffs. By endogenizing decision weights as a function of payoffs, our model provides a novel and unified account of many empirical phenomena, including frequent risk-seeking behavior, invariance failures such as the Allais paradox, and preference reversals.”
    Verbatim“a lottery's salient payoffs are those which differ most strongly from the payoffs of alternative lotteries, and the decision maker's mind focuses on salient payoffs when making a choice.”
    See also: Compromise Effect and Similarity Effect, all three are context-dependent choice theories; salience is the broadest, general-attention mechanism, while the other two describe specific, well-documented patterns salience-style theories are sometimes used to help explain.
    Tested as an experiment: Does naming a savings pocket keep the money there?, a picturable label winning by contrast against the generic ones around it, tested as a live product change.
    A specific case worth its own entry: Law of Round Numbers, a round number is a specific, reliable way to make one point on a scale more salient than its neighbours, strong enough to change behaviour on its own.
    22

    Left Digit Bias

    Why does $2.99 feel cheaper than $3.00 by so much more than one cent?

    $2.99 gets read as “two dollars something.” People latch onto the leftmost digit and down-weight everything after it, even when the gap to the next whole number is a single cent.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe first digit of a number does most of the work in how big it feels

    The psychology. Multi-digit numbers are encoded leftmost digit first, and that first encoding does most of the work in the magnitude judgment. Later digits are processed with far less weight. $2.99 and $3.00 differ by one cent in cash, but by a whole leading digit in the first encoding, so the felt gap is much larger than one cent.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Multi-digit numbers are encoded leftmost digit first, and that first encoding does most of the work in the magnitude judgment. Later digits are processed with far less weight. $2.99 and $3.00 differ by one cent in cash, but by a whole leading digit in the first encoding, so the felt gap is much larger than one cent.

    Where it causes errors

    Millions of real transactions show the pattern. A used car's price drops disproportionately the moment its odometer crosses a round 10,000-mile mark, even though one extra mile changed nothing about the car. The leftmost digit rolling over changed how buyers read the number.

    Where it can help

    Knowing the mechanism defuses it. Read a price's actual value before comparing options, including the digits after the first. For anyone pricing honestly, round, un-gamed numbers are the straightforward ethical alternative to exploiting the .99 effect.

    Spotted in the wild

    McDonald's own app prices a real current offer one cent under a full dollar, the exact pricing shape the cited study measures on car odometers.

    McDonald's, My McDonald's app. A “Buy a Large Sundae, get a Hashbrown for $0.99” offer, one cent under a full dollar. Captured 2026-08-28.

    This is McDonald's own current pricing, not evidence that the missing cent changed what anyone actually bought. The evidence for that is the cited study below.

    Lacetera, N., Pope, D. G., & Sydnor, J. R. (2012). “Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market.” American Economic Review, 102(5), 2206–2236
    22 million real used-car auction transactions.
    StrengthMore than 22 million wholesale used-car auction sales, real dollars in a real market, form the dataset. At each 10,000-mile odometer threshold the price series shows a discontinuous drop that a lab simulation would struggle to pin down at this resolution.
    WeaknessWholesale used-car auctions mix professional dealers with end consumers. The paper attributes the effect mainly to final customers rather than professional agents. Aggregate auction records still make a clean split between those groups hard.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Analyzing over 22 million wholesale used-car transactions, we find substantial evidence of this left-digit bias; there are large and discontinuous drops in sale prices at 10,000-mile thresholds in odometer mileage, along with smaller drops at 1,000-mile thresholds.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“We also investigate whether this heuristic behavior is primarily attributable to the final used-car customers or the used-car salesmen who buy cars in the wholesale market. The evidence is most consistent with partial inattention by final customers.”
    Also worth citing: Thomas, M., & Morwitz, V. (2005), “Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition,” Journal of Consumer Research, 32(1), 54–64, the classic lab demonstration behind familiar $X.99 pricing, showing the effect is strongest when the compared prices are otherwise close together, and that it isn't limited to prices alone.
    See also: Anchoring, related but distinct: anchoring is about a whole number shaping later judgments; this is specifically about which digit within a number does the heaviest lifting.
    Tested as an experiment: Does a home loan rate of 5.99% get remembered as a 5% loan, not almost 6%?, the same threshold effect, moved from a car's odometer onto a home loan's headline rate.
    23

    Ordering Effects

    Why does reshuffling the same options change which one gets picked?

    Identical options, shown in a new sequence, produce different picks. First and last slots pull extra attention and votes, whatever the underlying quality of those items.

    ›
    Likely mechanismWhat comes first and last gets remembered; what's in the middle gets lost

    The psychology. Primacy and recency stack. Early items get more careful processing before attention thins; the final item is still sitting in working memory when the choice is made. Middle items get neither boost. They are skimmed and recalled worse, quality aside.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Primacy and recency stack. Early items get more careful processing before attention thins; the final item is still sitting in working memory when the choice is made. Middle items get neither boost. They are skimmed and recalled worse, quality aside.

    Where it causes errors

    In real elections, print order alone moves vote share. The same candidate can pick up or lose several percentage points from sitting first versus lower down, especially in races where voters have almost nothing else to go on.

    Where it can help

    Rotate or randomise presentation order on ballots, surveys, search results, and menus. That cancels the slot advantage so the comparison runs on content rather than placement.

    Miller, J. M., & Krosnick, J. A. (1998). “The Impact of Candidate Name Order on Election Outcomes.” Public Opinion Quarterly, 62(3), 291–330
    Real 1992 Ohio ballot data across 118 races.
    Experiment Teardown
    118 down-ballot races
    Only whether a candidate was listed first changed
    Listed later
    Same candidate, printed lower on the ballot
    Listed first
    Same candidate, printed top of the ballot
    Result Later First Swing
    Avg. vote share vs. reference 0 (ref) → +2.5 pts +2.5

    Position alone moved real votes. In the roughly half of races where the effect showed up, simply being listed first was worth an average +2.5 percentage points, same candidate, same platform, different print order.

    Internal validityPrecincts received ballot positions through a fixed rotation rather than true random assignment. Direct checks found no meaningful differences in turnout or demographics across precinct groups, so the rotation works as a functionally random natural experiment on real votes.
    External validityThe effect concentrated in low-information down-ballot races. The authors neither expect nor claim the same size in high-salience races where voters already have strong independent cues.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Reliable name-order effects appeared in 48 percent of 118 races, nearly always advantaging candidates listed first, by an average of 2.5 percent.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“These effects were stronger in races when party affiliations were not listed, when races had been minimally publicized, and when no incumbent was involved.”
    Also worth citing: Murdock, B. B. (1962), “The Serial Position Effect of Free Recall,” Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 64, 482–488: the classic lab demonstration of the underlying memory mechanism: people best recall the first and last items in any list, whatever the content.
    See also: Order Effect, related but different: this is about which item gets selected from a set by its position in it; that one is about how information order changes the judgement of a single target.
    24

    Chunking

    Why does 5551234567 slip away when 555-123-4567 sticks?

    Split a long string into small groups (a phone number, a password, a to-do list) and it becomes far easier to keep in mind. No new facts are added; only the grouping changes.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe mind can only hold a handful of grouped pieces of information at once

    The psychology. Working memory takes a small count of independent units, not a fixed count of raw digits. The limit is on chunks, and each chunk can hold a lot. Turning 9472163 into 947-216-3 leaves the information intact while cutting the units the mind must juggle from seven to three.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Working memory takes a small count of independent units, not a fixed count of raw digits. The limit is on chunks, and each chunk can hold a lot. Turning 9472163 into 947-216-3 leaves the information intact while cutting the units the mind must juggle from seven to three.

    Where it causes errors

    Unbroken instructions, an ungrouped 16-digit account number, or a form that asks for a dozen separate inputs at once can overload working memory. The information itself need not be hard. Formatting alone raises errors and abandonment.

    Where it can help

    Chunking what people see respects working-memory limits and cuts errors and drop-off in measurable ways. Group digits, split a long form into short steps, and present instructions as a short numbered list. Every fact stays; only the packaging changes.

    Spotted in the wild

    A real financial-disclosure form, chunked exactly this way, in Up Home's own borrowing-power tool.

    Up Home, The Home Zone. Never presented as one long form: split into four labelled steps, Your Deposit, Your Home, You, Your Finances.

    Full decode: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers? A large ask broken into several smaller ones clears a mental bar the whole amount, presented at once, wouldn't.

    Miller, G. A. (1956). “The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information.” Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97
    The foundational paper on working-memory capacity and chunking.
    StrengthThree different task families point at the same capacity limit: absolute judgment of single stimuli, memory span for sequences, and rapid counting. Independent methods converge on a similar number of processable units, so the claim does not rest on one paradigm alone.
    WeaknessMiller synthesises and reinterprets earlier studies by other researchers, which used varied methods and materials. There is no single new controlled experiment of his own. The force of the paper is the pattern across that older work, and it inherits each study's original limits.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Everybody knows that there is a finite span of immediate memory and that for a lot of different kinds of test materials this span is about seven items in length. I have just shown you that there is a span of absolute judgment that can distinguish about seven categories and that there is a span of attention that will encompass about six objects at a glance.”
    Verbatim“Since the memory span is a fixed number of chunks, we can increase the number of bits of information that it contains simply by building larger and larger chunks, each chunk containing more information than before.”
    Decoded on The Science Behind: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers?, where a long borrowing-power form and a six-figure deposit target are each split into several smaller, labelled steps.
    Special report built on this: Breaking a Form Into Steps Changes How It Feels. It Doesn't Always Change How It Performs., where this exact mechanism is one of two explaining the Progress Flow form pattern, never tested on a form directly.
    25

    Translating Information

    Why does “$2 a day” feel cheaper than the same $730 a year?

    One total cost can feel cheap or dear depending on the unit it is stated in. A $600 yearly charge and “less than $2 a day” are the same figure, rewritten.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA cost gets compared to whatever similar expense comes to mind first

    The psychology. People rarely price a cost from first principles. They match it against the nearest similar expense that comes to mind. Stated per day or per coffee, it gets compared with other small, frequent spends. Stated as one large total, it gets compared with big, infrequent spends. The same number can clear or fail that check based only on which frame was shown.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    People rarely price a cost from first principles. They match it against the nearest similar expense that comes to mind. Stated per day or per coffee, it gets compared with other small, frequent spends. Stated as one large total, it gets compared with big, infrequent spends. The same number can clear or fail that check based only on which frame was shown.

    Where it causes errors

    A $600 yearly subscription restated as “less than $2 a day” can feel almost free, while the identical amount as one $600 charge can feel large enough to refuse. The money has not moved. Only the comparison set has.

    Where it can help

    The same reframing works honestly in reverse. Restating a small recurring charge as its real annual total (“that is $600 a year”) helps people spot subscriptions and fees that feel tiny one by one but add up to something that matters. That use undoes the distortion instead of leaning on it.

    Gourville, J. T. (1998). “Pennies-a-Day: The Effect of Temporal Reframing on Transaction Evaluation.” Journal of Consumer Research, 24(4), 395–408
    The paper that names and formally tests the “pennies-a-day” effect.
    StrengthMultiple studies ran the reframing effect across a wide spread of real product and donation categories. Alongside that, the authors proposed and tested a two-step mechanism: which comparison prices get retrieved, then how the transaction is judged against them.
    WeaknessLab tasks asked for hypothetical willingness to consider a purchase or donation. Real purchases over time were not tracked. Whether reframing changes long-run payment behaviour, beyond that first evaluation, still needed field confirmation.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedFraming an identical cost as a small, recurring “pennies-a-day” amount rather than one large aggregate charge produced more favourable evaluations of the transaction at small daily amounts, but the effect reversed at larger daily amounts, a pattern found across a range of product and charitable-donation categories.
    Verbatim (abstract)“The PAD framing of a target transaction is shown to systematically foster the retrieval and consideration of small ongoing expenses as the standard of comparison, whereas an aggregate framing of that same transaction is shown to foster the retrieval and consideration of large infrequent expenses. This difference in retrieval is shown to significantly influence subsequent transaction evaluation and compliance.”
    See also: Price Transparency, related but different: that's about whether the full cost is shown at all; this is about which unit an already-visible cost gets expressed in.
    26

    Emergency Reserves (“Extra Lives” for Goals)

    Why does building in permission to fail once make quitting less likely?

    Add a small, pre-approved allowance for slipping up, a “skip day,” a spare life, and people stick with a goal longer than when that same goal required perfection.

    ›
    Likely mechanismOne missed day can feel like the whole goal is already broken (the “what-the-hell effect”)

    The psychology. An all-or-nothing goal leaves no room for one miss. A single skipped day or broken streak can make the whole goal feel already lost. That kicks off the “what-the-hell effect”: guilt and rule-abandonment that turn one small lapse into quitting entirely. A pre-approved reserve changes what a slip means. It is no longer a broken rule, only an event that was already budgeted for, so the goal and the sense of still being on track stay intact.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    An all-or-nothing goal leaves no room for one miss. A single skipped day or broken streak can make the whole goal feel already lost. That kicks off the “what-the-hell effect”: guilt and rule-abandonment that turn one small lapse into quitting entirely. A pre-approved reserve changes what a slip means. It is no longer a broken rule, only an event that was already budgeted for, so the goal and the sense of still being on track stay intact.

    Where it causes errors

    A savings plan, diet, or habit tracker with zero tolerance for a missed day tends to fail in a familiar pattern. One bad day triggers a much larger collapse than that day warranted, because the person now treats the whole goal as already broken rather than delayed by a single day.

    Where it can help

    This principle is almost entirely a constructive one. Baking a small number of pre-approved “passes” into a goal, a skip day, a spare life, a grace period, measurably lengthens how long people keep going. Set that against an identical goal with no slack. The target itself does not need to get any easier.

    Sharif, M. A., & Shu, S. B. (2017). “The Benefits of Emergency Reserves: Greater Preference and Persistence for Goals that Have Slack with a Cost.” Journal of Marketing Research, 54(3), 495–509
    Six studies on goal slack, one tracking real day-by-day persistence over a week.
    StrengthSix studies make up the package: mostly online scenarios, plus one incentive-compatible task that tracked real behaviour for seven days. Goals that included a built-in emergency reserve were set against otherwise identical goals with none. Persistence differences can then be tied to the reserve.
    WeaknessUsing a reserve carried a real cost by design, so the skip was never a free pass, and commitment could stay intact. A costless skip might work differently and could even weaken the goal. The paper flags that boundary instead of treating reserves as always helpful.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedPeople persisted longer at goals with a small emergency reserve built in than at objectively equivalent goals with no reserve, and also reported preferring goals structured with a reserve over otherwise identical goals without one.
    ParaphrasedThe persistence effect ran through resistance to using the reserve itself: people with a reserve pushed harder specifically to avoid having to dip into it, even when using it carried no real downside, and that resistance, not a feeling of being back on track, is what the studies identified as driving the extra effort.
    Also worth citing: This is the constructive flip side of the “what-the-hell effect” / abstinence violation effect: Marlatt, G. A., & Gordon, J. R. (1985), Relapse Prevention: Maintenance Strategies in the Addictive Behavior Change, and Cochran, W., & Tesser, A. (1996), in Striving and Feeling (Eds. Martin & Tesser), the well-documented failure mode where one lapse in an all-or-nothing goal triggers total abandonment rather than a simple, recoverable setback.
    See also: Goal Gradient Effect, related goal-pursuit mechanism: that's about accelerating effort as a goal nears; this is about surviving the moments effort lapses instead.
    27

    Pain of Paying

    Why does the same coffee taste better on a subscription than paid for by the cup?

    The more directly and vividly someone feels the act of paying, the less they enjoy and the less they consume, even when the price itself is unchanged.

    ›
    Likely mechanismPaying hurts in proportion to how visible the act of paying is, not the amount

    The psychology. The act of paying carries its own small negative jolt, separate from the price. That jolt scales with how salient, immediate, and attention-grabbing the payment method is. Cash counted note by note hurts more than a card tap, which hurts more than a pre-authorised subscription charge that never appears. The pain tracks how vividly paying registers, not the amount.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    The act of paying carries its own small negative jolt, separate from the price. That jolt scales with how salient, immediate, and attention-grabbing the payment method is. Cash counted note by note hurts more than a card tap, which hurts more than a pre-authorised subscription charge that never appears. The pain tracks how vividly paying registers, not the amount.

    Where it causes errors

    Metered, pay-per-use pricing (by the bite, the minute, the click) can suppress use of something people would enjoy more of, simply because each unit re-announces the cost. A flat, prepaid, or bundled price removes that friction and can raise how much of the same thing people use.

    Where it can help

    Businesses can use this honestly by stripping needless payment friction from things that genuinely help the customer, for example a wellness app billed once a year instead of nagging weekly. That is different from using the same lever only to dull awareness so people overspend on subscriptions they would cancel if paying stayed more visible.

    Prelec, D., & Loewenstein, G. (1998). “The Red and the Black: Mental Accounting of Savings and Debt.” Marketing Science, 17(1), 4–28
    The paper that formalised and named the pain of paying.
    StrengthThe contribution is a full “double-entry” mental accounting model. Prepayment preference, flat-rate bias, and credit-card overspending, findings once treated as separate, fall out as consequences of one mechanism.
    WeaknessEvidence comes from existing consumer patterns and earlier experiments. The paper itself is a theoretical synthesis, without a new controlled study of its own. Each prediction has needed separate empirical tests since.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Such pay-before sequences confer hedonic benefits because consumption can be enjoyed without thinking about the need to pay for it in the future.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“our model predicts that consumers will find it less painful to pay for, and hence will prefer, flat-rate pricing schemes such as unlimited Internet access at a fixed monthly price, even if it involves paying more for the same usage.”
    See also: Mental Accounting, the broader model this principle is one application of: how payment method itself changes which mental account an expense gets charged to. Also see Payment Transparency, the more specific mechanism (rehearsal and immediacy) behind why some payment methods hurt more than others.
    28

    Peak-End Rule (& Duration Neglect)

    Why does memory of a vacation hang on its worst afternoon, not its ten good days?

    People remember an experience mainly by its worst (or best) moment and how it ended, not by how long it lasted or how intense it was on average.

    ›
    Likely mechanismMemory keeps the most intense moment and the ending, and drops almost everything else

    The psychology. Memory does not keep an experience as a continuous tape. It compresses it into a few representative snapshots. The most intense moment (the peak) and the final moments (the end) dominate that summary. Duration barely counts. An experience twice as long, with the same peak and end, is remembered almost the same way.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Memory does not keep an experience as a continuous tape. It compresses it into a few representative snapshots. The most intense moment (the peak) and the final moments (the end) dominate that summary. Duration barely counts. An experience twice as long, with the same peak and end, is remembered almost the same way.

    Where it causes errors

    A service that was mostly good can be remembered as worse because of one badly timed moment near the close: a rushed goodbye, a clumsy last step. A long stretch that went well gets little credit in memory for all that time, because duration is not what memory tracks.

    Where it can help

    Deliberately shaping a strong, positive closing moment, a real thank-you, a small unexpected touch right at the end, reliably lifts how the whole experience is remembered, without changing anything earlier. It is one of the most replicated, low-cost levers in service design.

    Redelmeier, D. A., Katz, J., & Kahneman, D. (2003). “Memories of Colonoscopy: A Randomized Trial.” Pain, 104(1–2), 187–194
    The follow-up randomised trial: deliberately extends the procedure to test whether a milder ending changes memory.
    Experiment Teardown
    682 colonoscopy patients
    Only how the procedure ended differed
    Standard procedure
    Ends as soon as the scope is withdrawn
    Extended procedure
    Scope held still an extra interval: mild, not zero, discomfort
    Result Standard Extended Swing
    Final pain 2.5 → 1.7 −0.8
    Overall rating 4.9 → 4.4 −0.5

    A longer, more painful procedure, remembered as better. Adding a milder tail end lowered both the final-moment pain and the overall retrospective score, even though total pain and duration both increased.

    Internal validityA randomised trial (n=682, standard vs. extended) recorded pain in real time during the procedure as well as in later recall.
    External validityThis trial used colonoscopy. The original 1996 study recovered the same peak/end pattern in a different procedure, lithotripsy, which points to a mechanism that is not tied to one medical setting.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedIn this 2003 trial itself, patients' retrospective ratings of how bad the overall procedure was correlated with peak pain and final-minute pain, but the duration of the procedure barely predicted the rating at all (r = 0.10 and 0.09 for the two retrospective measures), the same pattern the original 1996 study first identified.
    ParaphrasedPatients in the extended-procedure group also returned for a repeat colonoscopy at a higher rate over a median 5.3-year follow-up (odds ratio 1.41) than patients in the standard-procedure group, the better memory measurably changed later behaviour, not just the retrospective rating.
    Also worth citing: Redelmeier, D. A., & Kahneman, D. (1996). “Patients’ Memories of Painful Medical Treatments: Real-Time and Retrospective Evaluations of Two Minimally Invasive Procedures.” Pain, 66(1), 3–8, the original paper (n=154 colonoscopy, n=133 lithotripsy) that first established the peak/end correlation and duration neglect, setting up the randomised follow-up trial above.
    29

    Illusory Truth Effect

    Why does hearing a lie twice make it start to feel true?

    A repeated claim starts to feel truer, even when people do not consciously recall the repetition, and even when they correctly flagged it as false the first time.

    ›
    Likely mechanismRepetition alone makes a claim feel more true, even without any new evidence

    The psychology. Familiarity stands in for accuracy. Statements that feel easier to process because they have been heard before get misread as more likely to be true, even when that ease came only from repetition, not from evidence. Much of this runs below awareness; knowing the mechanism does not fully protect against it.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Familiarity stands in for accuracy. Statements that feel easier to process because they have been heard before get misread as more likely to be true, even when that ease came only from repetition, not from evidence. Much of this runs below awareness; knowing the mechanism does not fully protect against it.

    Where it causes errors

    Misinformation that gets repeated, including repetition meant to debunk it, can grow more believable through exposure alone, whether or not anyone consciously accepts it. Advertising and political messaging that simply restate a claim exploit the same path.

    Where it can help

    The same mechanism serves true and useful material worth remembering: a genuine safety instruction, a real key fact. Repeating an accurate message across several honest touchpoints raises how confidently and correctly people recall it.

    Hasher, L., Goldstein, D., & Toppino, T. (1977). “Frequency and the Conference of Referential Validity.” Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 16(1), 107–112
    The founding demonstration of the effect.
    StrengthSame participants judged the same statements on three occasions spaced two weeks apart, a true longitudinal setup. Belief that a statement was true climbed with repeated exposure across those weeks. A single sitting would miss that climb.
    WeaknessThe materials were plausible trivia, without personal or political stakes. Later work had to test whether motivated belief or disbelief changes the size of the effect.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“As can be seen from Table 2, the average rating assigned to repeated statements increased across successive sessions, while the rating assigned to nonrepeated statements diminished slightly.”
    Verbatim“The increase in validity ratings with repetition was equivalent for true and for false statements, despite the fact that subjects succeeded in discriminating between them.”
    Also worth citing: Fazio, L. K., Brashier, N. M., Payne, B. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2015), “Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth,” Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, found the effect persists even for statements people could correctly identify as false based on their own prior knowledge, showing repetition can override what someone already knows.
    30

    Illusion of Control

    Why do people blow on dice or pick their own lottery numbers?

    People behave as if they can steer outcomes that are random or already fixed, and that belief can last indefinitely when nothing ever corrects it.

    ›
    Likely mechanismSkill cues misapplied to chance outcomes

    The psychology. In ordinary skill settings, involvement really does raise control, so the mind treats skill-like cues, choice, competition, involvement, familiarity, as a shortcut for inferring control even in pure chance. Add any of those cues to a random process and confidence in influencing the outcome rises, with no change in the odds.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    In ordinary skill settings, involvement really does raise control, so the mind treats skill-like cues, choice, competition, involvement, familiarity, as a shortcut for inferring control even in pure chance. Add any of those cues to a random process and confidence in influencing the outcome rises, with no change in the odds.

    Where it causes errors

    People keep believing an action still matters, a button, a ritual, a specific strategy, long after it stopped doing anything, or never did. Nothing forces a direct test of the belief.

    Where it can help

    There is little ethical upside to manufacturing this illusion in others on purpose. The useful move runs the other way: noticing where someone might be pressing a metaphorical dead crosswalk button. Checking a phone repeatedly, refreshing a page, a superstitious pre-decision ritual: test whether the action actually changes anything.

    Langer, E. J. (1975). “The Illusion of Control.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(2), 311–328
    The foundational series of studies.
    StrengthControlled experiments changed one skill-like cue at a time inside otherwise pure-chance games: choosing a ticket number, facing a weak versus strong opponent, familiarity with the materials. That isolates which cues inflate confidence.
    WeaknessFive of six studies ran in workplaces or at a public racetrack, outside a lab. Stakes stayed modest (a few dollars per ticket), aside from one genuine $2,000 scholarship. Separate work still had to check whether the illusion is as large for life-changing financial or health decisions.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“The mean amount of money required for the subject to sell his ticket was $8.67 in the choice condition and only $1.96 in the no-choice condition.”
    Verbatim“This illusion may be induced by introducing competition, choice, stimulus or response familiarity, or passive or active involvement into a chance situation. When these factors are present, people are more confident and are more likely to take risks.”
    Also worth citing: New York City deactivated roughly three-quarters of its pedestrian crosswalk buttons starting in the 2000s without telling the public, many kept being pressed for years, an illusion of control persisting purely because it was never corrected (reported by the New York Times, 2004; discussed in Stuart Vyse's The Uses of Delusion, 2022).
    31

    Hindsight Bias

    Why does every crisis look obvious in hindsight, right after it happens?

    Once the outcome is known, it feels as if people basically saw it coming, even on questions that were genuinely uncertain beforehand.

    ›
    Likely mechanismMemory of prior uncertainty reconstructed after the fact

    The psychology. New outcome information does not simply sit beside prior beliefs in memory. It reshapes the memory of what people believed before, shrinking how large past uncertainty felt. They are not inventing a false prediction; their memory of earlier uncertainty has been edited without them noticing.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    New outcome information does not simply sit beside prior beliefs in memory. It reshapes the memory of what people believed before, shrinking how large past uncertainty felt. They are not inventing a false prediction; their memory of earlier uncertainty has been edited without them noticing.

    Where it causes errors

    A decision that was reasonable given what was known at the time gets judged as careless or obvious once the result is in (“how did nobody see this coming”). That discourages honest post-mortems and can punish sound decision-making that simply drew a bad outcome.

    Where it can help

    Write down predictions, confidence levels, and reasoning before the outcome is known, then review that written record afterward instead of relying on memory. That is the direct, low-cost countermeasure, and standard practice in well-run forecasting and decision-review processes.

    Fischhoff, B. (1975). “Hindsight ≠ Foresight: The Effect of Outcome Knowledge on Judgment Under Uncertainty.” Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 1(3), 288–299
    The founding paper, still the standard citation fifty years on.
    StrengthUsing real historical events described ahead of time, the design compared what people claimed they would have predicted with the forecasts they had actually made. Measuring both sides of that gap is stronger than collecting only after-the-fact confidence.
    WeaknessPrior beliefs were self-reported under experimental instruction, reconstructed after the fact. Later prospective designs recorded what people believed before the study began, closing that gap.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“In each of the 24 cases, reporting an outcome increased its perceived likelihood of occurrence.”
    Verbatim“Experiment 2 has shown that subjects are either unaware of outcome knowledge having an effect on their perceptions or, if aware, they are unable to ignore or rescind that effect.”
    32

    Survivorship Bias

    Why did WWII engineers almost armour the wrong part of the returning bombers?

    Looking only at survivors of a selection process, the funds that did not collapse, the planes that made it home, the founders who succeeded, yields a systematically warped picture. The failures that would correct it never show up.

    ›
    Likely mechanismNon-random sample created by invisible failures

    The psychology. This is less an active illusion than a data-collection blind spot. When failures also vanish from view, whatever remains is, by definition, a non-random and misleading sample. The mind treats a vivid, available set of examples as representative, without checking whether a whole class of counter-examples was ever visible.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    This is less an active illusion than a data-collection blind spot. When failures also vanish from view, whatever remains is, by definition, a non-random and misleading sample. The mind treats a vivid, available set of examples as representative, without checking whether a whole class of counter-examples was ever visible.

    Where it causes errors

    Studying only successful companies, funds, or people to extract “lessons for success” routinely yields confident advice that merely describes what survivors happened to share. Those same traits often show up just as often among the failures nobody studied, because those cases did not survive to be studied.

    Where it can help

    Actively hunt the missing failure data before drawing a conclusion: the funds that closed, the products that were discontinued, the applicants who were rejected. That is exactly the move that made Wald's WWII analysis correct where the intuitive version ran backwards.

    Mangel, M., & Samaniego, F. J. (1984). “Abraham Wald’s Work on Aircraft Survivability.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(386), 259–267
    The paper that reconstructs and formalises Wald's original wartime reasoning.
    StrengthRebuilds Wald's statistical method from his original wartime reports. The reconstruction recovers the real mathematics behind the well-known conclusion to “armour the parts with no bullet holes.” The popularised retelling leaves that out.
    WeaknessThe piece is a historical and methodological reconstruction of a WWII analysis. Wald's original military data and reasoning carry the evidentiary weight, and they were never built as a public, replicable dataset.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedWald recognised that damage data collected only from planes that returned from combat systematically excluded the planes that didn't return, and that the correct conclusion was to reinforce the areas showing the least damage on survivors, since planes hit in the heavily-damaged areas were the ones not coming back.
    Verbatim“Wald's methods were used in World War II and by the Navy and Air Force during the wars in Korea and Vietnam.”
    33

    Take-the-Best Heuristic (Less-Is-More)

    Why does one strong cue sometimes beat a model that weighs every input?

    A simple rule built on one strong piece of information can out-predict a complicated model that tries to weigh everything. More inputs are not always more accurate.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA simple rule can predict better than a complex one, because it isn't fooled by noise in the data

    The psychology. Complex models fit their training data well but can overfit, absorbing noise along with signal. A simple “take the best single cue and stop” rule uses less information, so it is less exposed to that noise. Under real uncertainty, the simpler rule can generalise better precisely because it asks less of the data.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Complex models fit their training data well but can overfit, absorbing noise along with signal. A simple “take the best single cue and stop” rule uses less information, so it is less exposed to that noise. Under real uncertainty, the simpler rule can generalise better precisely because it asks less of the data.

    Where it causes errors

    Assuming a more complex decision process will always beat a simple one leads people to distrust genuinely good simple heuristics. It also leads them to build overengineered processes that underperform a well-chosen simple rule, especially in noisy real-world conditions.

    Where it can help

    Where information is genuinely limited or noisy, pick the single most predictive cue and build the decision rule around it. That can be easier to use and more accurate than weighing a dozen partly reliable inputs. That approach stands on its own rather than splitting the difference with a heavier model.

    Gigerenzer, G., & Goldstein, D. G. (1996). “Reasoning the Fast and Frugal Way: Models of Bounded Rationality.” Psychological Review, 103(4), 650–669
    The foundational paper on fast-and-frugal heuristics.
    StrengthThe simple Take-the-Best algorithm faced five other statistical models, including full multiple regression, in roughly 858 million simulated head-to-head comparisons. The comparisons used one real dataset: populations of Germany's 83 largest cities.
    WeaknessThe domain was unusually tidy (city populations, which the nine cues predict well), and the choosers were simulated. Multiple regression got every advantage: true population figures and individually optimised weights for each case. Its tie with Take-the-Best is striking for that reason, though the result is still one demonstration in one environment.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“The Take The Best algorithm matched or outperformed all competitors in inferential speed and accuracy.”
    ParaphrasedThe advantage traced to the recognition principle. Models that folded every cue, including recognition, into one weighted sum sometimes ranked an unfamiliar city above a familiar one, simply because the familiar city carried more negative cue values on record. Take-the-Best and simple tallying let recognition act as its own single cue and avoided that mistake. That is also why every algorithm's accuracy peaked partway through learning, when a person recognized some cities but not all eighty-three, exactly the paper's less-is-more effect.
    34

    Choice Bracketing (Diversification Bias)

    Why do snack picks differ when choosing for the whole week at once versus one day at a time?

    Choosing once for a whole set of future decisions yields different picks than making each decision fresh, one at a time. Same options, different outcome, driven only by how the choices are grouped.

    ›
    Likely mechanismChoosing several things at once favours variety; choosing them one at a time repeats the favourite

    The psychology. When several choices are considered together (bracketed broadly), the mind treats them as ingredients in a varied whole and reaches for contrast, which pushes toward more variety. When the same choices are made one at a time (bracketed narrowly), each decision is judged on its own immediate merits, usually the same favourite, repeated.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    When several choices are considered together (bracketed broadly), the mind treats them as ingredients in a varied whole and reaches for contrast, which pushes toward more variety. When the same choices are made one at a time (bracketed narrowly), each decision is judged on its own immediate merits, usually the same favourite, repeated.

    Where it causes errors

    Picking a week's snacks or meals in advance reliably produces more variety than most people want in the moment they eat each one. The future self, bracketed broadly, wants variety in the abstract. The present self, choosing once, usually just wants the thing it likes.

    Where it can help

    Choose which bracket fits the decision on purpose. Commit in advance to one simple pick for a recurring choice that does not benefit from variety. Leave room for in-the-moment choice where variety and mood genuinely matter. That steers around the mismatch instead of falling into it by default.

    Read, D., & Loewenstein, G. (1995). “Diversification Bias: Explaining the Discrepancy in Variety Seeking Between Combined and Separated Choices.” Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 1(1), 34–49
    The paper that names diversification bias and identifies choice bracketing as one of its causes.
    StrengthSeveral rival accounts, including satiation and simple utility-maximising logic, were tested and discarded before choice bracketing and time-contraction remained as the mechanisms. The paper works by elimination across that sequence.
    WeaknessThe experiments use low-stakes, easily repeated consumption choices such as snacks and soft drinks. Separate work still had to check whether the same bracketing pattern holds for larger, less frequent decisions.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“If people make combined choices of quantities of goods for future consumption, they choose more variety than if they make separate choices immediately preceding consumption.”
    Verbatim“All 13 children in the combined choice condition chose two different candy bars, compared with only 48% (12 of 25) in the separate choice condition.”
    35

    The Precision Effect

    Why does $21,947 sound more like a real number than $22,000?

    A precise number ($21,947) and a round one ($22,000) trigger different reactions in a negotiation, and precision doesn't always help: it can make a novice seem more credible, but make an expert seem less competent.

    ›
    Likely mechanismPrecision read as a competence signal, until it isn't

    The psychology. A precise number implies the person behind it did real, careful work to arrive at it, a useful signal when the audience assumes competence is genuine. Among experts who know the domain, an unusually precise number can instead read as artificial confidence, or the tell of someone padding a number to look rigorous rather than actually being so. The same signal flips from a credibility boost into a credibility cost.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A precise number implies the person behind it did real, careful work to arrive at it, a useful signal when the audience assumes competence is genuine. Among experts who know the domain, an unusually precise number can instead read as artificial confidence, or the tell of someone padding a number to look rigorous rather than actually being so. The same signal flips from a credibility boost into a credibility cost.

    Where it causes errors

    Assuming more precision always signals more credibility can badly misfire when negotiating with someone who actually knows the domain. An experienced negotiator on the other side of the table may read your carefully-precise opening figure as overcompensation, not rigor.

    Where it can help

    Matching the precision of a number to the actual sophistication of the audience uses the same finding honestly rather than by accident. Use more precision for people who'll take it as a genuine effort signal. Use rounder figures, or precise ones that are explicitly justified, for experts who might otherwise read excess precision as posturing.

    Loschelder, D. D., Friese, M., Schaerer, M., & Galinsky, A. D. (2016). “The Too-Much-Precision Effect: When and Why Precise Anchors Backfire With Experts.” Psychological Science, 27(12), 1573–1587
    Five experiments, 1,320 participants including real professional negotiators.
    StrengthFive experiments covered real professional domains (real estate, jewellery, car sales, human resources) with 1,320 participants in total, including working domain experts alongside students. That spread gives the finding breadth across contexts.
    WeaknessExperiments 1 and 2 compared professional groups (real-estate agents and jewellers versus people with no negotiation experience) without randomly assigning expertise. Other group differences could therefore explain part of the gap. Experiment 4 anticipated that worry by comparing car salespeople with mechanics who share product knowledge but differ in negotiation experience. The same pattern appeared. That narrows the concern for the real-estate and jewellery findings without fully closing it.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“For amateurs, WTP and counteroffers increased linearly with precision of the first offer. For experts, WTP and counteroffers increased with precision only up to a point, after which greater precision backfired.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Anchor precision backfired because experts saw too much precision as reflecting a lack of competence.”
    See also: Left Digit Bias, related but different: that's about which digit in a number dominates how it's read; this is about what a number's overall precision signals about the person offering it.
    36

    Default Effect

    Why can changing one checkbox move a country's organ donation rate from 4% to 99%?

    The pre-selected option wins far more often than the same option wins when people must actively choose it. That gap holds even when the switch would take seconds and nothing blocks the change.

    ›
    Likely mechanismStaying with the default feels safer, easier, and like the recommended choice

    The psychology. A default needs no decision, so several forces stack behind it. It reads as an implied recommendation. It skips the small cost of choosing. It also skips the chance of regretting an active pick that turns out worse. Those pressures favour staying put even when switching is easy.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A default needs no decision, so several forces stack behind it. It reads as an implied recommendation. It skips the small cost of choosing. It also skips the chance of regretting an active pick that turns out worse. Those pressures favour staying put even when switching is easy.

    Where it causes errors

    People remain on a randomly assigned default even when it fits them poorly and switching costs only a little effort and attention. The pull of the default survives experiments built to rule out every other plausible reason for staying.

    Where it can help

    The same mechanism has a clear constructive use. Make the default the option that serves most people best (retirement auto-enrolment, organ-donor registration) and outcomes improve while anyone can still opt out.

    Brot-Goldberg, Z. C., Layton, T. J., Vabson, B., & Wang, A. Y. (2023). “The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D.” American Economic Review, 113(10), 2718–2758
    A genuine natural experiment using randomly-assigned real defaults.
    StrengthThe paper uses a real natural experiment: new low-income Medicare beneficiaries receive a government-assigned default prescription drug plan at random. The default itself is randomly assigned in a high-stakes setting.
    WeaknessThe sample is low-income Medicare beneficiaries in a subsidised programme, a group that may face particular attention or capacity constraints. Separate confirmation was still needed for higher-resource populations facing other kinds of defaults.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“We estimate that when a beneficiary’s default is exogenously changed from one year to the next, 96% of beneficiaries follow that default.”
    Verbatim“These results provide strong evidence that consumers follow defaults in this market, no matter what that default may be, and largely reject the hypothesis that the high levels of choice persistence in this program are explained by consumers actively choosing to remain in their plans in order to avoid real switching costs.”
    See also: Smart Defaults, the deliberate version of the same lever. This principle is about the power of whatever's pre-selected, passive by default; that one is about choosing when a default takes effect and what it's measured against, so it works with someone's biases instead of against them.
    See also: Every Default Decides Who Pays for Doing Nothing, a full report placing this principle on a wider spectrum: forced choice, opt-in, opt-out, timed defaults, and personalised defaults, each with its own real study and its own honest catch.
    37

    Mental Accounting

    Why does the same $20 feel different when it was found rather than earned?

    People file money into separate mental accounts by source or purpose (a windfall, a grocery budget, a ticket already paid). A dollar in one account feels worth less than the identical dollar in another.

    ›
    Likely mechanismMoney gets mentally sorted into separate buckets, even though it all spends the same

    The psychology. Textbook economics treats money as fungible: a dollar is a dollar wherever it came from. Real budgets work differently. Money gets sorted by source (bonus versus paycheck) or intended use (rent versus entertainment). Those category walls change how freely it gets spent, even when shifting dollars across categories would leave someone better off.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Textbook economics treats money as fungible: a dollar is a dollar wherever it came from. Real budgets work differently. Money gets sorted by source (bonus versus paycheck) or intended use (rent versus entertainment). Those category walls change how freely it gets spent, even when shifting dollars across categories would leave someone better off.

    Where it causes errors

    The everyday version: carrying high-interest credit card debt while cash sits in a low-interest savings account. “Savings” and “debt repayment” stay in separate mental accounts and never get netted, even though the arithmetic favouring repayment is obvious.

    Where it can help

    Used on purpose, that partitioning is a savings tool. Putting money for a house deposit or emergency fund in a separate, named account makes raiding it for everyday spend feel harder. The person builds the commitment themselves; it is a concrete form of the wider lever in Precommitment Devices.

    Spotted in the wild

    A sharper version of the same mental account, live on Up's own app: not a named balance, a photo of the actual thing.

    Up Bank, Maybuys. Saving towards a photo of the actual product, imported straight from a listing, not just a named balance like “Home Deposit” or “Holiday.”

    Full decode: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers? Money filed against a real, pictured thing is harder to casually spend than money sitting in an unlabelled balance.

    Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1984). “Choices, Values, and Frames.” American Psychologist, 39(4), 341–350
    Two independent samples, surveyed with one-sentence changes to which mental account a $10 loss was charged to.
    Experiment Teardown
    383 respondents, two independent samples
    Only which mental account the $10 loss was charged to differed
    Lost the ticket
    A $10 ticket, already bought, is lost before entering
    Lost the cash
    $10 in cash is lost before any ticket is bought
    Result Ticket Cash Swing
    Would still buy 46% → 88% +42

    The identical $10 loss, filed under a different mental account, nearly doubled people's willingness to spend. Losing the ticket felt like overspending on “the theatre”; losing the equivalent cash didn't touch that account at all.

    Internal validityThe headline 46%/88% contrast came from two large independent samples (n=200 and n=183) randomly assigned, between subjects, to one framing or the other. When the same respondents later saw both versions, the ticket answer moved after the cash version came first, and the reverse order did not produce that shift. That pattern is evidence people treated the two scenarios as connected once they could compare them.
    External validityThe vignette was hypothetical; no real money was at stake, a real limit of this particular study. Later work has since found the same asymmetry when the money was real.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedRespondents told they'd lost the $10 theatre ticket itself were much less willing to pay $10 for a replacement than respondents told they'd lost an equivalent $10 bill on the way to the theatre, even though both groups faced an identical net cost.
    Verbatim“Buying a second ticket increases the cost of seeing the play to a level that many respondents apparently find unacceptable. In contrast, the loss of the cash is not posted to the account of the play, and it affects the purchase of a ticket only by making the individual feel slightly less affluent.”
    Also worth citing: Thaler, R. (1985). “Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice.” Marketing Science, 4(3), 199–214, the paper that formalised mental accounting into a full theoretical model, already cited on this site as the foundation for Pain of Paying.
    See also: Pain of Paying, a direct application of the same mental-accounting model to how payment method itself changes spending, and Payment Transparency, the separate mechanism (rehearsal and immediacy) that governs whether a payment gets tracked into any mental account at all.
    Tested as an experiment: Does naming a savings pocket keep the money there?, a live-product test of this mechanism, built on the high school field session.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: Why does GoalSaver's 4.75% bonus feel like money you'd be losing, not money you haven't earned yet?, where a named, goal-labelled GoalSaver balance is the real, everyday version of a separate mental account.
    Also decoded on The Science Behind: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers?, where Up's Maybuys saves towards a photo of the actual product a customer wants, not just a labelled balance.
    38

    Endowment Effect

    Why does owning a mug, even briefly, make people demand more money to give it up?

    Brief ownership raises how much someone values an item. Sellers ask more to part with it than they would have paid to buy the identical thing as a non-owner.

    ›
    Likely mechanismOwning something makes giving it up feel like a loss, which looms larger than an equivalent gain

    The psychology. Loss aversion attaches to ownership. Giving up what someone already holds registers as a loss, and losses sting more than matched gains feel good. That lifts the minimum selling price above what a neutral buyer would pay for the same object. The gap comes from which side of the trade the person sits on.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Loss aversion attaches to ownership. Giving up what someone already holds registers as a loss, and losses sting more than matched gains feel good. That lifts the minimum selling price above what a neutral buyer would pay for the same object. The gap comes from which side of the trade the person sits on.

    Where it causes errors

    Free trials and generous return windows lean on this. After two weeks in the house, sending the product back feels like a loss. Perceived value rises past what the person would have paid cold, and people keep (and pay for) things they would never have bought from scratch.

    Where it can help

    A genuine no-obligation trial still has an informational use: people can check real fit before committing. Naming the bias personally also helps. Asking whether they would buy the item today, at this price, if they did not already own it cuts through the ownership pull when deciding to sell, renew, or keep.

    Spotted in the wild

    NRMA's member magazine, Open Road, is exactly the kind of object this principle predicts people would rather hold onto than scroll past.

    NRMA, Open Road magazine, Spring 2026 issue: cover story “Australia in Bloom: Four Spectacular Wildflower Road Trips,” plus a “Best Value Car Awards” sidebar. Photographed August 2026.

    NRMA keeps printing and mailing this instead of moving to digital-only, consistent with a physical copy carrying the ownership pull this principle describes. That's a real company's ongoing choice, not a controlled test of the endowment effect itself. Full case: Printing costs more than digital. The paper copy still wins.

    Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., & Thaler, R. H. (1990). “Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem.” Journal of Political Economy, 98(6), 1325–1348
    The classic Cornell coffee-mug experiment, replicated across several trials within the same paper.
    StrengthReal goods and real money, with random assignment to seller, buyer, or chooser roles. The core comparison ran across several independent trials with different objects (mugs, pens, chocolate).
    WeaknessThe exact reservation-price gap moved around across the paper's replications. What holds up is the direction and rough size: sellers demand roughly twice what buyers offer. The finding does not hang on one precise dollar figure.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“The median selling prices in the mug and pen markets were more than twice the median buying prices.”
    Verbatim“The close similarity of results for buyers and choosers indicates that there was relatively little reluctance to pay for the mug.”
    See also: Loss Aversion, the general asymmetry this is a specific case of: giving something up is felt more sharply than gaining the identical thing, ownership or not. Also Mental Accounting and IKEA Effect, the same family, applied to how money and self-made objects get valued.
    39

    IKEA Effect

    Why does a wobbly shelf someone built beat a better store-bought one in their own ranking?

    Building or partly creating something raises how much people value the finished result relative to an identical item they never touched. Labour itself creates attachment, separate from how good the result is.

    ›
    Likely mechanismPutting in the effort makes the finished result feel more valuable than it objectively is

    The psychology. Effort invested becomes a cue of value through self-signalling. Finishing a task produces a sense of authorship and competence. That feeling folds into how the finished object looks: pride in the process, plus an inflated read of the product's quality.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Effort invested becomes a cue of value through self-signalling. Finishing a task produces a sense of authorship and competence. That feeling folds into how the finished object looks: pride in the process, plus an inflated read of the product's quality.

    Where it causes errors

    A business can shift real assembly or setup onto the customer under the banner of “customisation,” at full price. The customer then defends and overvalues the result because they did the labour, regardless of whether the product improved.

    Where it can help

    Letting customers customise or assemble part of a product (a meal kit, a build-your-own bundle) can produce real satisfaction and a better sense of fit. That holds when the labour is optional and clearly does not stand in for a fair price.

    Norton, M. I., Mochon, D., & Ariely, D. (2012). “The IKEA Effect: When Labor Leads to Love.” Journal of Consumer Psychology, 22(3), 453–460
    Four studies, IKEA boxes, origami, and Lego sets, testing where the effect holds and where it breaks.
    StrengthFour different build tasks checked that the effect was not tied to one object type. A key boundary condition: elevated valuation vanished when the creation was destroyed or left incomplete, so successful completion drives the result more than effort alone.
    WeaknessValuations were self-reported liking and willingness-to-pay for low-stakes household objects, in the lab or online. Expensive or high-stakes purchases were outside the design.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Builders reporting greater liking (M = 3.81, SD = 1.56) than non-builders (M = 2.50, SD = 1.03), t(50) = 3.58, p < .001.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Our account suggests that labor leads to increased valuation only when labor results in successful completion of tasks; thus when participants built and then destroyed their creations, or failed to complete them, the IKEA effect dissipated.”
    Also worth citing: Ling, I.-L., Liu, Y.-F., Lin, C.-W., & Shieh, C.-H. (2020). “Exploring IKEA Effect in Self-Expressive Mass Customization: Underlying Mechanism and Boundary Conditions.” Journal of Consumer Marketing, 37(4), 365–374. Extends the original assembly-based finding to design-choice customisation tools specifically: offering more real choice in a customisation toolkit gave shoppers more room for self-expression, which in turn raised how much they valued the finished product.
    See also: Endowment Effect, related but distinct: that's valuation inflated by mere ownership; this is valuation inflated specifically by the labour of creating something.
    40

    Ostrich Effect

    Why do people stop checking a bank balance exactly when checking would help most?

    People skip information that might be bad news (an account balance, a bill, a test result) even though looking changes only awareness, not the underlying fact.

    ›
    Likely mechanismInformation avoidance to dodge anticipated negative emotion

    The psychology. The expected sting of confirming bad news is unpleasant enough that avoiding the information becomes a coping move, even when the data is free and actionable. Short-term emotional relief trades off against worse decisions, because ignorance does not stop the problem from growing.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    The expected sting of confirming bad news is unpleasant enough that avoiding the information becomes a coping move, even when the data is free and actionable. Short-term emotional relief trades off against worse decisions, because ignorance does not stop the problem from growing.

    Where it causes errors

    Investors who stop opening their portfolio in a downturn miss the chance to rebalance or cut losses. Someone who never opens a subscription's usage-versus-cost page keeps paying for something no longer worth it, because checking would confirm what they already suspect.

    Where it can help

    Products that surface bad news calmly, without requiring the user to go looking, route around the ostrich effect. A bank that sends a gentle “your balance is lower than usual” nudge does the checking the person would otherwise skip.

    Karlsson, N., Loewenstein, G., & Seppi, D. (2009). “The Ostrich Effect: Selective Attention to Information.” Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 38(2), 95–115
    Real brokerage and retirement-account login records from Scandinavian and American investors.
    StrengthActual account-login records from two independent datasets in different markets. The measure tracks what investors did with their accounts.
    WeaknessThe paper reports a regression coefficient, not a single before-and-after percentage. In the Vanguard data, a 1 percentage point rise in the prior four-day return linked to 18,000 to 23,000 extra daily logins, about 5 to 6% of the daily average. That is a precise effect size without collapsing into one tidy “X% more likely to check” headline.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“In both datasets, investors monitor their portfolios more frequently in rising markets than when markets are flat or falling.”
    ParaphrasedThe pattern held across two independent datasets, Scandinavian and American investors, suggesting it isn't specific to one brokerage platform or one market.
    41

    Order Effect

    Why does “smart, then difficult” leave a different impression from “difficult, then smart”?

    The same facts about a person or product, listed in a different order, produce a different overall impression. Whatever arrives first shapes how later details get read.

    ›
    Likely mechanismEarly information anchors how later information gets read

    The psychology. Early information builds a first hypothesis about a person or thing. Later details get interpreted through that frame instead of being weighed evenly. The same fact lands differently depending on whether it fits or complicates the story already underway.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Early information builds a first hypothesis about a person or thing. Later details get interpreted through that frame instead of being weighed evenly. The same fact lands differently depending on whether it fits or complicates the story already underway.

    Where it causes errors

    A performance review that opens with weaknesses before strengths leaves a more negative overall impression than the identical content in reverse order. Neither version lies, but the read differs. That is why the “compliment sandwich” exists as a workaround.

    Where it can help

    Leading with the most decision-relevant, honestly earned positive information, when that is the right place to start, can stop an unfairly negative first impression from colouring the whole evaluation. Later facts still appear; they are not hidden or spun.

    Asch, S. E. (1946). “Forming Impressions of Personality.” Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 41(3), 258–290
    The founding demonstration that reordering identical facts changes the overall impression they create.
    StrengthAmong the earliest controlled demonstrations that identical factual content, only reordered, shifts a global impression of a person. The change lands on the overall evaluative read as well as on which details people remember.
    WeaknessThe original method used short, decontextualised adjective lists read aloud, far from a real conversation or review. Later replications of this paradigm find a smaller, more context-dependent effect size than the 1946 results suggested.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“The impression produced by A is predominantly that of an able person who possesses certain shortcomings which do not, however, overshadow his merits. On the other hand, B impresses the majority as a ‘problem,’ whose abilities are hampered by his serious difficulties.”
    ParaphrasedOn the specific trait “happy,” 32% of participants who heard the positive-first ordering later described the person that way, versus only 5% of participants who heard the identical traits in negative-first order.
    See also: Ordering Effects, related but different: that's about which item gets selected from a set by its position in it; this is about how information order changes the judgement of a single target.
    42

    Shooting the Messenger

    Why does the doctor who delivers a diagnosis absorb blame that belongs to the disease?

    Bearers of bad news get judged more harshly: less likeable, less trustworthy, even when everyone agrees they did not cause the news.

    ›
    Likely mechanismBad news creates a bad feeling, and that feeling gets pinned on whoever delivered it

    The psychology. Bad news creates an unpleasant emotional state. That feeling gets misattributed onto whoever is socially linked to delivering it. Blame slides from the news onto its bearer, even when the bearer's innocence is explicit and known.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Bad news creates an unpleasant emotional state. That feeling gets misattributed onto whoever is socially linked to delivering it. Blame slides from the news onto its bearer, even when the bearer's innocence is explicit and known.

    Where it causes errors

    A support agent, doctor, or manager who has to relay unwelcome news (a delay, a diagnosis, a rejection) absorbs a likability penalty they did not earn. That can push people to delay or avoid necessary bad news, so the recipient finds out later and in worse shape.

    Where it can help

    The same research found the penalty shrinks when a messenger signals benevolent intent. Framing bad news around genuine care (“I'm telling you now because I think you'd want to know”) softens an unfair reaction without rewriting the news itself.

    John, L. K., Blunden, H., & Liu, H. (2019). “Shooting the Messenger.” Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 148(4), 644–666
    Eleven experiments testing whether innocent messengers of bad news get penalised, and why.
