    StrengthFive studies plus field donation data, covering gambling, effort, giving, and purchasing, converge on one mechanism. The pattern survived designs built to kill simpler accounts: no prize for finishing the set, a real cost to complete it, and an explicit statement that the grouping was arbitrary.
    WeaknessStudy 1, the cleanest quantified contrast, is still a nickel-stakes lab gamble. Generalisation beyond coin-flip play rests on the remaining four studies and the field donation evidence. There is no single large field trial here that reports a hard revenue figure.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Significantly more participants in the pseudo-set condition accepted all four gambles (29%) than in the control condition (16%).”
    Verbatim (abstract)“These effects persist in the absence of any reward, when a cost must be incurred, and after participants are explicitly informed of the arbitrariness of the set.”
    See also: Goal Gradient Effect, a related but distinct completion pull: that one is about accelerating as the real distance to a goal shrinks, this one is about a group feeling incomplete regardless of distance, based only on how it's framed.
    61

    Smart Defaults (Save More Tomorrow)

    Why would someone refuse a pay cut today, then agree to save more from a raise that had not arrived?

    A savings default timed so the increase arrives with a future raise. Accepting it costs nothing that shows up in today’s take-home pay.

    ›
    Likely mechanismCommitting today to a raise you haven't got yet means the increase never has to feel like a loss

    The psychology. Three biases usually block higher saving. Present bias makes a felt cut in today’s pay outweigh a benefit decades out. Loss aversion makes that cut sting more than a matching future gain would please. Inertia then holds whatever rate is already set. Save More Tomorrow steps around all three in one design.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Three biases usually block higher saving. Present bias makes a felt cut in today’s pay outweigh a benefit decades out. Loss aversion makes that cut sting more than a matching future gain would please. Inertia then holds whatever rate is already set.

    Save More Tomorrow steps around all three in one design. People commit now; the increase waits for a future, already-scheduled raise, so today’s paycheck does not move and present bias has nothing to fight. The raise still lands; only a slice is redirected, so take-home pay keeps rising and no loss registers. Once enrolled, the same inertia that once locked in a low rate now locks in a rising one.

    Where it causes errors

    The design dodges a felt pay cut only when escalation rides on a real raise. Many auto-escalation programmes bump the contribution rate on a fixed calendar date instead. That bump can land in a year when pay did not rise.

    In a pay freeze, or when a raise lags inflation, the automatic bump becomes the felt cut the original design was built to avoid. The same inertia that once protected a rising savings rate then protects a shrinking paycheck nobody chose to shrink. Retirement-industry guidance on 401(k) auto-escalation is blunt: tie the increase to an actual raise, or the mechanism becomes the loss it was meant to prevent.

    Where it can help

    Run as designed, this remains one of the most consequential nudges in the field. At the manufacturer where it was first tested, employees who joined moved average savings from 3.5% of pay to 13.6% across four raises, about 40 months. None of that rise registered as a pay cut. Opt-out stayed open at every raise, and some people used it. The decision moved earlier: made today about a raise still in the future, rather than at the raise itself, when loss aversion is primed to fight the change.

    Thaler, R. H., & Benartzi, S. (2004). “Save More Tomorrow™: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving.” Journal of Political Economy, 112(S1), 164–187
    A real field intervention inside one mid-size manufacturer's actual payroll and 401(k) system, tracked across four real pay raises.
    StrengthThis was a live payroll intervention: real deductions, followed through four actual pay raises over about 40 months at one employer. It is neither a lab task nor a stated-intention survey.
    WeaknessWorkers who entered SMarT had already cleared two filters: they were still below the recommended saving rate, and they had refused an immediate contribution hike. That twice-selected group may have been unusually open to a delayed, painless version of the same request. The paper does not test the design on a workforce that never saw the harder first ask.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedOf 162 employees who had just declined an immediate increase to their contribution rate, 78% agreed to the SMarT plan instead: an increase timed to their next four pay raises, capped at 14% of pay.
    ParaphrasedEmployees who joined raised their average savings rate from 3.5% to 13.6% of pay over the course of four raises, roughly 40 months, and 78% of those who joined were still enrolled by the fourth raise.
    A note on sourcing: the published paper sat behind this site's network restrictions, so both findings above are paraphrased from the abstract and secondary academic summaries, not quoted verbatim.
    See also: Default Effect, the passive version of the same lever. That principle is about the power of whatever's pre-selected; this one is about when and against what a default gets set, so it works with someone's biases instead of against them.
    See also: Good Friction, which removes friction from the enrolment step itself, a single “yes” to join. Smart Defaults is a different lever: not how hard the decision is to make, but when it's made and what it's measured against.
    See also: Every Default Decides Who Pays for Doing Nothing, a full report placing this timed default on a wider spectrum alongside forced choice, opt-in, opt-out, and personalised defaults.
    Also worth reading: The Biases Draining Your Super Could Also Fill It, where Australia's legislated Superannuation Guarantee increases and MySuper's lifecycle investment defaults apply this exact logic to retirement savings.
    62

    Precommitment Devices (the Ulysses Contract)

    Why would people freely choose their own deadline, then pick an earlier date that fines them if they miss it?

    A constraint someone accepts today on their own later choices, so a future self with thinner willpower cannot casually undo the plan.

    ›
    Likely mechanismAnticipating a future lapse in willpower, people pay a real cost now to remove the tempting choice later

    The psychology. People are time-inconsistent: the planner today weighs the future differently from the person who must live the plan later. Present bias makes near-term comfort loom larger than a cost or benefit weeks away. Plans that lean only on willpower keep losing to whoever shows up on the day. A precommitment device moves the cost forward. It locks in a felt consequence now, so the future self inherits a constraint rather than a fresh open choice.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    People are time-inconsistent: the planner today weighs the future differently from the person who must live the plan later. Present bias makes near-term comfort (skipping the gym, delaying the assignment) loom larger than a cost or benefit weeks away. Plans that lean only on willpower keep losing to whoever shows up on the day.

    A precommitment device moves the cost forward. Rather than trusting a future self to pick the harder option, it locks in a felt consequence now: a forfeited deposit, a public pledge, a deadline with a grade penalty. The future self inherits a constraint rather than an open choice.

    Where it causes errors

    The device binds only when the cost is real and the timing is right, and people misjudge their future selves on both. Commitment-contract tools like StickK let someone pledge money to a cause they would hate funding if they miss a goal. Those tools work under one condition: the stake and the deadline must be as strict as an outsider would set them.

    Left to design their own constraint, people often set stakes too low or park deadlines too near the finish to bind. The same optimism about later self-control that fed the procrastination then softens the device meant to fix it.

    Where it can help

    Used well, this is one of the few self-directed levers on the site. An earmarked savings account named for a real goal works. So does a habit-app subscription with a real financial stake, or a costly public deadline on a piece of work. Each one works by giving a future self less room to slide.

    Nobody else has to be deceived. The person who sets the constraint and the person bound by it are the same person, choosing in advance to make the easier path harder to take.

    Ariely, D., & Wertenbroch, K. (2002). “Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment.” Psychological Science, 13(3), 219–224
    A real MIT Sloan executive-education class turning in graded term papers, paired with a controlled lab experiment paying real participants to proofread for real errors.
    StrengthThe result appears in two places. One is a live class with real grades and a real 1%-per-day late penalty. The other is a randomised lab experiment that puts the same three deadline structures under paid incentives. The claim therefore rests on both uncontrolled field evidence and a controlled lab isolation.
    WeaknessHyndman and Bisin's 2026 direct replication of the controlled lab half, with a different real subject pool, found a negligible effect of deadline structure on the same performance measures. That result puts real pressure on how far that half of the original finding travels.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“The grades in the no-choice section (M = 88.76) were higher than the grades in the free-choice section (M = 85.67), t(97) = 3.03, p = .003.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“People have self-control problems, they recognize them, and they try to control them by self-imposing costly deadlines. These deadlines help people control procrastination, but they are not as effective as some externally imposed deadlines in improving task performance.”
    ParaphrasedA 2026 direct replication of the same lab design, run with a different subject pool, found the deadline-structure manipulation had a negligible effect on the three original performance measures, and evenly spaced externally imposed deadlines did not stand out as more effective at reducing procrastination.
    A note on sourcing: Hyndman and Bisin's 2026 replication sat behind this site's network restrictions, so that finding above is paraphrased from its abstract and secondary academic summaries, not quoted verbatim. The original 2002 paper's findings above are now quoted directly from its full text.
    See also: Mental Accounting, whose earmarked savings account is one concrete, everyday version of this same lever.
    See also: The Credit Card Premium, where deliberately switching a temptation purchase to cash or debit is the same self-imposed constraint applied to a single spending decision.
    See also: Present Bias, the underlying reason this device is needed at all: the same person genuinely chooses differently once a reward becomes immediate, which is exactly what a precommitment device is built to route around.
    Also worth citing: Ashraf, N., Karlan, D., & Yin, W. (2006). “Tying Odysseus to the Mast: Evidence from a Commitment Savings Product in the Philippines.” Quarterly Journal of Economics, 121(2), 635–672, a randomised field trial of a real commitment savings account, restricting a client's own access to their money until a self-chosen goal or date. Average balances rose 81 percentage points more for the group offered the account than for a control group after twelve months, evidence this same lever works on money specifically, not only on deadlines.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: Why does GoalSaver's 4.75% bonus feel like money you'd be losing, not money you haven't earned yet?, where a bank's bonus-interest condition does the same job as a formal commitment account, without the paperwork.
    Also decoded on The Science Behind: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers?, where Locked Savers attaches a real 3-hour delay, plus an optional social cost, to a future withdrawal.
    63

    Crossmodal Correspondence (the coffee mug effect)

    Why did the same café latte taste sweeter in a blue mug than in a white one?

    Taste arrives as one blended experience. An unrelated touch or colour cue folds into how something is judged to taste, even when the substance itself is unchanged.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA touch or colour cue gets folded straight into the taste itself, not judged as a separate, later step

    The psychology. Flavour is not built from taste receptors alone. Sight, touch, sound, and smell combine with taste into one experience before conscious judgment starts. A cue from another sense can shift what someone reports tasting without ever registering as a separate influence. The error is one sense colouring another, which is a different problem from one belief colouring another belief.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Flavour is not built from taste receptors alone. Sight, touch, sound, and smell combine with taste into one experience before conscious judgment starts. A cue from another sense can shift what someone reports tasting without ever registering as a separate influence.

    The error is one sense colouring another, which is a different problem from one belief colouring another belief. That is why it is hard to correct: tasting more carefully cannot dodge a cue already folded into the taste itself.

    Where it causes errors

    Perceived quality can drop for reasons that have nothing to do with the product. Coffee in a flimsy-feeling cup can score lower than a chemically identical pour served differently. A snack in packaging whose colour clashes with the food can take the same hit. The substance stayed put. Only a cue in another sense moved.

    Where it can help

    Among principles on this list, this one is often benign, because the substance is real either way. A cup or package that accentuates a flavour already present, drawing attention to a coffee’s own sweetness rather than inventing one, amplifies something true. The line into manipulation is using the same cue to hide a real defect: stale or bitter product dressed in cues of freshness or sweetness it does not have.

    Van Doorn, G. H., Wuillemin, D., & Spence, C. (2014). “Does the Colour of the Mug Influence the Taste of the Coffee?” Flavour, 3, Article 10
    A real café latte, poured from the same jug, served to the same tasters in a white mug, a blue mug, and a clear glass.
    StrengthParticipants tasted a real beverage rather than a described or imagined one. Every cup was prepared under identical machine settings, so mug colour was the only systematic difference between groups.
    WeaknessBoth experiments used between-subjects assignment, so no taster compared mugs side by side. Experiment 1 put 18 volunteers six to a mug; Experiment 2 put 36 volunteers twelve to a mug. Each cell stayed small even with the replication.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“The coffee was rated as less sweet in the white mug as compared to the transparent and blue mugs.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“In experiment 1, the white mug enhanced the rated ‘intensity’ of the coffee flavour relative to the transparent mug.”
    ParaphrasedThe authors proposed colour contrast against the coffee's own brown colour as the likely driver for the white mug's effect. They explicitly ruled out the opposite idea, that blue would soften the contrast and taste sweeter because it's brown's complementary colour, since ratings for the blue mug and the clear glass never differed significantly in either experiment.
    Also worth citing: Ichimura, F., Motoki, K., Matsushita, K., & Ariga, A. (2023), “The Tactile Thickness of the Lip and Weight of a Glass Can Modulate Sensory Perception of Tea Beverage,” Food and Humanity, 1, 180–187, found the same kind of shift through touch instead of sight: identical tea tasted sweeter poured from a glass with a thick, heavy lip than from one with a thin, light lip.
    See also: Halo Effect, related but distinct: that's one already-known trait colouring belief about a different, unrelated trait of the same source; this is a cue from a different sense changing the direct sensory experience itself, with no belief or inference in between.
    64

    Meaningless Differentiation

    Why did the same jacket score as higher quality once its down filling got a made-up “Alpine Class” label?

    A visible, specific-sounding detail can be read as proof of a real benefit even when the detail changes nothing. Buyers assume a company would not invent it for no reason.

    ›
    Likely mechanismIf a company bothered to add a feature, buyers assume it must mean something, even when it plainly doesn't

    The psychology. When two products are hard to tell apart, a specific-sounding, hard-to-verify attribute gets treated as evidence by itself. Buyers infer that a firm would not invent a named, particular-looking detail unless it stood for something real, and lean on that inference instead of checking whether it does.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    When two products are hard to tell apart, a specific-sounding, hard-to-verify attribute gets treated as evidence by itself. Buyers infer that a firm would not invent a named, particular-looking detail unless it stood for something real, and lean on that inference instead of checking whether it does. The attribute needs no explanation for the inference to fire; specificity alone reads as meaningful.

    Where it causes errors

    A product can beat a functionally identical, or even better, rival because a firm invented a specific-sounding grade. The same pattern shows up with an in-house certification that has no external body behind it, or a numbered rating with no published standard. Buyers have no easy way to separate a decorative label from one backed by a real check. Harder-to-evaluate categories leave more room for the pattern to work.

    Where it can help

    A visible, specific detail is a fair way to signal a real difference a buyer would otherwise have to take on faith, when the underlying claim is true. A garment genuinely woven more slowly on a scarcer machine, or a material sourced to a stricter real standard, are examples. The test is whether the label still points at something that would be true if nobody ever asked about it.

    Carpenter, G. S., Glazer, R., & Nakamoto, K. (1994). “Meaningful Brands from Meaningless Differentiation: The Dependence on Irrelevant Attributes.” Journal of Marketing Research, 31(3), 339–350
    A set of controlled experiments testing whether an invented, functionally irrelevant product attribute could still shift how buyers rated quality.
    StrengthAcross several experiments the authors varied whether the irrelevant attribute appeared and how it was framed. That factorial approach shows when the meaningless-attribute inference holds and when it collapses, instead of hanging on a single one-shot contrast.
    WeaknessBoth experiments scored hypothetical brands: 99 master's students in the first, undergraduates in the second, marking preference scales for fictional products. No real purchase with money changing hands was measured, so the effect size on actual buying stays untested here.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“The average rating for the target brand with regular down fill in the subjective condition was 3.1; among those exposed to the same brand that included alpine class fill, the average brand rating climbed to 9.1.”
    ParaphrasedThe effect replicated across three unrelated product categories, down jackets, pasta, and CD players, each given its own fictional irrelevant attribute (alpine class fill, authentic Milanese style, a studio-designed signal processing system), suggesting the inference isn't limited to one kind of product.
    ParaphrasedThe effect weakened once the same attribute was explicitly and clearly labelled as irrelevant to the product's actual performance, suggesting the inference depends on the attribute's meaning staying ambiguous, not on buyers being deceived outright about what it was.
    See also: Signpost Effect, related but distinct: that reframes an already-meaningful fact to activate a goal that was sitting dormant; this takes a fact with no inherent meaning at all and reads it as meaningful purely because it's there.
    See also: Halo Effect, related but distinct: that extends one already-established trait to a different, unrelated trait of the same source; this manufactures the first impression out of an attribute that was never actually informative about anything.
    65

    Licensing Effect (moral licensing)

    Why did shoppers who had just imagined volunteering pick the $50 designer jeans over a vacuum at the same price?

    One virtuous or responsible act can leave a felt permission to indulge next, even when the two choices have no practical link.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA virtuous act temporarily boosts the sense of being a good person, and that boost gets spent on an indulgence next

    The psychology. An act that reflects well on the self (a donation, a workout, picking the healthy option) gives a short boost to self-concept. That boost behaves like credit. Having just looked good or responsible, someone feels free to spend some of it on a choice a plain evaluation would have blocked. The two acts do not feel contradictory, because they get treated as morally fungible even when they are practically unrelated.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    An act that reflects well on the self (a donation, a workout, picking the healthy option) gives a short boost to self-concept. That boost behaves like credit. Having just looked good or responsible, someone feels free to spend some of it on a choice a plain evaluation would have blocked. The two acts do not feel contradictory, because they get treated as morally fungible even when they are practically unrelated.

    Where it causes errors

    “Buy one, give one” and similar cause-linked campaigns can work this lever on the buyer as well as the recipient. A customer who has just funded a donation can feel more entitled to the indulgent version of what they were buying anyway.

    The effect can also shrink the good deed itself. In the cited study, people who first imagined a virtuous commitment later donated less, when they donated at all, than people given no prior commitment. The licence permitted indulgence and also took a bite out of the generosity that followed.

    Where it can help

    The useful read is spotting when a business’s own design accidentally hands out licences it never meant to give. Folding a virtuous choice and an indulgent one into a single decision, rather than two separate moments, removes the gap the effect needs. A real earned credential, a finished workout, or a paid-down balance can still be a fair motivating waypoint, provided it is not later used to wave through a choice that undoes the first one.

    Khan, U., & Dhar, R. (2006). “Licensing Effect in Consumer Choice.” Journal of Marketing Research, 43(2), 259–266
    Five lab studies, mostly asking participants to imagine a prior virtuous commitment before choosing between a luxury and a plain option priced identically.
    StrengthFive studies varied both the virtuous act and the later choice. A mediation analysis tied the shift to a temporary boost in self-concept. When the virtuous act was pinned on external pressure instead of free choice, the effect shrank. That supplies a real boundary, beyond another bare correlation.
    WeaknessIn most of the five studies the virtuous choice was imagined. Participants pictured volunteering; they did not actually do the work. How strongly the pattern holds when the prior good deed is real therefore stays open.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Significantly more people in the license condition chose the designer jeans (57.4%) than in the control condition (27.7%).”
    ParaphrasedThe same pattern replicated with a different pair of choices: 56.5% of participants in the license condition chose the more expensive, hedonic sunglasses, versus 27.7% in the control condition. In a separate study using a real donation instead of a hypothetical choice, among participants who did donate afterwards, average donations were lower in the licensing condition ($1.20) than in the control condition ($1.70).
    Paraphrased62% of participants chose the designer jeans when the earlier virtuous act was freely chosen, versus 40% in the control condition, but that gap disappeared (45% versus 40%, not significant) when the virtuous act was instead framed as a penalty for a driving violation. A separate mediation analysis supported a temporary boost to self-concept, not general mood, as the actual driver.
    Also worth citing: the broader “moral credentialing” finding this consumer-choice version builds on originates in social psychology, Monin, B., & Miller, D. T. (2001), “Moral Credentials and the Expression of Prejudice,” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(1), 33–43, though a 2026 registered replication report found no reliable evidence for that original, differently-scoped effect, worth knowing before leaning on the older paper specifically.
    See also: Present Bias, related but distinct: this is about which choice gets permitted after an earlier virtuous act; that's about why an immediate temptation wins even with no virtuous act anywhere in the picture.
    See also: Behavioural Economics vs. Behavioural Science vs. Psychology vs. UX, on why the applied practitioner name for this effect comes from Khan and Dhar's economics paper, not Monin and Miller's earlier psychology paper above.
    Tested as an experiment: Does directing a tax refund to pay down a credit card increase spending right after?, taking the same mechanism from an already-earned reward onto a real windfall and a real debt.
    66

    Present Bias (the present self vs. the future self)

    Why would the same person choose fruit a week ahead, then take the junk food the moment it arrived?

    A reward available right now outweighs the identical reward available later by more than the wait alone would justify. A calm advance choice and the choice made in the moment can contradict each other even when the options never changed.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe value of a reward drops steeply the moment it's delayed at all, so “now” beats “later” out of proportion to the actual wait

    The psychology. Standard theory assumes constant discounting: next week’s reward is valued almost like this week’s. Real choice drops steeply once any delay appears, then flattens further out. That shape lets the same person prefer the healthy option a week ahead, when both choices are equally delayed, then reverse once “now” is on the table.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Standard theory assumes constant discounting: next week’s reward is valued almost like this week’s. Real choice drops steeply once any delay appears, then flattens further out.

    That shape lets the same person prefer the healthy option a week ahead, when both choices are equally delayed, then reverse once “now” is on the table. Values did not flip in the abstract. Standing next to immediate temptation runs a present-favouring calculation that picturing the same choice in advance never triggers.

    Where it causes errors

    Someone joins a gym or a savings plan confident in a disciplined future self. When the moment to act arrives, an immediate competing priority wins through the same timing effect the cited study documents. The study’s term for the gap is an “empathy gap”: a calm, well-fed decision-maker cannot reliably predict what a hungry, in-the-moment self will choose.

    Where it can help

    That timing problem is why it helps to structure a choice so it is made once, calmly, in advance, rather than reopened at peak temptation. The specific tool for that is Precommitment Devices. Short of a binding commitment, defaulting to the advance choice unless someone deliberately overrides it in the moment already strips some of the free timing edge the present self would otherwise get.

    Read, D., & van Leeuwen, B. (1998). “Predicting Hunger: The Effects of Appetite and Delay on Choice.” Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 76(2), 189–205
    A real two-stage snack-choice study: participants chose between a healthy and unhealthy snack to be delivered a week later, then were offered the chance to change that choice the moment it actually arrived, either hungry or freshly fed.
    StrengthThe design compared each person's advance pick with their own in-the-moment pick for the same future reward, so decision timing was the manipulated variable. Real hunger at the moment of choice was also varied, testing the mechanism rather than merely noting a preference reversal.
    WeaknessThe stakes were a snack choice among 200 employees at their Amsterdam workplaces, outside a lab. Whether a reversal of the same size appears in higher-stakes financial or health decisions with larger consequences was left for later work.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“participants were dynamically inconsistent: they chose far more unhealthy snacks for immediate choice than for advance choice.”
    Verbatim“participants who were hungry during immediate choice (those in conditions HH and SH) chose more unhealthy snacks than did those who were satisfied (HS and SS).”
    ParaphrasedThe same individuals were measurably inconsistent across the two time points, what the authors call dynamic inconsistency, confirming the reversal was a real change in one person's revealed preference, not just a difference between two separate groups.
    See also: Precommitment Devices, related but distinct: that's the tool that removes the future self's ability to relitigate a choice; this is the underlying bias that makes relitigating so likely to go the present self's way.
    See also: Licensing Effect, related but distinct: that's about which choice gets permitted after an earlier virtuous act; this is about why immediate temptation wins even with no virtuous act anywhere in the picture.
    Also worth reading: The Biases Draining Your Super Could Also Fill It, on the 3.05 million Australians who withdrew $37.8 billion of retirement savings early during the pandemic.
    67

    Sunk Cost Fallacy

    Why does money already spent keep pulling more spending after it?

    Money, time, or effort already sunk into something keeps pulling people to continue, even after continuing is the worse forward-looking choice.

    ›
    Likely mechanismStopping after spending money on something feels like admitting that money was wasted, so people keep going instead

    The psychology. Standard economic theory says only future costs and benefits should matter. Money already spent is gone either way, so a purely rational choice would ignore it. Real decisions track how much has already gone into a project, purchase, or course of action. Stopping would mean admitting that earlier spending bought nothing, and that admission itself feels like a cost.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Standard economic theory says only future costs and benefits should matter. Money already spent is gone either way, so a purely rational choice would ignore it. Real decisions track how much has already gone into a project, purchase, or course of action. Stopping would mean admitting that earlier spending bought nothing, and that admission itself feels like a cost.

    Where it causes errors

    A renovation that has blown its budget keeps getting more, because stopping would leave the money already spent buying an unfinished house. A failing internal project gets another quarter of headcount because killing it would make the last four quarters look wasted, while the new quarter is no more likely to succeed. A gym membership someone stopped enjoying gets renewed because of what the first year cost, a cost the renewal cannot recover.

    Where it can help

    Knowing the effect is what makes a genuine “kill” decision possible. A business that sets a stop-loss review or kill criterion before a project starts, ahead of any spend, gives itself a rule that is not yet contaminated by sunk cost. That rule still holds once money is on the table. Building the checkpoint early improves the decision more than trying to resist the pull once it is already engaged.

    Arkes, H. R., & Blumer, C. (1985). “The Psychology of Sunk Cost.” Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35(1), 124–140
    The paper that named the effect, combining hypothetical decision scenarios with a real field experiment on actual theatergoers' behaviour.
    StrengthAt Ohio University, real season-ticket buyers were randomly assigned full price or a discount for the same season, then their attendance was tracked. Random assignment plus observed behaviour beats a vignette that only asks what people say they would do.
    WeaknessOther findings in the paper, including the often-cited “radar-blank airplane” vignette, ask what someone would choose in a hypothetical story. No real money was at risk there, so those figures describe stated intentions rather than observed acts.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedIn the hypothetical airplane scenario, 85% of participants chose to continue funding a doomed project once told $10 million had already been invested in it, compared with just 17% choosing to continue when the identical remaining decision was described with no mention of prior investment.
    Verbatim“The no-discount group used significantly more tickets (4.11) than both the $2 discount group (3.32) and the $7 discount group (3.29).”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Evidence that the psychological justification for this behavior is predicated on the desire not to appear wasteful is presented.”
    See also: Endowment Effect, a related but distinct pull: that's about overvaluing something because it's already owned, this is about continuing to invest because of what's already been spent, whether or not anything is owned yet.
    68

    Temporal Reframing

    Why does the same yearly cost feel smaller when restated as a daily amount?

    Restating a cost as a small recurring figure instead of one aggregate total changes which comparisons come to mind, and makes the identical spend easier to accept.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA cost framed as a daily amount gets compared to small daily expenses, not the big ones it's actually replacing

    The psychology. Judging whether a price is worth paying means comparing it with some other expense already in mind. Restating an aggregate as a small recurring amount changes which expenses show up for that comparison. “$300 a year” calls up other large, infrequent purchases. “85 cents a day” calls up coffee, a snack, spare change. The recurring frame wins because it is judged against cheaper rivals; the underlying maths never moved.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Judging whether a price is worth paying means comparing it with some other expense already in mind. Restating an aggregate as a small recurring amount changes which expenses show up for that comparison. “$300 a year” calls up other large, infrequent purchases. “85 cents a day” calls up coffee, a snack, spare change. The recurring frame wins because it is judged against cheaper rivals; the underlying maths never moved.

    Where it causes errors

    A subscription, extended warranty, or insurance add-on quoted as “just a few dollars a day” can win agreement it would not get as a real annual total. Someone can lock into an ongoing cost they would have hesitated over after seeing the aggregate first. The payment schedule stays the same. Only which number is shown, and which smaller expenses that number is measured against, changes.

    Where it can help

    The same reframe can make a beneficial habit feel achievable rather than daunting. A savings app that shows a retirement contribution as “the price of a coffee a day” shrinks a large number enough to start, while still showing the total. The honest version prints the real annual figure beside the daily one. The manipulative version shows only the smaller number and hopes nobody multiplies.

    Gourville, J. T. (1998). “Pennies-a-Day: The Effect of Temporal Reframing on Transaction Evaluation.” Journal of Consumer Research, 24(4), 395–408
    A series of lab studies testing the "pennies-a-day" (PAD) framing across a range of product and donation categories, and the two-step comparison process behind it.
    StrengthBeyond documenting the pennies-a-day effect, the paper probes the proposed two-step account: which comparison expenses people retrieve, and how that retrieval shifts evaluation of the transaction. The contribution is a specific causal account of how the effect arises.
    WeaknessThe studies measure stated willingness to agree or donate in the lab. They do not follow real long-term subscriptions or donations. How people feel about a cost after months of actual recurrence is outside what this design can settle.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“the percentage of subjects agreeing to donate was significantly higher under the PAD than under the aggregate framing (52 vs. 30 percent; X2(1) = 4.66, p < .05).”
    Verbatim (abstract)“The PAD framing of a target transaction is shown to systematically foster the retrieval and consideration of small ongoing expenses as the standard of comparison, whereas an aggregate framing of that same transaction is shown to foster the retrieval and consideration of large infrequent expenses. This difference in retrieval is shown to significantly influence subsequent transaction evaluation and compliance.”
    ParaphrasedGeneral support for the pennies-a-day effect held across a range of product categories tested in the paper's lab studies, not just the charity example.
    See also: Chunking, a related but distinct move: that's about breaking one large ask into several smaller ones over time, this is about restating the same single total in smaller-feeling units without changing the schedule at all.
    69

    Bundling

    Why does a discount printed on the bundle feel larger than the same dollars split across its parts?

    The same dollar saving feels like a better deal when it is stated once on a combined bundle price than when it is spread across separate item-level discounts.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA single discount stated on the combined price registers as one bigger gain than the identical amount split into smaller pieces

    The psychology. Perceived savings in a bundle come from two sources people track differently: what each item would have cost alone, and any extra saving stated on the bundle price itself. Dollar for dollar, the second carries more weight. It registers as one direct gain, rather than several smaller cuts a buyer has to notice and add up.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Perceived savings in a bundle come from two sources people track differently: what each item would have cost alone, and any extra saving stated on the bundle price itself. Dollar for dollar, the second carries more weight. It registers as one direct gain, rather than several smaller cuts a buyer has to notice and add up.

    Where it causes errors

    A retailer can make the same total discount feel far more generous by moving it from item level to bundle level. “Save an extra $20 when you buy both together” lands harder than “$10 off each,” even though total dollars saved stay identical.

    A buyer can pick the bundle over better-fitting individual items because the bundle saving was easier to feel, even when the bundle itself was the weaker deal.

    Where it can help

    When combined savings are real, stating the discount once on the bundle communicates the value more clearly. Several small per-item cuts are easier for a buyer to miss or skip adding up. The honest version states an accurate combined saving. The manipulative version inflates the bundle discount relative to what the items were worth apart.

    Yadav, M. S., & Monroe, K. B. (1993). “How Buyers Perceive Savings in a Bundle Price: An Examination of a Bundle's Transaction Value.” Journal of Marketing Research, 30(3), 350–358
    A study separating a bundle's perceived value into two distinct components, savings on the individual items and additional savings on the bundle itself, and testing how each one contributes.
    StrengthThe paper separates two kinds of “savings” that everyday bundle-pricing talk usually mixes, then tests each alone and in combination. That split yields a sharper account than a blanket claim that bundling raises perceived value.
    Weakness252 undergraduates at a state university rated a print ad for a garment bag and a pullman suitcase. As with most classic bundle-pricing work from the period, they judged a described pricing scenario rather than completing a real purchase.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Such perceptions of overall bundle savings may consist of two separate perceptions of savings, each with a different relative influence: (1) perceived savings on the individual items if purchased separately and (2) perceived additional savings on the bundle.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Results of an experiment indicate that additional savings offered directly on the bundle have a greater relative impact on buyers' perceptions of transaction value than savings offered on the bundle's individual items.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“The effect of each saving is also influenced by the magnitude of the other saving.”
    See also: Mental Accounting, a related but distinct habit: that's about which account a cost or saving gets filed under, this is about whether a saving gets stated once as a single gain or scattered across several smaller ones.
    70

    Clawback (Loss-Framed Incentives)

    Why did factory teams work harder to keep a bonus already paid than to earn the same bonus by hitting a target?

    The same reward moves people more when it is framed as already theirs and at risk of being taken back than when it is framed as still to be earned.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA reward framed as already yours and losable motivates harder than the same reward only promised ahead

    The psychology. A bonus is usually judged against a reference point of having nothing extra: hit the target and gain something not yet held. Loss aversion makes a loss against that reference hurt more than an equivalent gain pleases. Shifting the reference upward, even by saying the money is already theirs, turns the same future outcome into a potential loss rather than a potential gain. Missing the target then feels like losing money already held, rather than failing to earn a bonus.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A bonus is usually judged against a reference point of having nothing extra: hit the target and gain something not yet held. Loss aversion makes a loss against that reference hurt more than an equivalent gain pleases. Shifting the reference upward, even by saying the money is already theirs, turns the same future outcome into a potential loss rather than a potential gain. Missing the target then feels like losing money already held, rather than failing to earn a bonus.

    Where it causes errors

    The same mechanism turns punitive when the “already given” framing is not matched by money that stays put. Signing and relocation bonus clawback clauses are common in tech and finance hiring. They require an employee to repay money already spent if they leave before a set date, often years out.

    Executive-compensation clawback rules the SEC finalised in 2022 under the Dodd-Frank Act work the same way at larger scale. Incentive pay already paid out can be recovered from a current or former executive after an accounting restatement, sometimes years after it was earned. Both are real, disclosed policies, yet a reward reclaimable years later reads less like motivation and more like a debt that was never settled.

    Where it can help

    Used honestly, the same lever helps. Two Australian banks apply a near-identical loss frame to bonus interest: CommBank’s GoalSaver, and Savers from Up, an app-only neobank. Both structure the rate so a customer earns it by default each month and gets a plain-language warning before an easy lapse costs them the difference.

    Nothing is hidden or punitive. The condition is disclosed upfront, the warning leaves time to act, and the “loss” being protected is a rate the customer already qualifies for, not one invented to manufacture urgency. The same reference-point shift that makes a clawed-back executive bonus feel like betrayal makes a timely, honest warning feel like the bank is on the customer’s side.

    Spotted in the wild

    The honest version of this mechanism, live on Up's own app: a bonus already framed as the customer's, with a real warning before it lapses.

    Up Bank, “Talk to us” inbox. A proactive “Bonus Interest Qualification” message, sent with real time left to act, not a punitive clawback after the fact.

    Full decode: How does Up Bank's behavioural design pay off for both the bank and its customers? A real, disclosed condition and a genuinely timely warning, not the punitive version this principle also documents.

    Hossain, T., & List, J. A. (2012). “The Behavioralist Visits the Factory: Increasing Productivity Using Simple Framing Manipulations.” Management Science, 58(12), 2151–2167
    A real field experiment inside an operating Chinese high-tech manufacturing plant, run on actual production teams and their real weekly bonus pay, not a lab simulation or a survey.
    StrengthInside a working Nanjing factory, from July 2008 through January 2009, 165 workers faced real RMB 80 bonuses tied to measured output. That bonus was about USD 11.72, more than 20% of a week's pay for the lowest-paid staff. The design is a live field experiment rather than a hypothetical or stated-preference survey.
    WeaknessMeasurement sat at one Chinese high-tech plant, with its own labour market, culture, and task mix. Whether the same loss-frame edge appears at other bonus sizes, in other industries, or in individual white-collar work rather than team piece-work was not tested here.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“The magnitude of the effect is roughly 1%: that is, total team productivity is enhanced by 1% purely due to the framing manipulation.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Conditional incentives framed as both ‘losses’ and ‘gains’ increase productivity for both individuals and teams… neither the framing nor the incentive effect lose their importance over time; rather the effects are observed over the entire sample period.”
    See also: Loss Aversion, the broader phenomenon this is one specific, deliberately engineered application of: a reward reframed as a possession at risk, not a prospect still to win.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: CBA's GoalSaver and Up Bank both apply this same loss frame honestly to bonus interest, warning a customer before an easy lapse costs them a rate they'd already qualify for.
    71

    Disclosure Backfire (Sunlight That Doesn't Disinfect)

    Why did telling people their advisor had a financial stake in inflating the advice make that advice more biased afterward?

    Conflict-of-interest disclosure is meant to help the listener discount advice. It can instead free the advisor to lean further into bias, while the listener still under-corrects.

    ›
    Likely mechanismAdmitting a bias aloud can feel like licence to act on it more, not a check that reins it in

    The psychology. Conflicted advice usually rides on a real incentive: a commission, a referral fee, a stake in the outcome. Requiring disclosure is meant to help the listener discount, the way a reader discounts a sponsored review. Two frictions get in the way. Moral licensing lets a disclosed advisor feel the duty is already done, freeing them to lean into the bias. Listeners rarely discount enough to cancel that increase, partly because rejecting disclosed advice can feel like accusing the advisor of dishonesty to their face.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Conflicted advice usually rides on a real incentive: a commission, a referral fee, a stake in the outcome. Requiring disclosure is meant to help the listener discount, the way a reader discounts a sponsored review. Two frictions get in the way. First, moral licensing: after disclosing the conflict, an advisor can feel the duty is already done. That frees them to lean into the bias rather than correct for it, since the listener has, in theory, been warned.

    Second, the listener rarely discounts enough to cancel that increase. Rejecting disclosed advice can feel like accusing the advisor of dishonesty to their face, a social cost most people avoid more than a pure financial calculation would predict. The two effects compound: advice grows more biased, and the correction does not grow to match.

    Where it causes errors

    In most markets a commission-paid financial advisor must disclose that fact before recommending a product. The disclosure is real and the products are usually legitimate. The disclosure does not reliably make the recommendation less commission-driven.

    An advisor who has disclosed has, in a literal sense, done what the rule asked. A client who has just been told the advisor earns more if they buy still has to weigh the discomfort of pushing back against someone across the desk. The rule creates the appearance of a safeguard without necessarily changing the underlying incentive it was built to neutralise.

    Where it can help

    Better wording on the disclosure rarely solves it. Removing the incentive the disclosure was meant to flag does. A fee-only advisor, paid a flat rate regardless of what they recommend, can disclose compensation without the same backfire, because no percentage-based upside remains to feel licensed to lean into. The honest use of this principle is diagnostic: when disclosing a conflict is the primary fix on offer, the underlying incentive has usually not been dealt with yet.

    Cain, D. M., Loewenstein, G., & Moore, D. A. (2005). “The Dirt on Coming Clean: Perverse Effects of Disclosing Conflicts of Interest.” The Journal of Legal Studies, 34(1), 1–25
    A set of controlled lab experiments built around a real coin-jar estimation task, where advisors who could see the actual value gave advice to estimators who couldn't, with a real, sometimes-disclosed financial incentive for the advisor to advise high.
    Strength147 Carnegie Mellon undergraduates were randomly assigned advisor or estimator roles judging real jars of coins. Advisor pay rewarded inflated advice, so the conflict of interest was built into incentives rather than only described. That is a controlled experiment with real payoffs, where a survey vignette would have fallen short.
    WeaknessThe biased advisors were not licensed professionals facing reputation or compliance risk, and the dollars at stake were the modest sums typical of lab tasks. Whether a professional advisor with more on the line shows a backfire of the same size stays untested here.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“First, people generally do not discount advice from biased advisors as much as they should, even when advisors’ conflicts of interest are disclosed. Second, disclosure can increase the bias in advice because it leads advisors to feel morally licensed and strategically encouraged to exaggerate their advice even further.”
    Verbatim“estimators earned less money when conflicts of interest were disclosed than when they were not, and advisors made more money with disclosure than without disclosure.”
    Also worth citing: Loewenstein, G., Sah, S., & Cain, D. M. (2012). “The Unintended Consequences of Conflict of Interest Disclosure.” JAMA, 307(7), 669–670, a follow-up perspective piece by two of the same authors arguing the same dynamic helps explain why conflict-of-interest disclosure rules in medicine and finance haven't reliably improved outcomes for the patients and clients they're meant to protect.
    See also: The Fine Print Nobody Reads, a full report on why standard disclosure fails this way so often, and what research shows actually works instead.
    72

    Propinquity Effect

    Why did neighbours who shared a hallway become close friends four times as often as neighbours at opposite ends of the same hallway?

    People who keep crossing paths because they live or work near each other grow more familiar than they otherwise would. That familiarity often gets treated as trust or fit, even when the judgment was supposed to rest on merit alone.

    ›
    Likely mechanismRepeated, incidental contact from physical closeness breeds familiarity, and familiarity gets mistaken for a signal of trust or fit

    The psychology. Friendship can form from repeated chance encounters alone. A shared mailbox route or a hallway walked every morning produces many small, unplanned contacts. Familiarity from that layout can feel like genuine compatibility, even though neither person chose the floor plan.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Friendship can form from repeated chance encounters alone. A shared mailbox route or a hallway walked every morning produces many small, unplanned contacts. Neither person has to decide to seek the other out.

    What matters is functional distance: how often two paths actually cross given the shared layout, more than raw metres between doors. Someone next to a stairwell or mailbox that everyone passes gets named as a friend more often than straight-line distance would predict. The familiarity that follows can feel earned through genuine compatibility, even when an apartment plan neither person chose produced it.

    The same shortcut shows up far outside friendship. A scout, manager, or evaluator who crosses paths with one candidate more often develops a felt sense of “knowing” that person. That felt sense can leak into a judgment that was meant to rest on merit alone.

    Where it causes errors

    Major League Baseball’s amateur draft is run by each team’s own scouting director, scoring thousands of prospects against shared statistics, reports, and film. A 2022 study of the 2000–2019 drafts covered roughly 30,000 drafted players from a pool of over a million. Holding on-field skill constant with machine learning, it found that a player is measurably more likely to be drafted by a given team the closer he lives to that team’s scouting director.

    Those geographically favoured players were worse bets. They were 38% less likely to ever appear in a single MLB game than similarly drafted players without the proximity edge. The effect peaked in later rounds, where personal discretion is highest and outside scrutiny is lowest. Nobody set out to favour nearby players. The housing-complex mechanism was simply wearing a different job title.

    Where it can help

    The same lever can be aimed on purpose. Seat a new hire near the colleagues they will need to work with, rather than wherever a desk happens to be free. That builds the cross-team familiarity that makes a quick question or a real problem flag feel ordinary instead of awkward.

    A mentorship programme that puts a junior and senior colleague on the same recurring meeting, instead of hoping the relationship forms on its own, engineers familiarity deliberately. It creates the same repeated, low-stakes contact a shared mailbox creates by accident. The aim is to make an already-good working relationship easier to reach.

    Festinger, L., Schachter, S., & Back, K. (1950). Social Pressures in Informal Groups: A Study of Human Factors in Housing. Harper & Brothers
    A real field study, not a lab experiment: married WWII veterans attending MIT on the GI Bill were assigned, essentially at random, to units in the newly built Westgate and Westgate West housing complexes, and later asked to name their three closest friends within the complex.
    StrengthHousing units were assigned at random, which blocks the story that people simply moved next to friends they already liked. Friendship patterns that followed had to track the physical layout rather than self-sorting by compatibility.
    WeaknessThe sample was tightly bounded: married graduate-student veterans in one 1946 housing complex. Friendship was measured by asking couples for a short list of names, a self-report shaped by memory and social comfort as much as by an objective count of shared time.
    Key findings
    Paraphrased41% of next-door neighbours, roughly 19 feet apart, named each other as one of their three closest friends, compared with 22% of residents two doors apart and just 10% of residents at opposite ends of the same hallway, roughly 89 feet away.
    ParaphrasedAbout 65% of all the close friendships residents named were with someone living in the same building, even though residents had just as much opportunity to befriend people in the complex's other buildings.
    ParaphrasedResidents whose apartment sat next to a shared stairwell or mailbox, a spot everyone in the building had to pass, were named as a friend more often than their straight-line distance from others would predict, showing that how often paths actually crossed mattered more than raw physical distance alone.
    A note on sourcing: the original 1950 monograph isn't available as searchable full text on this site's network, so all three findings above are paraphrased from the book's long-standing, widely-replicated figures as reported across independent academic summaries, not quoted verbatim from the original page.
    Also worth citing: Ahmadi, M., Durst, N., Lachman, J., List, J. A., List, M., List, N., & Vayalinkal, A. (2022). “Nothing Propinks Like Propinquity: Using Machine Learning to Estimate the Effects of Spatial Proximity in the Major League Baseball Draft.” NBER Working Paper No. 30786, a modern corroborating study covering roughly 30,000 players drafted from 2000 to 2019, with player skill estimated by a machine-learning model built for the Chicago White Sox. A player is 7.1% more likely to be drafted by a given team for every 1,000 km he lives closer to that team's scouting director, controlling for skill, and that effect climbs to 11.8% in rounds 16 and later, where a director has the most personal discretion. Players who benefit from that proximity are 38% less likely to ever appear in an MLB game than a similarly drafted player without it, and their initial signing bonuses run 12% to 25% higher, conditional on draft order. Still a working paper rather than a peer-reviewed publication at time of writing.
    See also: How do you prove distance biased a decision when nobody can run a controlled trial on real MLB scouts?, a full breakdown of how the draft study argues its case without being able to randomly assign where a scout lives.
    Special report: Proximity Gets Mistaken for Merit reads the housing study and the draft study together, seventy years apart, as one argument.
    73

    Availability Heuristic

    Why did one attack on planes lead to hundreds of extra deaths on the highway?

    When an event is easy to picture or recall, a recent headline, a vivid story, a personal memory, it feels more common and more likely than the base rate supports. Ease of coming to mind gets treated as evidence of frequency.

    ›
    Likely mechanismEasily recalled examples feel more common than they really are

    The psychology. The mind does not keep a running count of how often events occur. Asked how common or risky something is, people substitute a simpler question: how fast do examples come to mind? Speed of recall then gets read as a measure of frequency.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    The mind does not keep a running count of how often events occur. Asked how common or risky something is, people substitute a simpler question: how fast do examples come to mind? A vivid story, a recent headline, or a memorable personal episode surfaces first, and that speed of recall gets treated as a measure of frequency.

    The substitution fails where memorability and actual frequency diverge. Dramatic, unusual, or emotionally loaded events (a plane crash, a shark attack, a fraud story from a friend) are easy to recall precisely because they are rare and vivid. The more available an example feels, the more people overestimate how often the category it stands for really occurs.

    Where it causes errors

    After the September 11 attacks, many Americans who would normally have flown chose to drive instead. The vivid memory of hijacked planes made flying feel like the greater danger. Economist Gerd Gigerenzer compared U.S. Department of Transportation crash data for October through December 2001 with prior years and estimated 353 additional road deaths in that quarter, more than the roughly 250 people killed on the four hijacked flights.

    A later reanalysis by Michael Sivak and Michael Flannagan put the shift nearer 1,000 additional traffic deaths. Flying had not become more dangerous per mile travelled. Driving was, and remains, far riskier. The easily recalled image of a hijacked plane made that risk feel urgent in a way an ordinary highway fatality rarely does.

    Where it can help

    The practical countermeasure is to stop relying on unaided memory for high-stakes routines. A 19-item checklist from the World Health Organisation was tested across eight hospitals on four continents, from a rural clinic in Tanzania to a teaching hospital in Toronto. It forces a surgical team to confirm steps that are easy to skip precisely because they rarely go wrong: patient identity, surgical site, timely antibiotics.

    Across roughly 8,000 patients, major complications fell from 11.0% to 7.0%, and in-hospital deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8%. The checklist does not make anyone smarter. It replaces whatever happens to come to mind with a fixed list that ignores what is vivid or recent.

    Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1973). “Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability.” Cognitive Psychology, 5(2), 207–232
    The paper that introduced the availability heuristic as a distinct judgment shortcut, alongside representativeness and anchoring, in Kahneman and Tversky's broader research programme on heuristics and biases.
    StrengthIn the letter-position task, the same 152 subjects judged five letters (K, L, N, R, V). Independent counts of each letter's frequency in real English supplied a checkable answer against which guesses could be scored, so the mechanism is isolated cleanly.
    WeaknessLetter-frequency judgments are an artificial lab task, far from real risk or purchase decisions. This paper alone does not size the effect when the judgment carries higher stakes; later work, including the traffic-fatality analysis cited below, supplies that bridge.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“Among the 152 subjects, 105 judged the first position to be more likely for a majority of the letters, and 47 judged the third position to be more likely for a majority of the letters… The median estimated ratio was 2:1 for each of the five letters. These results were obtained despite the fact that all letters were more frequent in the third position.”
    Verbatim“It is certainly easier to think of words that start with a K than of words where K is in the third position. If the judgment of frequency is mediated by assessed availability, then words that start with K should be judged more frequent.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“This paper explores a judgmental heuristic in which a person evaluates the frequency of classes or the probability of events by availability, i.e., by the ease with which relevant instances come to mind. In general, availability is correlated with ecological frequency, but it is also affected by other factors. Consequently, the reliance on the availability heuristic leads to systematic biases.”
    Also worth citing: Gigerenzer, G. (2004). “Dread Risk, September 11, and Fatal Traffic Accidents.” Psychological Science, 15(4), 286–287, the real-world traffic-fatality analysis referenced above; a later reanalysis, Sivak, M., & Flannagan, M. J. (2004). “Consequences for Road Traffic Fatalities of the Reduction in Flying Following September 11, 2001.” Transportation Research Part F, 7(4–5), 301–305, found an even larger shift.
    Also worth citing: Haynes, A. B., Weiser, T. G., Berry, W. R., et al. (2009). “A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population.” New England Journal of Medicine, 360(5), 491–499, the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist trial referenced above.
    74

    Diversification Heuristic

    Why does an even split of money track how many options sit on the menu more than what those options hold?

    Asked to divide money or attention across several unfamiliar options, most people split evenly across however many options appear. The rule tracks the count of boxes, not what each box contains.

    ›
    Likely mechanismWeighing what each option actually holds is hard, so people just split evenly by count instead

    The psychology. Comparing each option’s real risk, return, and overlap takes effort most people skip in the moment. The mind substitutes an easier question: how many options are there, and what is one divided by that? An even split then feels like diversification without a look inside.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Comparing each option’s real risk, return, and overlap takes effort most people skip in the moment. The mind substitutes an easier question: how many options are there, and what is one divided by that? An even split then feels like sensible diversification without checking what sits inside each option, or how alike the options are.

    That is why the rule is called naive diversification: it diversifies by count, not by content. Two menus holding the same underlying assets, one drawn as three funds and one as six, get split three ways or six ways under this rule. That produces two different final portfolios from the same building blocks, purely because of how many boxes the menu drew around them.

    Where it causes errors

    CommSec Pocket’s “Invest in” menu lists ten flat options side by side: Aussie Top 200, Aussie Dividends, Aussie Sustainability, Aussie Corporate Bonds, Global 100, Diversified Equities, Emerging Markets, Health Wise, Sustainability Leaders, and Tech Savvy. There is no default and no guidance on how much to put in each.

    A first-time investor chasing “a spread” who taps four or five of them is likely to split evenly across whichever ones they happened to pick. They miss that Diversified Equities already holds hundreds of companies across several markets, while Tech Savvy, Health Wise, and Emerging Markets are concentrated, higher-volatility single-theme bets. They also miss that Aussie Top 200 and Aussie Dividends likely already share many of the same large ASX names.

    Benartzi and Thaler found the same pattern in real employer retirement plans. The share of contributions held in stock funds tracked the share of stock funds among the funds the plan listed. A plan that listed mostly stock funds produced mostly-stock employee portfolios. A plan that listed mostly bond funds produced bond-heavy ones, almost independent of what employees said about their own risk tolerance.

    Where it can help

    Once it is clear that people will roughly divide evenly across whatever is offered, the menu itself becomes a design lever. A plan sponsor or app designer can offer a smaller, genuinely balanced set, or lead with one already-diversified default. That can produce a sensible outcome from someone who would otherwise equal-weight a messier list. Menu composition is a consequential design choice. Length for its own sake is not a neutral virtue.

    Spotted in the wild

    CommSec Pocket's real “Invest in” screen: ten flat options, no default, no grouping, and nothing telling a new investor how much of their money should go where.

    CommSec Pocket, “Invest in” menu. Ten options, equal visual weight, no indication of how they overlap or how concentrated each one is. Captured 2026-08-28.

    This screenshot shows a real, current menu, not a claim that any particular investor actually equal-weighted it. The evidence that people tend to do exactly that with menus shaped like this is the cited study below.

    Benartzi, S., & Thaler, R. H. (2001). “Naive Diversification Strategies in Defined Contribution Saving Plans.” American Economic Review, 91(1), 79–98
    The paper that named the “1/n” naive-diversification strategy in retirement saving.
    StrengthReal employer retirement-plan data show revealed behaviour with money on the line, and a companion menu experiment varies how many funds appear and of what type. The 1/n pattern surfaces under both real stakes and clean experimental control.
    WeaknessIn the field data, employers that list more stock funds also tend to hold more stock. Those employers may also differ in workforce demographics or risk philosophy in ways that push holdings up on their own. The companion experiment speaks to that worry without fully settling it for the observational half.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“We show that some investors follow the ‘1/n strategy’: they divide their contributions evenly across the funds offered in the plan.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Consistent with this naive notion of diversification, we find that the proportion invested in stocks depends strongly on the proportion of stock funds in the plan.”
    ParaphrasedIn a companion hypothetical-menu experiment, University of California employees offered a choice among four fixed-income funds and one stock fund allocated an average of 43% of their contributions to equities, while a separate group offered one fixed-income fund and four stock funds, the same mix TWA's pilot plan actually uses, allocated 68%, a 25-point gap the authors found statistically significant even though a rational, mean-variance-optimizing investor would only have moved a few points.
    Run this one live: Live Sessions: Diversification Heuristic, a real room tapping funds from CommSec Pocket's own flat 10-option menu versus a curated 3-option one, instead of the CommSec analogy alone.
    Also worth reading: The Biases Draining Your Super Could Also Fill It, applying this same naive “1/n” pattern to a superannuation fund's own investment menu.
    75

    Ambiguity Aversion

    Why would someone refuse a bet with unknown odds, even when those odds could beat a known but worse alternative?

    Faced with a risk whose odds are known and an otherwise identical risk whose odds are hidden, most people take the known one, even when the hidden odds could be equal or better.

    ›
    Likely mechanismAn unknown probability feels more threatening than a bad known one, so the unknown option gets avoided

    The psychology. Known risk and unknown odds are different problems for judgment, even when expected outcomes match. Offered a bet with stated odds and an otherwise identical bet with hidden odds, most people take the stated one, including bets they would normally reject. The aversion is to not being told the odds.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Known risk and unknown odds are different problems for judgment, even when expected outcomes match. Offered a bet with stated odds and an otherwise identical bet with hidden odds, most people take the stated one, including bets they would normally reject. The reaction is to missing information about the odds, not only to bad odds.

    That asymmetry breaks a basic consistency rule. Someone who will not bet on red from an urn with a hidden mix should then be willing to bet on black. Between the two colours, one has to be at least an even shot. Daniel Ellsberg’s 1961 demonstration showed people declining both bets on the ambiguous urn, a pattern no single, consistent probability judgment can produce. Aversion to ambiguity itself sits on top of ordinary risk aversion.

    Where it causes errors

    Ambiguity aversion helps explain a stubborn household-investing puzzle. Many people hold far less of their portfolio in stocks than a sensible risk calculation would suggest. What stock they do hold skews toward their own employer or their own country’s market, the setting whose rules feel familiar rather than opaque.

    A large US household survey found ambiguity-averse respondents were less likely to hold stocks at all. When they held stocks, they held a smaller share of assets in them, and held more of their employer’s stock specifically. Familiar risk gets tolerated; unfamiliar risk gets avoided, independent of which one pays more on average.

    Where it can help

    Stating the same policy plainly everywhere it appears removes an avoidable source of ambiguity aversion. A customer who can see exactly what they are agreeing to has less need to invent a worse hidden version. The same logic applies to decisions worth de-risking: an insurance product with a clear, simple contract, or a warranty with one stated term instead of several conditional ones. Cutting genuine ambiguity is what lowers the aversion. Reassurance without clearer terms does less.

    Spotted in the wild

    Real ambiguity doesn't always look hidden. Sometimes it's two different real numbers, both plainly published, with nothing telling the reader which one actually applies to them.

    Apple, Shopping Help: Returns & Refunds. Two return windows for two return methods on the same order: seven days for a Pick-up Point drop-off, 14 calendar days for an Apple Store return. Both real, both currently published, with nothing on the page explaining why they differ. Captured 2026-08-28.

    This is Apple's own published policy, not a claim that the difference confuses every reader or changes anyone's behaviour. It's a real instance of the kind of unresolved, unexplained variation that keeps a choice ambiguous rather than merely risky, the mechanism the cited study below actually tests.

    Ellsberg, D. (1961). “Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms.” Quarterly Journal of Economics, 75(4), 643–669
    The paper that first distinguished ambiguity (unknown probabilities) from ordinary risk (known probabilities) as things people respond to differently, illustrated with a thought experiment about drawing coloured balls from two urns.
    StrengthEllsberg's urns keep prize, ball count, and bet type fixed. The only material difference between urns is whether the colour split is known or hidden, which isolates ambiguity from every other reason someone might refuse a bet.
    WeaknessEllsberg's demonstration was informal: a small circle of Harvard and RAND colleagues, no random assignment, no fixed sample, no reported percentages. It worked as a philosophical challenge to expected-utility theory more than as a data study. Later experiments confirmed the pattern under controlled conditions.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedEllsberg described two urns, each holding 100 balls. Urn A is known to hold exactly 50 red and 50 black balls. Urn B holds red and black balls in some unknown ratio. Offered a bet that pays out for drawing red, most people he spoke with preferred betting on Urn A. Offered the identical bet for drawing black instead, most preferred Urn A again, a pattern that can't be reconciled with any single, fixed probability estimate for Urn B's contents.
    Verbatim“What is at issue might be called the ambiguity of this information, a quality depending on the amount, type, reliability and ‘unanimity’ of information, and giving rise to one's degree of ‘confidence’ in an estimate of relative likelihoods.”
    A note on sourcing: Ellsberg's original demonstration was an informal thought experiment described in his own paper, not a controlled study with a defined sample size or reported percentages; he reports typical responses (“if you are in the majority…”) rather than tabulated results.
    Also worth citing: Dimmock, S. G., Kouwenberg, R., Mitchell, O. S., & Peijnenburg, K. (2016). “Ambiguity Aversion and Household Portfolio Choice Puzzles: Empirical Evidence.” Journal of Financial Economics, 119(3), 559–577, the real, quantified measurement behind the investing example above: a representative US household survey that measured each respondent's own ambiguity aversion directly, using questions built on Ellsberg's urn structure, then tested it against their real portfolio data. Ambiguity-averse respondents were less likely to hold any stocks at all, held less in stocks when they did, held more of their own employer's stock specifically, and were more likely to sell out of stocks during the 2008 financial crisis.
    See also: Risk Aversion, the more familiar half of this picture: even with known odds, people weight a loss more heavily than a same-sized gain. Ambiguity aversion is what happens one level up, when the odds themselves aren't known.
    76

    Risk Aversion

    Why do most people take a guaranteed $40 over a coin flip that pays $0 or $100?

    Offered a certain amount and a gamble worth the same or more on average, most people take the certain amount. They give up expected value to keep certainty.

    ›
    Likely mechanismEach extra dollar of gain matters a little less than the last, so a sure amount can beat a gamble worth more on average

    The psychology. Classical economics says a gamble should be judged by expected value alone. Real choices bend that rule because each extra dollar of gain is worth a little less than the last. A sure amount already in hand can beat a gamble with a higher average payout.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Classical economics says a gamble should be judged by expected value alone, the probability-weighted average of payoffs. Real choices bend that rule because each extra dollar of gain is worth a little less than the last. A sure amount already in hand can beat a gamble with a higher average payout, simply because the value of money curves as amounts grow. That is diminishing marginal utility, a different mechanism from loss aversion’s asymmetry between losses and gains. Risk aversion appears even when no loss is possible, only a sure gain against a larger, less certain one.

    Strength of the effect depends on how real the money is. Charles Holt and Susan Laury ran the same menu of paired lottery choices at trivial payouts and at payouts scaled to serious money.
