People became measurably more risk averse as stakes moved from small to large and from hypothetical to real. Imagining a bigger number on paper does not reproduce the same shift. Actual money on the table does.

    Where it causes errors

    Risk aversion itself is a coherent preference. It turns into an error when it is aimed at the wrong horizon. A retirement saver who avoids stocks entirely because year-to-year swings feel threatening is applying a short-horizon risk judgment to a long-horizon decision. Over decades those swings mostly wash out. The aversion is real; the timeframe is where the mistake sits.

    Where it can help

    Products can reduce real risk, not only the feeling of it. A stated return policy is the clearest version. A published window to send back an unwanted purchase turns an irreversible bet into a reversible one, which directly lowers the risk of buying something unseen or untried.

    A 0%-interest instalment plan reduces a different risk: the payment itself. If the terms match what is stated, spreading a known total over fixed payments removes the risk of triggering interest. Either mechanism turns exploitative the moment it encourages a purchase someone could not otherwise afford or return, or hides a shortened window or a cost in the fine print.

    Spotted in the wild

    Two live examples of businesses reducing the real risk of a purchase, not just how risky it feels, on the exact pages where that risk aversion would otherwise kick in.

    Apple, Shopping Help: Returns & Refunds. A published 14-day return window for Apple Store purchases (seven days for a Pick-up Point drop-off) gives a shopper a real, stated right to undo the purchase, before they've even paid. Captured 2026-08-28.

    Apple.com, iPhone product page. Afterpay's “Pay Monthly” financing offer, 0% interest and no monthly fees for up to 24 months, sits directly above the phone line-up, reducing the payment risk of the same purchase instead. Captured 2026-08-28.

    Both are the retailer's own advertised terms, not independent verification of every order's actual outcome. A shopper still has to check the specific terms that apply to them. What the two screenshots show is the tactic itself, in two different forms. A return window removes the risk of being stuck with the wrong product. An instalment plan removes the risk of an unexpected interest cost. Either can lower the resistance risk aversion would otherwise create.

    Holt, C. A., & Laury, S. K. (2002). “Risk Aversion and Incentive Effects.” American Economic Review, 92(5), 1644–1655
    The paper that popularised the paired lottery-choice task now widely used to measure an individual's own risk aversion directly, by finding the exact point where they switch from the safer bet to the riskier one.
    StrengthEach subject saw the same ten paired lottery choices, safer lower-variance options against riskier higher-variance ones, at every step. Within a person, only the offered probabilities changed, which maps where that person's risk tolerance sits.
    WeaknessThe sample was 212 university students at Georgia State, Miami, and Central Florida, spread across five payoff-scale treatments. The two highest, most expensive treatments had only 19 and 18 subjects, so the high-stakes cells rest on thin numbers.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“With real payoffs, risk aversion increases sharply when payoffs are scaled up by factors of 20, 50, and 90.”
    Verbatim“Subjects facing hypothetical choices cannot imagine how they would actually behave under high-incentive conditions.”
    See also: Loss Aversion, a related but distinct asymmetry: risk aversion is about the curve of value itself, present even in a choice with no possible loss, while loss aversion is specifically about losses hurting more than same-sized gains help.
    See also: Ambiguity Aversion, the same caution taken one step further. Even once the odds are known, as they are in every choice above, most people still prefer the safer option. Hide the odds entirely, and the aversion gets stronger still.
    Also worth reading: The Biases Draining Your Super Could Also Fill It, a real case of exactly this: a short-horizon risk judgment applied to a decades-long retirement balance during the 2020 market crash.
    The formal name for this gap: Ecological validity: does the task even resemble the real thing?, on Five Ways an Experiment Can Be Right and Still Wrong, using this exact study as the case.
    77

    Positional Concern (Rank Beats the Number)

    Why did most people in a real survey choose to earn half as much money, so long as they still out-earned everyone around them?

    Offered an absolute amount of money and a smaller amount that still ranks above everyone else, many people take the smaller amount. Relative standing can matter as much as, or more than, absolute dollars.

    ›
    Likely mechanismBeating other people's amount can matter more than the actual amount received

    The psychology. Money is rarely judged in isolation. It is read against a reference group, and that comparison can carry weight of its own. Solnick and Hemenway measured how much: 257 Harvard School of Public Health students, faculty, and staff chose between two hypothetical worlds with prices held constant.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Money is rarely judged in isolation. It is read against a reference group, and that comparison can carry weight of its own. Solnick and Hemenway measured how much. They asked 257 Harvard School of Public Health students, faculty, and staff to choose between two hypothetical worlds with prices held constant. Option one: earning $50,000 a year while everyone else earns $25,000. Option two: earning $100,000 a year while everyone else earns $200,000.

    56% chose the first option: half the absolute income, in exchange for ranking above peers instead of behind them. The same pattern appeared for other goods the survey tested: education, physical attractiveness, a supervisor’s praise. Strength varied by domain. It was strongest for attractiveness and supervisory approval, and weakest for vacation time, where most respondents cared more about the actual days off than about beating anyone else’s total.

    Where it causes errors

    Positional concern can turn a genuinely good outcome sour through the frame it is compared against. A raise that objectively improves someone’s life can register as a loss once they learn a peer received a larger one, with relative slippage overriding the absolute gain.

    Pay-transparency rollouts hit this directly. Making salaries visible does more than surface fairness problems. It creates new positional comparisons that did not exist while the numbers were private, including for employees whose own pay never moved.

    Where it can help

    The mechanism can also be used without inventing a comparison that was not there before. Showing someone real progress against a relevant peer group, a savings rate against similar savers, a fitness goal against people at the same starting point, can motivate action that a purely absolute number does not.

    The honest version uses a real, representative reference group and states the comparison plainly. The dishonest version cherry-picks a reference group chosen to make the number look better or worse than it is.

    Solnick, S. J., & Hemenway, D. (1998). “Is More Always Better? A Survey on Positional Concerns.” Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 37(3), 373–383
    A survey of 257 faculty, students, and staff at the Harvard School of Public Health, asking respondents to choose between a lower-absolute/higher-relative outcome and a higher-absolute/lower-relative one, across income and several other domains.
    StrengthPrices and lifestyle costs were held constant across both hypothetical worlds, so relative standing was the only live difference between options. The same contrast ran across domains beyond income, including education, attractiveness, and vacation time.
    WeaknessEvery item was a hypothetical survey choice with no real money attached, the cheap-talk gap this site's Reading the Research coverage already flags. What people say they would pick need not match what they would do if their own income were truly at stake.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“Half of the respondents preferred to have 50% less real income but high relative income.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“Concerns about position were strongest for attractiveness and supervisor's praise and weakest for vacation time.”
    See also: Social Norm, a related but distinct comparison effect: Social Norm is about matching your own behaviour to what others are doing, Positional Concern is about how a payoff itself feels once you know what others got.
    See also: Cheap Talk & Hypothetical Bias, the same stated-vs-real gap this study's own hypothetical design runs into.
    78

    Warm-Glow Giving (Giving Without Being Watched)

    In a game where the choice stays private forever, why did most people still hand over almost a third of the money?

    Even with total, unaccountable control over money and no penalty for keeping all of it, most people still give some away. The act of giving tends to feel rewarding on its own, separate from anything the giver might receive back.

    ›
    Likely mechanismGiving itself feels rewarding, even when the giver could never be seen or repaid

    The psychology. A dictator game gives one person an endowment and total power over how much, if any, to pass to a second person who cannot retaliate or reward. Engel’s 2011 meta-analysis pooled 616 treatments and 20,813 reconstructed dictator decisions from 131 published studies.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A dictator game gives one person an endowment and total power over how much, if any, to pass to a second person who cannot retaliate or reward. Engel’s 2011 meta-analysis pooled 616 treatments and 20,813 reconstructed individual dictator decisions from 131 published studies. It remains the largest single look at behaviour when people are told, in effect, that nothing stops them from keeping everything.

    Nearly two-thirds gave something anyway, and the average dictator handed over about 28% of the pot. Andreoni’s label for this is warm-glow giving: a private reward from the act of giving itself, distinct from caring what happens to the person on the other end.

    Where it causes errors

    Warm glow rewards the feeling of having given, not the outcome the gift produces. It can steer a choice toward the option that feels most personally satisfying rather than the one that does the most good. Checkout round-up prompts, the “round up your total for charity” button many retailers and ride-share apps now show, run on exactly this mechanism. Tapping yes supplies the reward whether or not the shopper knows which cause receives the change or how effectively it is used.

    Where it can help

    Aimed honestly, the same mechanism can support real generosity toward someone the giver will never meet and will never be repaid by. Caffè sospeso, the Naples tradition of pre-paying for a stranger’s coffee, works because the giver never learns who receives it and asks for nothing back. That is the dictator game’s shape, built into a coffee bar instead of a lab.

    Engel, C. (2011). “Dictator Games: A Meta Study.” Experimental Economics, 14(4), 583–610
    A meta-analysis pooling 616 dictator-game treatments and 20,813 reconstructed individual decisions across 131 published studies, using regression to isolate the effect of specific design choices (anonymity, framing, recipient identity) while controlling for the others.
    StrengthMore than 20,000 real decisions pooled across a hundred-plus independent studies sidestep the small-sample limits of any one dictator-game paper. Regression then isolates which design features, beyond the vague category “dictator games,” actually raise or lower giving.
    WeaknessPooling a hundred-plus studies mixes unlike protocols: stake sizes, student versus non-student samples, face-to-face versus fully anonymous setups. The 28% average hides how far the studies disagree, from near zero in the most anonymous designs to well above that figure in the least.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“If one calculates the grand mean from all reported or constructed means per 616 treatments, dictators on average give 28.35% of the pie.”
    Verbatim“16.74% choose the equal split.”
    ParaphrasedGuaranteeing anonymity from the experimenter too, the double-blind design Hoffman, McCabe and colleagues introduced in 1994, made little difference on its own across Engel's pooled data. Only once the analysis controlled for whether the game was one-shot or repeated did double-blind designs show a weak, small reduction in generosity, suggesting full experimenter anonymity matters only in more complex designs, not as a blanket effect.
    Also worth citing: Hoffman, E., McCabe, K., & Smith, V. (1996). “Social Distance and Other-Regarding Behavior in Dictator Games.” American Economic Review, 86(3), 653–660. A related moderator: generosity fell further as the social distance between dictator and recipient grew, even without the full anonymity manipulation above.
    See also: Reciprocity, a related but distinct mechanism: Reciprocity is triggered by receiving something first, Warm-Glow Giving happens with no prior gift, no future interaction, and no possibility of being thanked.
    79

    Bulletproof Glass Effect

    Why can a company’s own privacy promise make customers trust it less?

    A prominent, detailed privacy or security notice can backfire. Instead of feeling safer, people infer that anything needing this much protection must be a real threat, and trust falls rather than rises.

    ›
    Likely mechanismExplaining a protection in detail implies the danger it guards against is real

    The psychology. Most managers expect a visible privacy or security notice to make customers feel safer. Brough, Norton, Sciarappa and John tested that prediction with a content analysis of real company notices, a manager survey, a field experiment at checkout, and five further online experiments.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Most managers expect a visible privacy or security notice to make customers feel safer. Brough, Norton, Sciarappa and John tested that prediction with a content analysis of real company notices, a manager survey, a field experiment with real customers at checkout, and five further online experiments.

    They found the opposite of what most managers predicted. A prominent, detailed notice made customers trust the retailer less and buy less, even when the notice described only protections the company genuinely had. The authors named it after bulletproof glass on a house: visitors do not feel safer seeing it; they wonder what the house expects to be protected from.

    Where it causes errors

    A team redesigning a checkout page for trust can do real damage with a well-meant security badge or a long data-protection paragraph. The added detail reads as a threat signal, and can suppress conversions the team never traces back to the change that caused them.

    Where it can help

    Privacy information still belongs on the page; its shape is what matters. A brief, benevolence-framed statement, saying plainly that the company protects customer data because it respects privacy, reassures without itemising defences in a way that implies a specific danger. Disclosure obligations can still be met in language that does not do the scaring for the company.

    Brough, A. R., Norton, D. A., Sciarappa, S. L., & John, L. K. (2022). “The Bulletproof Glass Effect: Unintended Consequences of Privacy Notices.” Journal of Marketing Research, 59(4), 739–754
    A multi-method study: a content analysis of publicly traded companies' actual privacy notices, a survey of managers' expectations, a field experiment with real customers at a real checkout, and five online experiments isolating the mechanism.
    StrengthThe field test measured real customers making real purchase decisions. Content analysis, a manager survey, the field test, and online experiments then checked the same finding from independent angles instead of resting on one study.
    WeaknessThe field effect was real but small in absolute terms. At Borrowell, a fintech whose sign-up already requested income and credit-report access, enrollment fell from 41.48% to 39.66% when the privacy notice was made more prominent, a 1.82-percentage-point drop. Holding in a setting already rich in sensitive financial data undercuts the idea that data category itself is a natural exemption. The boundary the studies identify is prior trust: Study 4 reversed the effect once customers already had reason to distrust the firm.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“formal privacy notices undermined consumer trust and decreased purchase interest even when they emphasized objective protection (Studies 2, 3, and 5) or omitted any mention of potentially concerning data practices (Study 6).”
    Verbatim (abstract)“These unintended consequences did not occur, however, when consumers had an a priori reason to be distrustful (Study 4) or when benevolence cues were added to privacy notices (Studies 5 and 6).”
    80

    Implementation Intentions (If-Then Planning)

    Why did deciding when and where to act more than double the odds of actually following through?

    Deciding in advance exactly when, where, and how to act on a goal, a specific if-then plan rather than a general intention, makes follow-through far more likely.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA specific plan hands control of the action to a cue, so it fires automatically

    The psychology. A general intention names a goal but not the moment of action. When to act is left for later, when hesitation, forgetting, or a competing demand can crowd it out. Gollwitzer and Brandstätter tested a sharper alternative: an implementation intention linking a specific future situation to a planned response.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A general intention names a goal but not the moment of action. When to act is left for later, when hesitation, forgetting, or a competing demand can crowd it out. Gollwitzer and Brandstätter tested a sharper alternative: an implementation intention. That is a plan of the form “when situation Y arises, I will do X,” linking a specific future moment to the intended response before the moment arrives.

    College students were asked to write a report on how they spent Christmas Eve and mail it within 48 hours of Christmas. Half the group also named exactly when and where they would sit down and write it. 71% of that group completed the report on time, versus 32% of the group given only the general goal: more than double, from the same intention, deadline, and task.

    Where it causes errors

    A specific plan solves forgetting or hesitating to start. It does not fix a problem the plan was never built for: lacking the skill, resources, or ability the goal requires. Forming a detailed if-then plan can feel like the hard part is done when the real barrier was never about remembering to begin.

    A separate research programme tested this directly. Implementation intentions helped with easy goals and with difficult goals whose main obstacle really was getting started. They showed no benefit for a class of genuinely difficult goals that the plan alone could not make achievable.

    Where it can help

    This is one of the more directly useful findings on the site. Naming the exact when and where for something already wanted is a small, low-cost way to close the gap between intending and doing. A savings transfer timed to the moment a paycheck lands is one example. So is a specific gym slot rather than “exercise more,” or a fixed time to review a subscription before it renews. All are the same plan structure, applied to something the person has already decided they want.

    Gollwitzer, P. M., & Brandstätter, V. (1997). “Implementation Intentions and Effective Goal Pursuit.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 73(1), 186–199
    Three studies: a correlational study of college students' own difficult goals; an experiment assigning the same difficult goal (writing and mailing a Christmas Eve report within 48 hours) to everyone, with half the group additionally specifying exactly when and where they would act; and a lab study testing whether people who had formed an implementation intention actually seized the specified opportunity the moment it appeared.
    StrengthGoal, deadline, and task were held fixed across both groups, so the written plan was the only systematic difference. Completion gaps cannot be blamed on one group getting an easier or different goal.
    WeaknessThe assignment was a one-off, low-stakes psychology report. It was not a recurring habit facing competing demands, temptation, or a real cost of failure. Whether an effect of the same size appears for harder ongoing goals (exercise, saving, medication) is a separate empirical question this study does not settle alone.
    Key findings
    Verbatim“When the goal intention of Study 2 was furnished with implementation intentions, however, completion rate drastically increased from 32% to 71%.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“In correlational Study 1, difficult goal intentions were completed about 3 times more often when participants had furnished them with implementation intentions.”
    Also worth citing: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). “Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of Effects and Processes.” Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119. A meta-analysis across dozens of studies, confirming implementation intentions work through several distinct processes, not just one, including goal shielding: naming a specific obstacle in advance and planning a response to it protects the original goal from that obstacle when it actually shows up.
    Also worth citing: Dewitte, S., Verguts, T., & Lens, W. (2003). “Implementation Intentions Do Not Enhance All Types of Goals: The Moderating Role of Goal Difficulty.” Current Psychology, 22, 73–89. The corroborating study behind the “Where it causes errors” section above.
    Also worth citing: Nickerson, D. W., & Rogers, T. (2010). “Do You Have a Voting Plan? Implementation Intentions, Voter Turnout, and Organic Plan Making.” Psychological Science, 21(2), 194–199. A real field experiment, 287,228 voters ahead of the 2008 US presidential election: a call that helped people form a specific voting plan (what time, coming from where, doing what beforehand) raised turnout by 4.1 percentage points overall, and by 9.1 points in single-voter households, a genuine, ethical, large-scale use of this exact mechanism.
    See also: Reminder Fatigue, the real cost of pushing this mechanism too far: a well-timed reminder helps follow-through, but each additional one carries a measurable risk of losing the relationship entirely.
    81

    Reminder Fatigue

    Why does a reminder that lifts compliance today also make people cut off contact for good?

    A repeated reminder raises compliance when it is sent. Each extra one also raises the odds the recipient opts out of all future contact. The two effects are often tracked separately, so the win is easy to see and the cost is easy to miss.

    ›
    Likely mechanismRepeating an ask reads as ignoring an earlier no, until people cut ties entirely

    The psychology. A reminder restates the ask and also signals something about the relationship: the sender is willing to contact again after silence. Below a threshold that can feel helpful. Past it, repetition starts to read as disregard for an earlier silence, and the response can be closing the channel entirely.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    A reminder restates the ask and also signals something about the relationship: the sender is willing to contact again after an unanswered first attempt. Below a threshold that can feel helpful, a nudge someone might genuinely have wanted.

    Past it, repetition starts to read as disregard for an earlier silence or decline. The response is no longer only a smaller no to this one ask. It can become a decision to close the channel for good, a larger cost than simply lowering the odds of any single future ask.

    Where it causes errors

    A campaign that measures only the metric it is nudging, this quarter’s donations, this month’s click-through, can look like a clean win. It can also be costing the business its highest-value, longest-tenured relationships, the ones with the most left to lose by leaving. The same trap applies to appointment reminders, renewal notices, and app push notifications: each extra nudge can lift the immediate number while raising the odds this person becomes unreachable forever.

    Where it can help

    The mechanism argues for restraint more than for cleverer wording. Cap how often a specific ask repeats, retire a reminder after a set number of ignores, and reserve repetition for genuinely time-sensitive asks. Do not default to repetition only because it lifts short-run metrics. A well-designed reminder system treats a permanent opt-out as a real cost of every message, weighed against the value of one extra nudge before the next one goes out.

    Damgaard, M. T., & Gravert, C. (2018). “The Hidden Costs of Nudging: Experimental Evidence from Reminders in Fundraising.” Journal of Public Economics, 157, 15–26
    A large-scale field experiment with a real charity's own donor list and reminder programme.
    StrengthThe authors ran a field experiment on a charity's actual donors rather than a lab simulation. Beyond reporting two separate percentages, they structurally estimated a welfare model that puts donation gains and unsubscribe costs into one comparable unit, dollars, so readers need not weigh the two informally.
    WeaknessThe evidence comes from one charity's email fundraising programme. Push notifications, phone calls, and text messages were not tested, and each channel has its own sending cost and its own cost of being ignored, which could rewrite the tradeoff.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“we find that reminders increase donations, but they also substantially increase unsubscriptions from the mailing list.”
    Verbatim (abstract)“reminders are welfare diminishing for the potential donors as non-givers incur a welfare loss of $2.35 for every reminder. The net benefit of every reminder to the charity is $0.18.”
    Verbatim“the Low Frequency treatment reduces the unsubscription rate from 0.49% to 0.30%.”
    Also worth citing: Ancker, J. S., Edwards, A., Nosal, S., Hauser, D., Mauer, E., & Kaushal, R. (2017). “Effects of Workload, Work Complexity, and Repeated Alerts on Alert Fatigue in a Clinical Decision Support System.” BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, 17, Article 36. A completely different domain, real clinical alerts inside electronic health records, found the identical shape of effect: the likelihood a clinician acted on a reminder dropped by roughly 30% for each additional reminder received in the same encounter.
    See also: Not Enough Choice, a related but distinct mechanism: that's resistance to a restricted set of options; this is resistance to being contacted again after an earlier silence or decline went unanswered.
    See also: Implementation Intentions, the mechanism this principle is a caution against overusing: a well-timed reminder or plan-prompt genuinely helps follow-through, but each additional one carries a real, measurable cost this site's own reminder-call and confirmation-screen experiments are built to respect.
    Decoded on Reading the Research: Backfires Have Six Different Causes, where this exact study appears as “The Charity Reminder Boomerang,” the sixth case in a roundup of interventions that looked like wins on the metric being watched.
    82

    Biased Assimilation

    Why did the same two conflicting studies leave two people who disagreed further apart than before?

    Shown identical mixed evidence, people do not converge. They accept what confirms what they already believed, pick apart what contradicts it, and finish more certain of their original view than when they started, on both sides at once.

    ›
    Likely mechanismEvidence that confirms a belief gets accepted; evidence that contradicts it gets picked apart

    The psychology. People do not apply one consistent standard when judging evidence. Material that fits what they already believe is accepted near face value. Material that contradicts it faces heavier scrutiny: sample too small, method flawed, comparison unfair. The same argument passes or fails depending on which side it supports.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    People do not apply one consistent standard when judging evidence. Material that fits what they already believe is accepted near face value. Material that contradicts it faces heavier scrutiny: the sample was too small, the method was flawed, the comparison was unfair. The same argument passes or fails a credibility test depending on which side it supports.

    That double standard compounds once someone reads a full mix of evidence, some for their view and some against. They keep the confirming half and discount the disconfirming half, so the same balanced set of facts leaves both sides more sure of their original position than before they read anything. Biased information is not required. Genuinely mixed evidence is enough on its own.

    Where it causes errors

    The death-penalty debate the original study used is still running, decades later, for this reason. Research on whether capital punishment deters murder has reached genuinely mixed conclusions: some studies find a measurable effect, some find none, some find the opposite. Each side of the public debate keeps citing whichever studies confirm prior belief and dismissing the rest as bad research. The same body of evidence that should narrow disagreement has barely moved it in decades.

    The pattern appears anywhere an ambiguous result gets treated as proof. Two people can look at the same sales dashboard, survey, or test result and each leave more convinced their prior read was right. Each graded the noisy parts of the data by the study’s own rule: convincing if it agrees, flawed if it does not.

    Where it can help

    The fix removes what biased assimilation needs: the ability to tell, before judging a result, which side it supports. A properly randomised experiment with one clear control group makes that much harder. There is one predetermined comparison everyone agreed to in advance, rather than a pile of ambiguous evidence each side can sift afterward. Blind peer review, where a reviewer judges a paper without knowing whose theory it supports, runs on the same principle.

    Lord, C. G., Ross, L., & Lepper, M. R. (1979). “Biased Assimilation and Attitude Polarization: The Effects of Prior Theories on Subsequently Considered Evidence.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(11), 2098–2109
    A lab experiment giving real undergraduate supporters and opponents of the death penalty two conflicting fictitious research studies to evaluate.
    StrengthThe two fictitious studies used distinct real designs: a cross-state comparison of death-penalty presence, and a before-and-after comparison inside one state that adopted it. Which conclusion rode with which design was swapped across participants. That swap blocks the simplest alternative, that one method simply looked more rigorous, because either method could carry either conclusion.
    WeaknessUndergraduates in one lab session read two short fictitious summaries on a single contested issue. Whether an effect of the same size appears when people weigh real, higher-stakes evidence over months (an investment thesis, a policy rollout, a medical diagnosis) was not tested here.
    Key findings
    Paraphrased48 students who identified as either strong supporters or strong opponents of the death penalty each read two fictitious research summaries: one concluding the death penalty lowers murder rates, one concluding it doesn't. Each side rated whichever study matched their existing belief as more convincing and better conducted than the one that contradicted it.
    ParaphrasedThe two fictitious studies used two genuinely different real-world research designs, a cross-state comparison and a within-state before-and-after comparison, and which conclusion was attached to which design was swapped across participants, so the pattern couldn't be explained by one design simply looking more credible on its own.
    ParaphrasedAfter reading the identical pair of mixed studies, both supporters and opponents of the death penalty rated themselves as more confident in their original position than before they'd read anything, even though the two studies, taken together, offered no net evidence either way.
    A note on sourcing: this site's network access blocked every attempt to reach the primary paper itself (university PDF mirrors and academic databases all returned network-policy errors), so every finding above is paraphrased from independently corroborating secondary sources describing the study's own design and results, not quoted verbatim from the original paper.
    See also: Availability Heuristic, a related but distinct judgment error: that's misjudging how common something is because examples of it are easy to recall; this is misjudging how convincing evidence is because of which side it happens to support.
    Run this one live: Live Sessions: Biased Assimilation, seeding two groups with opposite priors, showing both the identical result, then watching the room's ratings and excuses sort themselves by belief instead of evidence.
    83

    Probability Weighting (why a tiny chance of a huge prize outweighs its real odds)

    Why does a 1-in-a-million chance to win feel worth chasing?

    People do not weigh probabilities the way arithmetic says they should. A very small chance of a big prize is treated as far more likely than it is. A very high chance of the same outcome is treated as slightly less certain than it is.

    ›
    Likely mechanismThe mind turns a tiny real chance into a felt chance that's far bigger than the actual odds warrant

    The psychology. Standard decision theory gives a 1% chance exactly 1% of the weight in a choice, and a 99% chance exactly 99%. Real judgment bends that line. Low probabilities get inflated well past their true size; high probabilities get discounted slightly below theirs.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Standard decision theory gives a 1% chance exactly 1% of the weight in a choice, and a 99% chance exactly 99%. Real judgment bends that line. Low probabilities get inflated well past their true size, and high probabilities get discounted slightly below theirs. The felt gap between “impossible” and “a tiny chance” looms larger than the felt gap between “very likely” and “certain,” even when both gaps are the same few percentage points in arithmetic terms.

    The distortion runs both ways off the same tiny probability. Aimed at a gain, it makes a long-shot prize feel worth chasing. Aimed at a loss, the same-sized sliver of risk makes an unlikely disaster feel worth insuring against. That is why the same framework that explains lottery tickets also explains travel insurance for a flight that is very unlikely to be cancelled.

    The size of the distortion tracks how the prize feels, not only its odds. Later research found people overweight a small chance of something emotionally vivid, a kiss from a favourite celebrity, an electric shock, even more than an equally small chance of plain cash. The more a prize makes someone feel something before they have won anything, the harder the real odds are to weigh correctly.

    Where it causes errors

    A promotion that bundles a routine purchase with “a chance to win” a huge prize does not need stated odds for the effect to work, and often does not provide them. Almost any small number reads as similarly enticing once it is framed as a chance to win, so the actual likelihood barely shapes how attractive the deal feels. The same overweighting sells extended warranties on cheap appliances, add-on insurance for low-risk events, and scratch-card loyalty promotions whose true expected value is a fraction of a cent.

    Where it can help

    The same overweighting can be aimed at something the person and the business both want, and the upside is not only strategic. A real field experiment found that simply holding a lottery-style ticket measurably lifts happiness in the hours before the draw, whether or not it wins. The hope itself is a modest, genuine good.

    A charity or health service can raise participation by offering prize-draw entry for a blood donation, survey, or screening, often for less cost than paying everyone a small guaranteed fee. The felt value of a small chance at a big reward often beats the felt value of a certain small one, even when the certain payment is worth more on paper. Naming the real odds honestly, rather than hiding them, is what keeps this use encouraging rather than exploitative.

    Spotted in the wild

    A routine $2.50 fries deal, bundled with exactly this kind of unstated chance to win.

    McDonald's Australia's own promo page: “each deal is your chance to win free Macca's for life,” no odds stated anywhere on the screen, captured September 2026.

    The real prize count, on McDonald's own McGold Card page: eight winners nationwide, the actual odds a customer would need to weigh correctly and can't from the deal screen alone.

    Full decode: Why does a $2.50 fries deal come with a chance to win free food for life? A real, currently operating promotion, shown to illustrate the mechanism, not proof it drove any particular customer's purchase.

    Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). “Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk.” Econometrica, 47(2), 263–291
    One of the most cited papers in economics: a series of choice problems, each pitting a gamble against an equivalent sure outcome, run across groups of real respondents to map how people actually weigh probability rather than assuming they weigh it the way expected-utility theory says they should.
    StrengthOverweighting small probabilities and underweighting large ones recurred across dozens of differently worded choice problems and multiple respondent groups. Inside the study, that repetition is what makes the pattern hold. One question alone would leave it thin.
    WeaknessEvery choice was a hypothetical paper gamble with no real payout. Stated picks need not match behaviour under real stakes; later work with real-money incentives has tested that gap directly.
    Key findings
    Verbatim (abstract)“people underweight outcomes that are merely probable in comparison with outcomes that are obtained with certainty. This tendency, called the certainty effect, contributes to risk aversion in choices involving sure gains and to risk seeking in choices involving sure losses.”
    ParaphrasedThe paper's decision-weighting function shows small probabilities carrying more weight in a choice than their true value justifies, which the authors note helps explain why both long-shot gambling and insurance against rare losses feel more compelling than their real odds alone would predict.
    ParaphrasedPeople also simplify choices between multiple risky options by ignoring whatever the options share and focusing only on what differs between them, an “isolation effect” that can produce different preferences for the objectively identical choice depending only on how it's presented.
    See also: Illusion of Control, related but distinct: that's false confidence in a genuinely random outcome once skill-like cues are added to it; this is misjudging the raw odds themselves, before any skill framing enters the picture at all.
    Also worth citing: Rottenstreich, Y., & Hsee, C. K. (2001). “Money, Kisses, and Electric Shocks: On the Affective Psychology of Risk.” Psychological Science, 12(3), 185–190, the study behind the emotionally vivid prize comparison above: the same small probability gets weighted even more heavily once the outcome itself carries real emotional charge.
    Also worth citing: Burger, M. J., Hendriks, M., Pleeging, E., & van Ours, J. C. (2020). “The Joy of Lottery Play: Evidence from a Field Experiment.” Experimental Economics, 23(4), 1235–1256, the field experiment behind the anticipatory-happiness finding above: buying the ticket itself, not just winning, is where the measured wellbeing gain shows up.
    Also worth reading: The Lottery You Can't Lose, a real product built on this same overweighting of small probabilities, pointed at a savings goal instead of a wager.
    Decoded on The Science Behind: Why does a $2.50 fries deal come with a chance to win free food for life?, a real fast-food app promotion built on exactly this mechanism.
    Try this one live: Does a chance at 0% increase home loan applications more than the guaranteed discount alone?, an experiment blueprint testing the same mechanism at a much higher stake than a savings rate or a fries deal.
    84

    Curiosity Gap (information gap theory)

    Why does someone keep watching just to find out what happens next?

    Not knowing something one wants to know creates a real, felt discomfort, closer to an itch than a preference, and only the missing piece relieves it. The pull is strongest when someone knows just enough to sense the gap, not when they know nothing at all.

    ›
    Likely mechanismA noticed gap between what you know and what you want to know creates a felt discomfort until it's closed

    The psychology. Curiosity behaves like a drive state, closer to hunger than to a stable personality trait. It starts from a perceived gap between what someone currently knows and what they want to know. Discomfort from that gap, not general interest in the topic, is what pushes them to close it.

    The full write-up: study, numbers, and caveats›
    The psychology

    Curiosity behaves like a drive state, closer to hunger than to a stable personality trait. It starts from a perceived gap between what someone currently knows and what they want to know. Discomfort from that gap is what pushes them to close it, more than general interest in the topic. Knowing nothing at all about something does not create curiosity, because no gap is visible yet.

    The gap has to be sensed already for the pull to exist, which is why curiosity peaks at a specific point: knowing just enough to realise there is more one does not know. Knowing everything, or knowing nothing, both leave nothing to feel. A trivia question with a rough hunch needles far more than one with no idea attached or one already answered with certainty.

    Where it causes errors

    A headline can manufacture the felt gap without an answer worth the click, which is the entire mechanism behind clickbait. The size of the gap a headline promises has no necessary link to the size or value of the actual answer, so plenty of attention gets spent closing gaps that were never worth opening. The same move sells a cliffhanger episode that resolves into something thin, or a “you won’t believe what happened next” post that resolves into something ordinary.

    Where it can help

    Posing a real, specific question before teaching the answer, rather than stating the answer first, makes the material land harder and stick longer. That is an honest use of the same gap, opened by a real, answerable question rather than a manufactured one. The gap gets closed with something genuinely worth the attention it cost. That is the difference between this use and clickbait: same mechanism, opposite honesty about what waits on the other side.

    Loewenstein, G. (1994). “The Psychology of Curiosity: A Review and Reinterpretation.” Psychological Bulletin, 116(1), 75–98
    A wide-ranging theoretical synthesis, not a single experiment: it reviews decades of earlier, disconnected curiosity research and reinterprets it as one testable framework, information gap theory.
    StrengthThe paper folds drive-based and incongruity-based curiosity theories that had talked past each other into one model. It also yields a specific, falsifiable claim: curiosity should peak at intermediate knowledge, away from either extreme. That is sharper than an anecdotal description of curiosity.
    WeaknessAs a theoretical review it synthesises decades of prior findings and does not run a new controlled trial. Its central prediction therefore needed independent empirical confirmation, which is exactly what the Kang et al. follow-up below supplies.
    Key findings
    ParaphrasedCuriosity is reinterpreted as a form of cognitively induced deprivation, arising from a perceived gap between what someone knows and what they want to know, functioning as a genuine drive state rather than a stable trait or a simple preference for novelty.
    ParaphrasedThe theory predicts curiosity should be weakest at both extremes, when someone has no sense a gap exists and when no gap remains, and strongest at intermediate levels of knowledge, in between simply not knowing and already knowing.
    Also worth citing: Kang, M. J., Hsu, M., Krajbich, I. M., Loewenstein, G., McClure, S. M., Wang, J. T. Y., & Camerer, C. F. (2009). “The Wick in the Candle of Learning: Epistemic Curiosity Activates Reward Circuitry and Enhances Memory.” Psychological Science, 20(8), 963–973, the empirical follow-up confirming the 1994 theory's own prediction directly: using trivia questions and fMRI, curiosity tracked an inverted pattern against confidence, peaking at intermediate confidence, and higher curiosity while reading a question predicted better memory for its answer more than a week later.
